What this analysis says Validated

  • This overview lists the 48 reform issues identified for North Macedonia in RUN-2026-01: 14 under Chapter 2 (Freedom of movement for workers) and 34 under the cross-cutting technology and AI theme.
  • All values shown are judgements validated by the analyst at G6.
  • Nineteen issues are rated High priority (4 in Chapter 2 and 15 in the technology theme, one of them set to High by the analyst at G6), 24 Medium and 5 Low.
  • The dominant pattern is persistence: 33 of 48 issues have a persistent direction of travel, and no Chapter 2 issue is judged to be improving.
  • Five technology issues are improving: electronic public procurement tools, electronic communications law, the cybersecurity framework, electronic identification and trust services law, and customs IT systems.
  • Where the improvement is in law only, the issue briefs say so.
  • Two technology issues are worsening and one is new.
  • No issue's gap is closed: 20 gaps are open, 27 partly addressed, and one, on third-country workers, cannot be judged on the evidence.
  • Most issues are of Medium tractability.
  • The comparator pilot covered three High priority issues: nationality discrimination in access to employment (RI-FMW-001), the underused interoperability platform (RI-TEC-028) and the national e-services portal (RI-TEC-036).
2026 update: Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package No 2026 country report on North Macedonia is in the project yet, so every issue shows its 2025 position and the current validated judgements, and its 2026 update is marked as awaiting the package. 13 issues already draw on other 2026 official EU evidence (the 2026 Rule of Law country chapter, the 2026 economic reform programme assessment and conclusions, the third Reform Agenda payment assessment and the 2026 subcommittee), which is part of the validated alpha and is not a substitute for the Enlargement Package. Unresolved gap (open): What remains is equal treatment of EU workers in the law on access to the labour market, including an end to posts in private companies reserved for nationals.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its law on access to the labour market with the EU acquis, in particular on non-discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers in all sectors, so that by accession EU citizens can work there without restrictions such as work permits (MKD-EU-2025-001-0013; MKD-EU-2025-003-0025; MKD-EU-2025-003-0033). The Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners is in practice, and it was amended in 2021 and in April 2025, but the 2025 amendment only renames ministries and bodies, and further amendments on the employment of foreigners are listed only as proposed in machine-translated government reports (MKD-GOV-2021-001-0001; MKD-GOV-2025-001-0001; MKD-GOV-2025-003-0011; MKD-GOV-2026-001-0007). The Commission states that the law does not distinguish EU citizens from other foreigners and that some private sector posts are reserved for nationals (MKD-EU-2025-001-0097; MKD-EU-2025-001-0101). North Macedonia points to the ban on nationality discrimination in the Law on Labour Relations, which is adopted but not shown in application (MKD-EU-2025-003-0018; MKD-EU-2025-003-0019). No outcome has been assessed. The gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is High and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The core recommendation has barely changed. From 2020 to 2022 the Commission asked the country to continue adapting the legal framework on access to the labour market, in particular on non-discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers (MKD-EU-2020-001-0076; MKD-EU-2021-001-0060; MKD-EU-2022-001-0063). From 2023 it added the words "in all sectors", and in 2025 "adapt" became "align" (MKD-EU-2023-001-0090; MKD-EU-2024-001-0008; MKD-EU-2025-001-0013). Each report from 2020 to 2024 found no progress, and the 2025 report found no legislative developments (MKD-EU-2020-001-0079; MKD-EU-2024-001-0057; MKD-EU-2025-001-0096). The February 2025 screening report made the requirement more concrete: partial alignment, an end-point at accession with no work permit or residence permit for EU workers, and exclusion of EU citizens from the annual foreign worker quotas (MKD-EU-2025-003-0031; MKD-EU-2025-003-0025; MKD-EU-2025-003-0028).

Country response
  • Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners · in practice
  • Law Amending and Supplementing the Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners 2021 · adopted
  • Law Amending the Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners 2025 · adopted
  • Proposed amendments on the employment of foreigners · proposed
  • Law on Labour Relations · adopted
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Conflicting evidence
  • The Commission states that the law does not distinguish between EU citizens and other foreigners, while North Macedonia states that under the same law the quotas do not apply to EU citizens following a reciprocity agreement with the EU.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is equal treatment of EU workers in the law on access to the labour market, including an end to posts in private companies reserved for nationals. The foreigners law is itself the barrier, the 2025 amendment only renames bodies and the further amendments are only proposed with unknown content (all statuses are proposals; the two government items are machine translated, so capped at Medium), while the country's general ban on nationality discrimination is its own account and does not close the gap. The Commission's statement that the law makes no EU distinction conflicts with the country's account on quotas, which is reported and partly explained under RI-FMW-002.

Direction of travel: Sub-area wording on access to the labour market, which matches this issue, says no progress in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, and the 2025 report says there were no legislative developments. The 2025 screening finding of partial alignment is a first assessment of that kind and does not show a change.

Priority: A key recommendation on non-discrimination against EU workers is repeated in the 2020 to 2025 reports, and equal access is central to the chapter. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found in the evidence.

Tractability: The change is legal and within the government's control, and the same law was amended in 2021 and 2025. Against that, six reports record no alignment and the requirement runs to the time of accession, so there is no evidence of past progress.

Open questions
  • The Commission states that the foreigners law makes no distinction for EU citizens, while North Macedonia states that the quotas do not apply to EU citizens under a reciprocity agreement, and this confirmed conflict could be settled by the text of the law or the agreement and data on how permits are issued to EU citizens (MKD-EU-2024-001-0058; MKD-EU-2025-003-0010).
  • The content of the proposed amendments on the employment of foreigners, and whether they are the law adopted in April 2025, is not known from the machine-translated Employment Agency reports, so the draft or adopted text would settle it (MKD-GOV-2025-003-0011; MKD-GOV-2026-001-0007).
  • No source shows how the non-discrimination rule in the Law on Labour Relations is applied to foreign or EU workers, which inspection, court or complaints data could show (MKD-EU-2025-003-0018).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is a legal system for appointing EURES members and partners and access for private employment agencies.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to establish a system for appointing EURES members and partners and to give private employment agencies access to it, and its key recommendation asks the country to strengthen the Employment Service Agency and align legislation and good practice with the EURES and European Labour Authority regulations (MKD-EU-2025-003-0066; MKD-EU-2025-003-0067; MKD-EU-2025-001-0012). At screening, North Macedonia stated that the Agency will be the main EURES implementing body and National Coordination Office, and that it foresees an EU-funded analysis of harmonisation needs and stronger Agency capacity (MKD-EU-2025-003-0049; MKD-EU-2025-003-0060). The amendments needed to comply fully have a deadline of 2030, with implementation upon accession (MKD-EU-2025-003-0068). All four responding measures remain proposed, and the Commission reported no developments on EURES in November 2025 (MKD-EU-2025-001-0106). There is no outcome evidence. The validated judgements are priority High, direction of travel persistent, unresolved gap partly_addressed and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

From 2020 to 2022 the Commission recorded only that nothing had been done to prepare for joining EURES on accession (MKD-EU-2020-001-0083; MKD-EU-2021-001-0067; MKD-EU-2022-001-0069). From 2023 the key recommendation asked the country to strengthen the Employment Service Agency and align legislation and good practice with EURES and European Labour Authority rules, in near-identical words in 2023, 2024 and 2025 (MKD-EU-2023-001-0089; MKD-EU-2024-001-0007; MKD-EU-2025-001-0012). The 2025 screening report made the requirement specific: an appointment system for EURES members and partners, and access and adequate connection for private employment agencies (MKD-EU-2025-003-0066; MKD-EU-2025-003-0067; MKD-EU-2025-003-0070). It also rated preparation as good and alignment as good at IT and structural levels (MKD-EU-2025-003-0062; MKD-EU-2025-003-0069).

Country response
  • Strengthening of Employment Agency capacities · proposed
  • Designation of the Employment Service Agency as EURES National Coordination Office · proposed
  • Amendments to national legislation to comply with EURES standards · proposed
  • Analysis of harmonisation needs · proposed
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is a legal system for appointing EURES members and partners and access for private employment agencies. The Commission credits good alignment on IT and structural levels, but every responding intervention is only proposed (these statuses are themselves proposals), with legislative amendments on a 2030 deadline and implementation at accession.

Direction of travel: Sub-area wording on EURES, which matches this issue, says no developments or measures in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025, and the 2023 key recommendation still asks for alignment. The screening report's 'good level of preparation' sits in tension with these and with its own finding that no appointment system exists; it is the only rating of this kind, so I do not read it as improvement, and I report the tension rather than resolve it.

Priority: Alignment with EURES is named in the key recommendation in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and EURES is one of the chapter's main strands. The recommendation is a composite one, so the repetition is of one sentence and not of independent findings.

Tractability: One lead body is planned and the IT and structural base is credited, which helps. However, no legal step has been reported in six years, the country's own timetable runs to 2030 and implementation is tied to accession.

Open questions
  • The screening report's rating of a good level of preparation sits in tension with its own finding that no appointment system exists and with the annual reports of no developments, and the analysis reports this tension rather than resolving it; the Commission's next assessment or a statement of the basis for the rating would settle it (MKD-EU-2025-003-0062; MKD-EU-2025-003-0058; MKD-EU-2025-001-0106).
  • No source shows whether the planned analysis of harmonisation needs, the designation of the Agency as National Coordination Office or the capacity strengthening has started, and Agency or government progress reports would settle this (MKD-EU-2025-003-0049; MKD-EU-2025-003-0060).
  • The content and timing of the legislative amendments within the 2030 deadline are unknown, and a draft law or a dated legislative plan would show whether the appointment system and private agency access are covered (MKD-EU-2025-003-0068).

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to negotiate and conclude bilateral social security coordination and healthcare insurance agreements with EU Member States and to put in place administrative measures to prepare for accession (MKD-EU-2021-001-0061; MKD-EU-2024-001-0009; MKD-EU-2025-001-0014). The ministry lists agreements it describes as in force and applied, including with 13 Member States, but this list is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence and gives no case data (MKD-GOV-2023-001-0001; MKD-EU-2025-003-0085). Negotiations with Italy, the USA and Greece began in 2023, yet the Commission reports no new agreements signed in any year from 2021 to 2025 (MKD-EU-2024-001-0065; MKD-EU-2021-001-0072; MKD-EU-2022-001-0070; MKD-EU-2023-001-0097; MKD-EU-2024-001-0066; MKD-EU-2025-001-0107). The agreements are judged to have worked, with Medium attribution, in a narrow sense: the Commission rates preparation on coordination as good because of that experience (MKD-EU-2025-003-0090). What remains is agreements with the other Member States and administrative measures for accession. The validated assessment is partly_addressed, with priority High, direction of travel persistent and tractability Low.

EU requirement

The core request has been stable since 2021, with small shifts in verb and scope. In 2021 the Commission asked the country to take steps to conclude further bilateral agreements and to identify administrative measures for accession (MKD-EU-2021-001-0061). In 2022 it asked it to step up signature of agreements with EU Member States, now naming healthcare insurance (MKD-EU-2022-001-0064). From 2023 the wording became to continue negotiating and concluding agreements and to put in place administrative measures (MKD-EU-2023-001-0091; MKD-EU-2024-001-0009). The 2025 report adds preparation for electronic exchange of social security data (MKD-EU-2025-001-0014). The 2025 screening report states that further agreements need to be signed, specifically with EU Member States (MKD-EU-2025-003-0106; MKD-EU-2025-003-0091).

Implementation and outcome
  • Bilateral social security agreements: Experience from bilateral agreements gives North Macedonia a good level of preparation on social security coordination. · success worked, attribution Medium
Conflicting evidence
  • The 2020 report gives 14 social security agreements with EU Member States and the 2021 report gives 13 out of the same total of 23, while the 2021 report also states there were no changes in this area (MKD-EU-2021-001-0068).
  • The 2023 report gives 23 bilateral agreements, while North Macedonia states 22 in the screening report, whose bilateral meeting took place in March 2023, and no item under this issue records an agreement ending.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is agreements with the other Member States and the administrative measures to prepare for accession. Agreements with 13 Member States are in force, by the government's own list and the Commission's count, but the negotiations with Italy and Greece are only proposed and no outcome is recorded; these statuses are proposals. Adopting further agreements would not by itself close the gap.

Direction of travel: The chapter scale was context only, and the 2025 'good level of preparation' for coordination is a single rating with nothing before it. No new agreements are recorded in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 or 2025, despite negotiations started in 2023. Two confirmed count contradictions stand (14 against 13 EU agreements; 23 against 22 in total); they do not change this view and are not resolved here.

Priority: Concluding agreements is in the key recommendation in the 2021 to 2025 reports, and social security coordination is a main strand of the chapter. The Commission's good preparation rating lowers the urgency but not the repeated requirement, so reviewers may reasonably weigh centrality differently.

Tractability: Progress depends on other states agreeing, not only on the government. No new agreement is recorded from 2021 to 2025, including after the negotiations started in 2023.

Open questions
  • Two confirmed conflicts on the number of agreements stand unresolved, 14 against 13 with EU Member States between the 2020 and 2021 reports and 23 against 22 in total between the 2023 report and the screening report, and a current official list checked against the Commission's count would settle them (MKD-EU-2020-001-0084; MKD-EU-2021-001-0069; MKD-EU-2023-001-0098; MKD-EU-2025-003-0085).
  • The ministry's list of agreements in force and applied is machine translated and gives no case data, so figures on claims handled, periods aggregated or benefits exported under each agreement would be needed to show the agreements working in practice (MKD-GOV-2023-001-0001).
  • No outcome of the negotiations with Italy and Greece begun in 2023 is recorded, and a report of signature or ratification would settle their status (MKD-EU-2024-001-0065; MKD-EU-2025-001-0107).
  • The Commission's good preparation rating is a single 2025 finding with no earlier rating to compare, and later Commission assessments would show whether readiness is changing (MKD-EU-2025-003-0090).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is removing citizenship conditions from the pension and health insurance laws, aligning with the regulations and putting administrative measures in place by accession.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to put in place administrative measures to prepare for accession and for electronic exchange of social security data, and to align its pension and disability and health insurance laws with the coordination regulations by accession, including on nationality conditions (MKD-EU-2025-001-0014; MKD-EU-2025-003-0107). The Commission finds the national framework partly aligned and notes that both laws in some cases require citizenship for access to insurance (MKD-EU-2025-003-0093; MKD-EU-2025-003-0094; MKD-EU-2025-003-0104). The pension, health insurance and unemployment insurance laws and the 2023 law on the register of mandatory social insurance are assessed as adopted, with no evidence on how they are applied or that the register exists (MKD-EU-2024-001-0067; MKD-EU-2025-003-0083; MKD-EU-2025-003-0084). The country plans within five years to analyse its law, capacity and IT infrastructure, amend the law and define EESSI access points, assessed as proposed (MKD-EU-2025-003-0097). The Commission rates preparation on coordination as good because of experience with bilateral agreements, assessed as worked with Medium attribution but narrow in scope (MKD-EU-2025-003-0090; MKD-EU-2025-003-0105). The gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is High and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The key recommendation on administrative measures has run through every report since 2020. In 2020 to 2022 the Commission asked the country to identify which administrative measures would be needed before accession, with 2021 and 2022 adding further bilateral agreements on coordination and health insurance (MKD-EU-2020-001-0077; MKD-EU-2021-001-0061; MKD-EU-2022-001-0064). From 2023 the wording shifts from identifying measures to putting them in place, which was assessed as a change of wording rather than a reported step (MKD-EU-2023-001-0091; MKD-EU-2024-001-0009). The 2025 report adds electronic exchange of social security data (MKD-EU-2025-001-0014). The February 2025 screening report adds a specific legal requirement: removing citizenship conditions from the pension and health insurance laws by accession (MKD-EU-2025-003-0095; MKD-EU-2025-003-0107).

Country response
  • Law on the register of mandatory social insurance · adopted
  • Law on Employment and Insurance in Case of Unemployment · adopted
  • Law on Health Insurance · adopted
  • Law on Pension and Disability Insurance · adopted
  • Preparations for EESSI access points · proposed
Implementation and outcome
  • Bilateral social security agreements: Experience from bilateral agreements gives North Macedonia a good level of preparation on social security coordination. · success worked, attribution Medium
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is removing citizenship conditions from the pension and health insurance laws, aligning with the regulations and putting administrative measures in place by accession. The Commission finds the framework partly aligned, but the plan to amend the legislation is only proposed within five years (a status that is itself a proposal).

Direction of travel: The chapter scale was context only, and the 2025 ratings have nothing earlier to compare with. The recommendation on administrative measures recurs from 2020 to 2025, and the shift from identifying measures to putting them in place reflects wording, not a reported step.

Priority: Administrative measures for coordination are in the key recommendation in each report from 2020 to 2025, and alignment with the regulations is central to this strand of the chapter. The screening report requires alignment, including on nationality conditions, by accession.

Tractability: The named legal changes are within national control, and the register law adopted in 2023 shows some related legislative activity. However, it spans the pension and health systems, needs prior analysis and has a plan of up to five years.

Open questions
  • No item shows the register of mandatory social insurance established after the 2023 law, so evidence of the register in operation would settle whether the law has gone beyond adoption (MKD-EU-2024-001-0067).
  • The description of how the health insurance and unemployment insurance laws work comes only from the country's own presentation at screening, so independent evidence on their application, for example to EU or other foreign workers, is missing (MKD-EU-2025-003-0083; MKD-EU-2025-003-0084).
  • The five-year plan to amend the legislation and define EESSI access points has no reported steps, and a draft amendment, the planned analysis or an EESSI readiness report would show whether it is moving (MKD-EU-2025-003-0097).

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission requires that, by accession, EU citizens can access North Macedonia's labour market without restrictions such as work permits, can reside for work without a visa or residence permit, and are specifically excluded from the annual quotas for foreign workers (MKD-EU-2025-003-0025; MKD-EU-2025-003-0028). The Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners has been in force since 2015 and was amended in 2021 and 2025, but the 2025 amendments only rename ministries and bodies (MKD-GOV-2015-001-0001; MKD-GOV-2021-001-0001; MKD-GOV-2025-001-0001; MKD-GOV-2025-001-0002). The Commission reports that the Employment Agency issues work permits under annual quotas, set at 10 000 for 2025 (MKD-EU-2023-001-0093; MKD-EU-2025-001-0099). A law on seasonal work allows EU citizens access, but the Commission states that the conditions remain to be set in implementing legislation (MKD-EU-2025-001-0102; MKD-EU-2025-001-0103). Further amendments are listed only as proposals (MKD-GOV-2025-003-0011; MKD-GOV-2026-001-0007). The validated judgements are priority Medium, direction of travel persistent, unresolved gap open and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's description of the regime has hardly changed: from 2020 its reports state that the country sets annual work permit quotas, and the 2024 and November 2025 reports repeat this (MKD-EU-2020-001-0081; MKD-EU-2024-001-0059; MKD-EU-2025-001-0099). What changed is how explicit the requirement became. In 2024 the Commission asked only for further alignment of the Law on work and employment of foreigners (MKD-EU-2024-001-0048). The February 2025 screening report then set out the requirement in full: no work permit, no visa or residence permit for work, and explicit exclusion from the quotas (MKD-EU-2025-003-0025; MKD-EU-2025-003-0028). In November 2025 the Commission added that the conditions for EU citizens in seasonal work remain to be specified (MKD-EU-2025-001-0103).

Country response
10 interventions and their validated implementation status
  • Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners · in practice
  • Law Amending and Supplementing the Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners 2021 · adopted
  • Law Amending the Law on Employment and Work of Foreigners 2025 · adopted
  • Proposed amendments on the employment of foreigners · proposed
  • Law on Foreigners · adopted
  • 2019 amendments to the Law on Foreigners · implemented
  • Single application procedure for work permits · implemented
  • Annual quota of work permits for foreigners · in practice
  • Law on the Work Engagement of Individuals · adopted
  • secondary legislation under the 2021 amending law · insufficient evidence
Implementation and outcome
  • 2019 amendments to the Law on Foreigners: Foreign workers can obtain work permits through a single application to one authority, simplified by Law on Foreigners amendments from May 2019. · success mixed, attribution Medium
Conflicting evidence
  • The Commission states that the law does not distinguish between EU citizens and other foreigners, while North Macedonia states that under the same law the quotas do not apply to EU citizens following a reciprocity agreement with the EU.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is access for EU citizens without work permits or residence permits, with their explicit exclusion from quotas, and no responding intervention is linked (statuses are proposals). The confirmed contradiction stands: the Commission says the law does not distinguish EU citizens, while the country says quotas do not apply to them under a reciprocity agreement. Art. 5(2) point 1 of the 2015 law (machine translated, so capped at Medium, and used under LIM-0024) partly explains this, because it does exempt foreigners given equality under such an agreement, but it is conditional, no item identifies a concluded agreement or shows it applied, and the Commission still requires the exclusion.

Direction of travel: The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is part of the chapter and no sub-area wording matches; Commission items describe annual quotas and work permits unchanged from 2020 to 2025, and the 2025 seasonal work law leaves conditions for EU citizens to be specified. Permit counts (755 in 2021, some 8 900 in 2024) are not used as a trend, because the bases appear to differ: the 2021 figure sits beside 3 242 separate opinions in a machine-translated agency report, capped at Medium.

Priority: Permits and quotas are central to the chapter, but they are named as requirements only in the 2024 report and the screening report, not in the annual key recommendation, which is why this is central with thin support. If the reviewers read the key recommendation on non-discrimination as covering permits and quotas, this would be High; the large item count is mostly the law's own text and did not count.

Tractability: The change needs only national law, but it involves two laws and the interior and labour ministries and the Employment Agency, and an international organisation reports overlapping mandates between the laws. The law was amended in 2021 and 2025 without touching this requirement, and the proposed amendments have unknown content.

Open questions
  • The Commission states that the law does not distinguish EU citizens from other foreigners, while North Macedonia states that the quotas do not apply to EU citizens under a reciprocity agreement, and this confirmed conflict stands; evidence that such an agreement was concluded and applied would settle it (MKD-EU-2024-001-0058; MKD-EU-2025-003-0010; MKD-GOV-2015-001-0026).
  • The legal provision that partly explains the country's position, Article 5(2) of the 2015 law, is available only in machine translation and is capped at Medium confidence, so an official English text or a checked translation is needed (MKD-GOV-2015-001-0026).
  • Whether the secondary legislation due within 30 days under the 2021 amending law was adopted is not shown (insufficient evidence), and its publication in the Official Gazette would settle this (MKD-GOV-2021-001-0032).
  • The permit counts of 755 for 2021 and about 8 900 for 2024 appear to rest on different bases, so a consistent annual series of permits by type, with any figures for EU citizens, would be needed to read a trend (MKD-EU-2022-001-0068; MKD-EU-2025-001-0104; MKD-GOV-2022-002-0005).

RI-FMW-003 · Chapter 2Validated Flagged for re-review

Public sector posts closed to EU citizens beyond the public authority exception

Priority MediumDirection persistentGap openTractability Medium

Assessment: The Commission asks North Macedonia to ensure that, by accession, restrictions on access to the public sector apply only to posts directly involving the exercise of public authority and the safeguarding of the general interest of the State, in line with the case law of the Court of Justice.

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is limiting the restriction to posts involving public authority and the general interest of the State, in line with case law of the Court of Justice.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to ensure that, by accession, restrictions on access to the public sector apply only to posts directly involving the exercise of public authority and the safeguarding of the general interest of the State, in line with the case law of the Court of Justice (MKD-EU-2025-003-0026; MKD-EU-2025-003-0035). The Commission reports each year that EU citizens cannot access public administration posts other than a short list of positions in healthcare and higher education (MKD-EU-2024-001-0060; MKD-EU-2025-001-0100). The screening report records that foreigners have no access to public employment, with exemptions for medical, dental and pharmacy experts in health and for higher education (MKD-EU-2025-003-0021; MKD-EU-2025-003-0023). No intervention responding to this issue is linked in the evidence, so there is no implementation status and no outcome to assess. The gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is Medium and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's finding has stayed essentially the same. In 2020 it stated that EU citizens do not have access to public administration posts, and from 2021 it added the exception for some positions in health and education (MKD-EU-2020-001-0080; MKD-EU-2021-001-0064). The 2022 and 2023 reports say EU citizens "still" cannot access these posts, and the 2024 and 2025 reports describe the exceptions as a short list in healthcare and higher education (MKD-EU-2022-001-0066; MKD-EU-2023-001-0094; MKD-EU-2024-001-0060; MKD-EU-2025-001-0100). The explicit requirement appears only in the February 2025 screening report, which sets the public authority test, asks the country to examine which civil service categories could be reserved for nationals, and links both to case law (MKD-EU-2025-003-0026; MKD-EU-2025-003-0027; MKD-EU-2025-003-0035).

Country response

No country intervention is linked to this issue in the evidence.

Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is limiting the restriction to posts involving public authority and the general interest of the State, in line with case law of the Court of Justice. No responding intervention is linked, so there is no status to compare, and the existing exemptions for health and higher education are the country's account and are narrower than the requirement.

Direction of travel: The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is part of the chapter and no sub-area wording matches. The finding that EU citizens cannot take public administration posts, apart from some in health and education, is unchanged in each report from 2020 to 2025.

Priority: This is a repeated finding central to the chapter, but public sector posts are named as a requirement only in the screening report and not in an annual key recommendation. If the reviewers read 'in all sectors' in the 2023 to 2025 key recommendation as covering them, this would be High.

Tractability: The work is national and depends on no outside party, but it requires a careful review of civil servant categories across the public service against case law. There is no evidence of past progress and no responding intervention.

Open questions
  • It is not settled whether the words "in all sectors" in the 2023 to 2025 key recommendation cover public sector posts, which would raise the priority to High, and a statement from the Commission or the reviewers' reading of the wider report would settle it (MKD-EU-2023-001-0090; MKD-EU-2025-001-0013).
  • The evidence contains no government plan, review of civil servant categories or draft law on this issue, so a national response document would be needed before any status could be assessed (MKD-EU-2025-003-0027).
  • The scope of the health and higher education exemptions rests on the country's account in the screening report, and the legal texts or data on EU citizens employed under them would confirm how they work (MKD-EU-2025-003-0021; MKD-EU-2025-003-0022; MKD-EU-2025-003-0023).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is updated EURES training after staff turnover, with connection of private employment agencies and later ESCO mapping.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to strengthen the Employment Service Agency through continued training and to align legislation and the exchange of good practice with EURES and European Labour Authority rules (MKD-EU-2023-001-0089; MKD-EU-2024-001-0007; MKD-EU-2025-001-0012). The Commission reports that capacity building for civil servants on EURES and the European Labour Authority took place in 2023 (MKD-EU-2023-001-0087; MKD-EU-2023-001-0096), and the 2025 screening report states that all main IT elements for EURES are in place and that administrative capacity is satisfactory (MKD-EU-2025-003-0063; MKD-EU-2025-003-0064). The capacity building and the Agency's web portal are assessed as implemented, but no source shows how the training or the portal is used, so no result is established (MKD-EU-2025-003-0053). What remains is updated EURES training after staff turnover, connection of private employment agencies and, later, ESCO mapping (MKD-EU-2025-003-0065; MKD-EU-2025-003-0070; MKD-EU-2025-003-0055). The validated assessment is partly_addressed, with priority Medium, direction of travel persistent and tractability High.

EU requirement

The key recommendation is nearly unchanged from 2023 to 2025: in each report the Commission asks the country to strengthen the capacity of the Employment Service Agency by continuing training, and to align legislation and the exchange of good practices with EURES and ELA regulations (MKD-EU-2023-001-0089; MKD-EU-2024-001-0007; MKD-EU-2025-001-0012). The 2025 wording differs only in spelling out the two acronyms, and the 2025 report states that the previous recommendations were not implemented (MKD-EU-2025-001-0011). The February 2025 screening report adds more specific points: it finds the IT elements in place and capacity satisfactory, but asks for the 2014 to 2015 twinning training to be updated, for private employment agencies to be given access and adequately connected, and for ESCO mapping at a later stage (MKD-EU-2025-003-0063; MKD-EU-2025-003-0064; MKD-EU-2025-003-0065; MKD-EU-2025-003-0067; MKD-EU-2025-003-0070; MKD-EU-2025-003-0055).

Country response
  • Employment Service Agency web portal · implemented
  • Upgrade of the Employment Service Agency IT system · implemented
  • Capacity building on EURES and the European Labour Authority · implemented
  • Strengthening of Employment Agency capacities · proposed
  • Twinning project training on EURES (2014-2015) · implemented
  • Analysis of harmonisation needs · proposed
  • Memorandum of cooperation on access and exchange of information · adopted
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is updated EURES training after staff turnover, with connection of private employment agencies and later ESCO mapping. The Commission finds the main IT elements in place and capacity satisfactory, and capacity building and IT upgrades are proposed here as implemented while further strengthening is only proposed; all these statuses are proposals.

Direction of travel: The chapter scale was context only. The key recommendation to strengthen the Employment Service Agency is nearly unchanged in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, which sets the default, and the 2025 report says the previous recommendations were not implemented. Training took place in 2023 and the screening report calls capacity satisfactory, but no earlier rating exists to show a rise from.

Priority: Agency capacity is named in the key recommendation in three reports, so the requirement is repeated. It is not central now, because the Commission finds capacity satisfactory and the IT elements in place.

Tractability: The remaining work rests mainly with one agency, does not depend on other countries and builds on training and IT delivered before. Past capacity building is reported by the Commission, not only by the government.

Open questions
  • No source shows the EURES training or the Agency's web portal being used, so independently checked data on vacancy exchange or online service use would be needed to judge results (MKD-EU-2023-001-0096; MKD-EU-2025-003-0053).
  • The planned upgrade that would let the Agency take data from private employment agencies and act as the single point for EURES exchange is not shown as delivered, and an Agency or Commission report on that specific function would settle it (MKD-EU-2025-003-0061).
  • Whether private employment agencies have been connected to the system is not reported, and a later Commission assessment of EURES readiness would show it (MKD-EU-2025-003-0067; MKD-EU-2025-003-0070).
  • The planned strengthening of the Agency's capacities and the EU-funded analysis of harmonisation needs are only proposed, and evidence that they were carried out would be needed to update the gap (MKD-EU-2025-003-0060).

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is aligning national law with the regulation and preparing the State Labour Inspectorate for coordinated tasks.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to further align its legislation and exchange of good practice with the EURES and European Labour Authority regulations, and its screening report finds national law not aligned with the regulation establishing the Authority (MKD-EU-2025-001-0012; MKD-EU-2025-003-0076; MKD-EU-2025-003-0079). The Commission reports that capacity building for civil servants on EURES and the Authority took place, and this training is assessed as implemented, but no source shows the knowledge in use and it does not align the law (MKD-EU-2023-001-0087; MKD-EU-2023-001-0096). The country states medium-term plans to harmonise, with full implementation on accession, and to prepare the State Labour Inspectorate for tasks coordinated by the Authority, including inspections and undeclared work; both are assessed as proposed (MKD-EU-2025-003-0077; MKD-EU-2025-003-0078; MKD-EU-2025-003-0080). No outcome has been assessed. The gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is Medium and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The European Labour Authority first appears in the evidence in the 2023 report, inside a key recommendation mainly about strengthening the Employment Service Agency through training, further alignment of legislation and exchange of good practice in line with the EURES and Authority regulations (MKD-EU-2023-001-0089). The 2024 and 2025 reports repeat this recommendation almost word for word, with the 2025 report only spelling out the full names of EURES and the Authority (MKD-EU-2024-001-0007; MKD-EU-2025-001-0012). The only direct findings on the Authority come from the February 2025 screening report, which states twice that North Macedonia is not aligned with the regulation establishing it (MKD-EU-2025-003-0076; MKD-EU-2025-003-0079). The requirement is therefore unchanged in substance since 2023.

Country response
  • Capacity building on EURES and the European Labour Authority · implemented
  • Preparations of the State Labour Inspectorate for European Labour Authority tasks · proposed
  • Harmonisation with the regulation establishing the European Labour Authority · proposed
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is aligning national law with the regulation and preparing the State Labour Inspectorate for coordinated tasks. Both responses are only proposed for the medium term, and the implemented training does not align the law; these statuses are proposals.

Direction of travel: The chapter scale was context only. The composite recommendation naming the European Labour Authority is nearly unchanged in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and the only direct findings, in the screening report, say national law is not aligned.

Priority: The authority is named in a key recommendation in three reports, but only as part of a sentence mainly about the employment service. The direct support is one source and the issue is not central to the chapter.

Tractability: Harmonisation is within national control and plans exist, but the plans only run in the medium term, with full implementation at accession. They also need institutional and procedural preparation by the labour inspectorate as well as legal change.

Open questions
  • No source shows that the training on EURES and the Authority is being used in practice, so evidence of trained staff applying it, for example in the Employment Service Agency or the labour inspectorate, would settle whether it has had any effect (MKD-EU-2023-001-0096).
  • The content and timing of the medium-term harmonisation plan are not set out, so a draft law, action plan or timetable would show whether alignment is under way (MKD-EU-2025-003-0077; MKD-EU-2025-003-0080).
  • No item shows the institutional, procedural and administrative preparations of the State Labour Inspectorate being carried out, which inspectorate reports or Commission findings could confirm (MKD-EU-2025-003-0078).

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is the human and IT capacity to exchange social security data through EESSI and to process EHIC data electronically.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to develop human capacity and upgrade its IT capacity so that it can exchange social security data with Member States through EESSI, and to step up its capacity to use EHIC data electronically so that it is ready at accession (MKD-EU-2025-003-0092; MKD-EU-2025-003-0103; MKD-EU-2025-003-0108). The Commission finds the country still at an early stage on EESSI (MKD-EU-2025-003-0098). The country reports plans for a single unified registry of insured persons within two years, financed by a World Bank loan, and for an analysis of law, capacity and IT infrastructure leading to defined EESSI access points within five years (MKD-EU-2025-003-0096; MKD-EU-2025-003-0097). Both are assessed as proposed, and no source shows either in operation. The country also reports that its healthcare facilities have no EHIC reader, so the data cannot be processed electronically (MKD-EU-2025-003-0101). The unresolved gap is assessed as open. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is insufficient_evidence and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The requirement appears in the evidence only from 2025, so no change over 2020 to 2025 can be traced. The February 2025 screening report states that North Macedonia is "still at an early stage" on EESSI and asks it to step up alignment, develop human capacities, upgrade IT capacities and increase its capacity to use EHIC data electronically (MKD-EU-2025-003-0098; MKD-EU-2025-003-0099; MKD-EU-2025-003-0092; MKD-EU-2025-003-0103; MKD-EU-2025-003-0108). The November 2025 annual report then adds administrative preparation for electronic exchange of social security data to its key recommendation, alongside concluding bilateral agreements (MKD-EU-2025-001-0014). The word "still" suggests the issue predates 2025, but the earlier reports in the evidence do not state it.

Country response
  • Single unified social insurance registry · proposed
  • Preparations for EESSI access points · proposed
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is the human and IT capacity to exchange social security data through EESSI and to process EHIC data electronically. The registry and the EESSI preparations are only proposed (statuses that are themselves proposals), and the country reports no EHIC reader in its healthcare facilities.

Direction of travel: The sub-area rating 'still at an early stage' matches this issue but appears only in the 2025 screening report, and the annual key recommendation adds electronic exchange only in 2025. The word 'still' suggests the issue is not new, so I do not call it new, and a single year cannot show a trend.

Priority: Electronic exchange is central to applying coordination at accession, and the Commission asks for stepped-up effort. The support is thin, however, as it comes from the screening report and one annual key recommendation.

Tractability: The planned registry has a stated World Bank loan and two-year horizon, but it rests on the country's own account. Several institutions are involved, EESSI access points follow later analysis over five years, and connection also involves the EU side, with no past progress recorded.

Open questions
  • Direction of travel is insufficient_evidence because the rating rests on a single year of Commission assessment, and earlier Commission or government material on EESSI readiness would be needed to show a trend.
  • The registry and its World Bank financing rest on the country's own account in the screening report, and loan documents or project progress reports would show whether the plan has moved forward (MKD-EU-2025-003-0096).
  • No source reports progress on defining EESSI access points or on equipping healthcare facilities with EHIC readers, and later Commission reports or ministry and Health Insurance Fund updates would be needed to settle whether either has begun (MKD-EU-2025-003-0097; MKD-EU-2025-003-0101).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is access through EHIC for citizens of the other Member States.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission reports each year that citizens of only some Member States can use the European Health Insurance Card or access medical services in North Macedonia (MKD-EU-2024-001-0068; MKD-EU-2025-001-0108). From 2020 to 2024 the reports record nine agreements or nine Member States, and the 2024 and 2025 reports state there has been no development on the EHIC (MKD-EU-2020-001-0087; MKD-EU-2021-001-0071; MKD-EU-2022-001-0072; MKD-EU-2023-001-0100; MKD-EU-2024-001-0068; MKD-EU-2025-001-0108). Use of the card with these nine states is assessed as in_practice, and the bilateral social security agreements as implemented. The Commission finds alignment with the technical needs of the EHIC satisfactory (MKD-EU-2025-003-0102), and the outcome is assessed as mixed success with Medium attribution, because coverage is limited to nine Member States. Access for citizens of the other Member States remains, and the gap is assessed as partly_addressed. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is persistent and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's finding has changed little. From 2020 to 2023 the reports record nine agreements, or nine Member States, allowing use of the card, and in 2021 the Commission notes that no new EHIC agreements were concluded (MKD-EU-2020-001-0087; MKD-EU-2021-001-0071; MKD-EU-2021-001-0072; MKD-EU-2022-001-0072; MKD-EU-2023-001-0100). In 2024 it states plainly that there has been no development, with citizens of only nine Member States having access (MKD-EU-2024-001-0068). The 2025 screening report adds a more positive note, finding technical alignment satisfactory (MKD-EU-2025-003-0102). The November 2025 report again states no development but lists fourteen Member States with access to medical services (MKD-EU-2025-001-0108; MKD-EU-2025-001-0109); this was assessed as a difference of scope, not growth, because the five added states have agreements that do not include EHIC use (MKD-EU-2025-003-0198).

Country response
  • European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) · in practice
  • Bilateral social security agreements · implemented
Implementation and outcome
  • Bilateral social security agreements: Alignment with EHIC technical needs is satisfactory, with bilateral agreements allowing EU citizens to use the EHIC. · success mixed, attribution Medium
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is access through EHIC for citizens of the other Member States. Use with nine Member States is proposed as in practice (a status that is itself a proposal), and the Commission finds technical alignment satisfactory, but the card's use rests on separate arrangements and not on general entitlement.

Direction of travel: The chapter scale was context only. Nine agreements or nine Member States are recorded in each report from 2020 to 2024, and no development in 2024 and 2025. The 14 Member States in the 2025 report is a noted difference of scope, not growth, because the five added have agreements that do not include EHIC.

Priority: This is a repeated finding across six reports, but the EHIC is not named in the key recommendation, which refers only to healthcare insurance agreements. The Commission treats technical alignment as satisfactory and it overlaps with RI-FMW-008.

Tractability: The sources describe the basis differently: the country says unilateral use and the Commission says bilateral agreements, which matters because the first would be within national control and the second depends on others. The country reports that agreements could soon be reached with three more states, but no new agreement or development has been recorded.

Open questions
  • The sources describe the basis for EHIC use differently, with the country stating unilateral use and the Commission stating bilateral agreements, and the agreement texts or a Health Insurance Fund statement would be needed to settle which applies (MKD-EU-2025-003-0100; MKD-EU-2025-003-0102).
  • The country reports that agreements could soon be reached with Hungary, Romania and Croatia, but no source records a new agreement, so later Commission reports or ministry lists would show whether this has happened (MKD-EU-2025-003-0100).
  • The status of the bilateral agreements rests on government reporting alone, and independent confirmation of how they are applied, such as data on EHIC claims handled by healthcare institutions, would strengthen the assessment.
  • No outcome data show how many EU citizens actually use the card in the country, and usage or reimbursement figures from the Health Insurance Fund would help to judge results.

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is a signed integrity policy, a person to implement it, a reinforced internal audit department and controls in the institutions concerned.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to strengthen the framework for preventing corruption in free movement of workers, and in particular asks the Employment Agency to sign an integrity policy, nominate a person to implement it, reinforce its internal audit staff and ensure controls, documentation and monitoring (MKD-EU-2025-003-0114; MKD-EU-2025-003-0116; MKD-EU-2025-003-0195; MKD-EU-2025-003-0118). The Commission states that the agency applies the code for civil servants but has not adopted an integrity policy, and that it had planned to sign one but had not done so (MKD-EU-2024-001-0070; MKD-EU-2025-003-0113; MKD-EU-2025-001-0110). No country intervention responding to this issue is linked in the evidence, so there is no implementation status or outcome to report. The Commission describes the framework as weak and the country as still at an early stage in this domain (MKD-EU-2024-001-0069; MKD-EU-2025-003-0111; MKD-EU-2025-003-0117). The validated assessment is that the gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is Medium and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The requirement first appears in the evidence in 2023, when the Commission states that the Employment Service Agency needs to adopt an integrity policy document (MKD-EU-2023-001-0101). In 2024 the Commission adds that the specific framework for preventing corruption in free movement of workers remains weak (MKD-EU-2024-001-0069; MKD-EU-2024-001-0070). The 2025 screening report widens and sharpens the wording: it asks for the policy to be signed, for a person to be nominated to implement it, for internal audit staff to be reinforced, for controls within the institutions involved and for the Ministry of Labour and Social Policy's capacities to be reinforced, and it rates the country as still at an early stage (MKD-EU-2025-003-0116; MKD-EU-2025-003-0195; MKD-EU-2025-003-0118; MKD-EU-2025-003-0112; MKD-EU-2025-003-0117). The November 2025 report repeats that no integrity policy has yet been adopted (MKD-EU-2025-001-0110).

Country response

No country intervention is linked to this issue in the evidence.

Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is a signed integrity policy, a person to implement it, a reinforced internal audit department and controls in the institutions concerned. No responding intervention is linked, so there is no status to compare, and the country's stated plan to sign has not been shown to be carried out.

Direction of travel: The sub-area rating 'still at an early stage' matches this issue but appears only in 2025, so it is used with the issue's own items. The integrity policy is outstanding in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and the framework is called weak in 2024 and again in the screening report.

Priority: The requirement is repeated by the Commission in three reports, but it is not in a key recommendation for the chapter or central to it. The issue's scope is limited to free movement of workers, and general anti-corruption policy is outside it.

Tractability: Signing the policy and naming a person are small steps for one agency, but no report shows them done, though the agency reportedly planned to do so. Reinforcing audit staff, ministry capacity and controls across institutions is wider.

Open questions
  • The evidence contains only Commission statements, so it does not show whether the agency has since signed the integrity policy or named a person to implement it; a government or agency document recording the signature and appointment would settle this (MKD-EU-2025-003-0113; MKD-EU-2025-001-0110).
  • No source reports the current staffing of the agency's internal audit department or the controls in place, so the scale of the remaining capacity gap is unknown; audit reports or staffing data for the agency would settle it (MKD-EU-2025-003-0116).
  • Two screening report items rest on Medium confidence evidence, so a second source confirming the planned signature and the weakness of the framework would strengthen the record (MKD-EU-2025-003-0113; MKD-EU-2025-003-0111).

insufficient evidence Validated

Low Validated

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is designating an institution to support EU mobile workers and improving the system that informs them of their rights.

View detail
Assessment in brief

In its 2025 screening report the Commission asks North Macedonia to improve the system that informs EU workers of their rights in the country and to designate an institution responsible for supporting EU mobile workers (MKD-EU-2025-003-0029; MKD-EU-2025-003-0030; MKD-EU-2025-003-0034). No country intervention responding to this requirement is linked in the evidence, so there is no implementation or result to report. A 2026 regional report by an international organisation states that complaint mechanisms are available only in local languages in most Western Balkan contexts and that workers have no way to navigate the several institutions sharing responsibility for their protection, but these items concern migrant workers generally and cannot alone support a finding about North Macedonia (MKD-IO-2026-001-0016; MKD-IO-2026-001-0018). What remains is designating the institution and improving the information system. The validated assessment is open, with priority Low, direction of travel insufficient_evidence and tractability High.

EU requirement

The requirement cannot be traced over time, because all the Commission's items on this issue come from one document, the February 2025 screening report (MKD-EU-2025-003-0029; MKD-EU-2025-003-0030; MKD-EU-2025-003-0034). In that report the Commission states that efforts should be made to improve the system informing EU workers about their rights and that an institution responsible for supporting EU mobile workers should be designated, and it repeats the call to designate such an institution in a separate sentence (MKD-EU-2025-003-0029; MKD-EU-2025-003-0034). No item from the annual reports of 2020 to 2025 is recorded for this issue, and the requirement is not named in a key recommendation, so there is no earlier wording to compare.

Country response

No country intervention is linked to this issue in the evidence.

Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is designating an institution to support EU mobile workers and improving the system that informs them of their rights. No responding intervention is linked, so there is no status to compare.

Direction of travel: The chapter scale was context only, and the issue's EU items come from one report, the 2025 screening report, so there is no sequence to read. The 2026 items are regional, concern migrant workers generally and cannot alone support a finding about the country.

Priority: The requirement appears in one report, in repeated sentences, and is not named in a key recommendation. The regional items do not raise this, as they concern other workers.

Tractability: Designating an institution is a single national decision, with no dependence on others and few actors. There is no evidence of past progress, so this rests on the nature of the task and is less certain for the wider information system.

Open questions
  • Direction of travel cannot be assessed because the requirement appears in only one report, and the Commission's next assessment of this point would show whether it is moving (MKD-EU-2025-003-0029).
  • No source says whether any body has been designated or is preparing to support EU mobile workers, and a government decision or Commission finding on such an institution would settle whether the gap is being addressed (MKD-EU-2025-003-0034).
  • The regional evidence on complaint mechanisms and on navigating institutions concerns migrant workers generally, so country-specific evidence on how EU workers in North Macedonia obtain information on their rights would be needed before it can be used (MKD-IO-2026-001-0016; MKD-IO-2026-001-0018).

Low Validated

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is alignment with Directives 98/49/EC and 2014/50/EU, apart from cross-border membership and equal treatment in voluntary funds.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission's 2025 screening report finds North Macedonia's legislation not aligned with Directive 98/49/EC or Directive 2014/50/EU on supplementary pension rights, apart from cross-border membership and equal treatment of incoming and outgoing EU workers in voluntary pension funds (MKD-EU-2025-003-0044; MKD-EU-2025-003-0047). Those two elements are provided in national law but enter into force only on the date of accession (MKD-EU-2025-003-0045). The country states that the Law on Voluntary Fully Funded Pension Insurance sets the legal framework for the voluntary scheme; the law is assessed as adopted, and no evidence of its application is given (MKD-EU-2025-003-0037). The screening report also states that the responsible unit has only one person working in it and calls for thorough training of the teams in charge (MKD-EU-2025-003-0043; MKD-EU-2025-003-0046). What remains is alignment with both directives beyond those two elements. The validated assessment is open, with priority Low, direction of travel insufficient_evidence and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

The requirement cannot be traced over time, because every Commission item on this issue comes from one document, the February 2025 screening report. There the Commission states that the legislation is not aligned with Directive 98/49/EC or Directive 2014/50/EU, and that the country is not aligned with most of the supplementary pensions acquis apart from cross-border membership and equal treatment in voluntary funds (MKD-EU-2025-003-0044; MKD-EU-2025-003-0047). It also describes features of the current scheme, such as access for people aged 15 to 70, keeping an occupational account after employment ends and limits on early withdrawal, and recommends thorough training (MKD-EU-2025-003-0038; MKD-EU-2025-003-0039; MKD-EU-2025-003-0040; MKD-EU-2025-003-0046). No item from the annual reports of 2020 to 2025 is recorded for this issue.

Country response
  • Law on Voluntary Fully Funded Pension Insurance · adopted
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: What remains is alignment with Directives 98/49/EC and 2014/50/EU, apart from cross-border membership and equal treatment in voluntary funds. Those two exceptions are provided in law but enter into force only at accession, and no responding intervention is linked, so adoption does not count as closure.

Direction of travel: All items come from one report, the 2025 screening report, so there is no sequence to read and the chapter scale cannot help.

Priority: The requirement is raised only in the screening report and in no key recommendation, and supplementary pensions are peripheral to the chapter compared with its main strands. It remains a stated acquis gap, so Low does not mean it can wait past accession.

Tractability: Legal alignment is within national control and part of the framework is already drafted into law. However, the responsible unit is reported to have only one person and the Commission calls for thorough training.

Open questions
  • Direction of travel cannot be read from a single report, and the Commission's next assessment of supplementary pensions would show whether alignment is moving (MKD-EU-2025-003-0044).
  • No source reports a plan, draft law or timetable for aligning with the two directives, and a government plan or draft amendment would show whether the gap is being addressed (MKD-EU-2025-003-0047).
  • No evidence shows how the Law on Voluntary Fully Funded Pension Insurance is applied, for example to workers leaving or joining occupational funds, and supervisory or fund data would settle this (MKD-EU-2025-003-0037).
  • The staffing constraint rests on one Medium-confidence statement, and current staffing figures for the responsible unit would confirm whether it remains a constraint (MKD-EU-2025-003-0043).

Unresolved gap (insufficient evidence): A regional claim that laws are EU-aligned does not name the country and sits uneasily with the Commission's finding of partial alignment for EU workers.

View detail
Assessment in brief

No Commission recommendation on third-country workers under Chapter 2 appears in the evidence, so this issue is raised mainly by international organisations, partly at regional level (MKD-IO-2024-001-0075; MKD-IO-2026-001-0004). They report an ageing population and skilled emigration that increase the need for foreign workers, alongside regulatory barriers to their immigration (MKD-IO-2024-001-0003; MKD-IO-2024-001-0098). For North Macedonia they report quota-based admission, passport retention, wage deductions of up to 30% and systematic underreporting of exploitation (MKD-IO-2026-001-0004; MKD-IO-2026-001-0012; MKD-IO-2026-001-0017). They also describe permits tied to one employer and under-resourced, reactive labour inspection (MKD-IO-2026-001-0011; MKD-IO-2026-001-0015; MKD-IO-2026-001-0023). No intervention by North Macedonia is linked to this issue and no outcome is recorded. The validated unresolved gap is insufficient_evidence and the direction of travel is insufficient_evidence. Priority is Low and tractability is Medium, the latter a provisional view.

EU requirement

The fact pack contains no EU requirement item from a Commission document for this issue, so there is no Commission wording whose change between 2020 and 2025 or 2026 can be traced. The concerns about third-country workers come from international organisations and one research study rather than from the Commission (MKD-IO-2024-001-0075; MKD-RES-2023-001-0036). The validated judgements note that the Commission's Chapter 2 assessment concerns the access of EU workers, not workers from outside the EU, and that a regional claim that laws are EU-aligned does not name the country (MKD-IO-2026-001-0023; MKD-EU-2025-003-0031).

Country response

No country intervention is linked to this issue in the evidence.

Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: No EU requirement item exists for this issue, so the comparison the gap requires cannot be made and no responding intervention is linked. The international organisations report, for North Macedonia, regulatory barriers, passport retention, wage deductions, underreporting and overlapping laws, which is what remains on their account; other items are regional. A regional claim that laws are EU-aligned does not name the country and sits uneasily with the Commission's finding of partial alignment for EU workers.

Direction of travel: The evidence is from international organisations, with one research study, and partly regional, and no measure of this issue repeats over time for the country. The doubling of permits is regional and cannot alone support a finding here, and the Commission's permit counts have unclear bases. The chapter scale was not decisive, as it concerns EU workers' access.

Priority: The issue is mainly raised by others: the evidence is from international organisations and partly regional, with no Commission recommendation on third-country workers in Chapter 2. The labour shortage it describes may matter for the country, but that is not the test for importance to accession.

Tractability: The rules and inspection are national matters, without dependence on the EU, but the international organisation evidence, partly regional, points to several institutions, under-resourced inspection and permits tied to one employer. No item shows past progress for the country, so this is a provisional view.

Open questions
  • Whether conditions for third-country workers in North Macedonia are improving or worsening is unsettled, because no measure repeats over time for the country and the doubling of work permits is a regional figure (MKD-IO-2026-001-0001); country-level permit and complaint series over several years would settle it.
  • The size of the remaining gap cannot be assessed without an EU requirement item, so a Commission position on third-country workers, or a confirmed decision that none applies, is needed.
  • The scale of rights violations after legal entry rests on international organisation reports that point to underreporting (MKD-IO-2026-001-0012; MKD-IO-2026-001-0017); labour inspectorate records or a country survey of third-country workers would settle it.
  • The Commission's permit counts have unclear bases (MKD-EU-2022-001-0068; MKD-EU-2025-001-0104), so official permit statistics with stated definitions are needed.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asked North Macedonia from 2020 to 2024 to finalise and adopt a long-term ICT strategy, and since 2022 it has asked for stronger ministry capacity to coordinate digital transformation (MKD-EU-2020-001-0105; MKD-EU-2024-001-0015; MKD-EU-2022-001-0099; MKD-EU-2025-001-0128). The Commission reports that a Ministry of Digital Transformation was set up and that a long-term ICT strategy and action plan were adopted in 2025 (MKD-EU-2025-001-0045; MKD-EU-2025-001-0127). Adoption is not improvement in governance: national audit and strategy texts, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, report under half of ministry IT posts filled, no confirmed National Council activity in 2023 and no central register of ICT systems (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0037; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0070; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0082). The Commission still asks for more IT staff and better coordination, and encouraged a digital agency whose need the country said it would reassess (MKD-EU-2025-001-0052; MKD-EU-2025-014-0004; MKD-EU-2025-004-0004). The validated assessment is partly_addressed, with priority High, direction of travel persistent and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

The key recommendation to finalise the long-term ICT strategy appeared in 2020 and, as finalise and adopt, in every report from 2021 to 2024, with the 2022 and 2024 versions adding alignment with electronic communications and network security rules and, in 2024, adoption of the cybersecurity strategy (MKD-EU-2020-001-0105; MKD-EU-2021-001-0083; MKD-EU-2022-001-0087; MKD-EU-2023-001-0119; MKD-EU-2024-001-0015). It left the list in 2025, when the Commission reported the strategy adopted (MKD-EU-2025-001-0127). The capacity request has been stable since 2022, moving from the Ministry of Information Society and Administration to the Ministry of Digital Transformation (MKD-EU-2022-001-0099; MKD-EU-2023-001-0149; MKD-EU-2024-001-0080; MKD-EU-2025-001-0128). In 2025 the Commission added a call to recruit and retain more IT staff, while its screening assessment described the institutional set-up as well structured (MKD-EU-2025-001-0052; MKD-EU-2025-004-0005).

Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The latest EU items report the strategy adopted but still ask for stronger ministry capacity, more IT staff and the digital agency, which remains proposed and which the country has said it will reassess; these statuses are themselves proposals, and that of the National Council is unclear because the 2024 audit found no 2023 activity while the strategy cites its formation. What remains is applying the strategy, building coordinating capacity and IT staffing, and settling the agency question. The Commission's well-structured set-up and the national vacuum are a noted difference of scope, not a conflict.

Direction of travel: The only movement is that the key recommendation to finalise and adopt the ICT strategy, unchanged from 2020 to 2024, ended in 2025 because the strategy was adopted, and adoption is not improvement in governance. The Commission's wording that the ministry needs stronger capacity is unchanged across 2022 to 2025, which sets the default to persistent, and the 2025 report adds a call for more IT staff. The chapter scale (some progress 2020, limited 2021 to 2024, some 2025) is context only and was not decisive.

Priority: The ICT strategy was a Chapter 10 key recommendation in five successive reports, and the ministry capacity ask has recurred in four reports to 2025, on an issue central to the digital transformation theme. The key recommendation itself left the list after adoption in 2025 and the capacity ask sits in body text, so High rests on treating adoption as the start rather than the end of the requirement. National plans and audits were not counted towards this rating.

Tractability: A new ministry and an adopted strategy show that institutional steps can be taken, but the strategy took over five years and coordination depends on many institutions that have offered limited cooperation. IT posts are about half filled and public pay rules limit competition with the private sector, which the ministry cannot change alone. The staffing and working group evidence is machine translated and capped at Medium.

Open questions
  • The Commission's 2025 statement that a long-term ICT strategy was adopted is linked to SMART/MK: 2030 only by timing, and whether the earlier unadopted drafts became that strategy is not stated, so a text naming the adopted strategy would settle it (MKD-EU-2025-001-0127; MKD-GOV-2025-011-0005).
  • Sources differ on the National Council for Digital Transformation, which the 2025 strategy describes as formed to plan and coordinate while the State Audit Office could not confirm any activity in 2023, and records of its meetings and decisions since then would show whether it functions (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0167; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0070).
  • Whether a national digital agency will be set up is unresolved, since the Commission encouraged it and the country said it would reassess the need, and a government decision either way would settle it (MKD-EU-2025-014-0004; MKD-EU-2025-004-0004).
  • The staffing and coordination evidence rests on machine-translated national texts capped at Medium confidence, and current IT staffing figures and evidence of the adopted strategy being carried out would be needed to judge whether governance is improving (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0037; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0078; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0169).

RI-TEC-004 · Technology & AIValidated

Core e-government building blocks missing

Priority HighDirection persistentGap partly addressedTractability Medium

Assessment: The Commission asks North Macedonia to put in place the basic systems that e-government needs, and the Reform Agenda ties payments to three steps: legislation allowing electronic documents to be archived, data storage infrastructure with an e-platform for record keeping and archival work, and a single document management system for all central institutions.

2025 report: 1 item2026 update: Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is application of the law, the storage and record-keeping platform, the single document system across all central institutions and the digital mailbox.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to put in place the basic systems that e-government needs, and the Reform Agenda ties payments to three steps: legislation allowing electronic documents to be archived, data storage infrastructure with an e-platform for record keeping and archival work, and a single document management system for all central institutions (MKD-EU-2023-003-0044; MKD-EU-2024-007-0011; MKD-EU-2024-007-0012; MKD-EU-2024-007-0013; MKD-GOV-2024-002-0014; MKD-GOV-2024-002-0015; MKD-GOV-2024-002-0016). Parliament adopted the Law on Archival Material and Archival Activity in June 2025 and the Commission considers that step achieved, but the law applies only from 1 June 2026 and its by-laws remain proposed (MKD-EU-2025-011-0039; MKD-EU-2025-011-0045; MKD-EU-2025-011-0043). The Commission's technical checks found the document management system only partially operational, and the government reports that 22 institutions use a very small part of it, on machine-translated figures (MKD-EU-2025-011-0046; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0076). The Commission's statement that adoption facilitates e-government is judged too early to show success (MKD-EU-2025-001-0047). The validated assessment is that the gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is High and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

In 2020 and 2023 the Commission's wording in this area concerns the human resources management information system, whose use it says increased but could be further exploited (MKD-EU-2020-001-0010; MKD-EU-2023-001-0214). In July 2023 the Commission states more broadly that basic systems such as a digital mailbox need to be put in place to advance e-government (MKD-EU-2023-003-0044). From October 2024 the requirement becomes concrete and conditional: the Reform Agenda sets three payment conditions on archiving legislation, storage infrastructure with an archival e-platform, and a single document management system for all central institutions (MKD-EU-2024-007-0011; MKD-EU-2024-007-0012; MKD-EU-2024-007-0013). In October 2025 the Commission explains the purpose, stating that the legal framework and a complete document management system will let institutions exchange and store documents electronically without printing (MKD-EU-2025-011-0044).
