Implementation and outcome
  • Law on Archival Material and Archival Activity 2025: Adopting electronic archiving legislation makes it easier to use e-government tools. · success too early, attribution insufficient evidence
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: Of the three Reform Agenda requirements, the law is adopted and the Commission treats that step as achieved, but it applied only from June 2026 with by-laws still proposed, the e-platform is proposed and the document system is only partially operational; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is application of the law, the storage and record-keeping platform, the single document system across all central institutions and the digital mailbox. No item in the input shows whether the 2026 deadlines were met.

Direction of travel: The change since the Commission's 2023 call for basic systems is the adoption of the electronic archiving law in 2025 and the Reform Agenda steps themselves, and adoption alone does not show improvement. The Commission's technical checks found the document system only partially operational, and use has barely moved, from 21 institutions in 2022 to 22 in 2025, on machine-translated national figures capped at Medium. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive.

Priority: The archiving law, the storage platform and the single document system are named Reform Agenda steps with payments attached, and these shared systems are central to the digital government theme. The rating rests on those EU conditions, not on the many national plan items.

Tractability: The tasks are bounded, led by one ministry and backed by payment incentives, and the legal step was achieved by its 2025 deadline. Roll-out is harder: it needs hardware, licences, training and change of working habits in many institutions, and earlier piloting left 22 institutions using a small part of the system. The national evidence on use is machine translated and capped at Medium.

Open questions
  • No item shows whether the June 2026 and December 2026 Reform Agenda deadlines for the storage platform and the single document management system were met, so a Commission payment assessment or technical check after those dates would settle the status (MKD-GOV-2024-001-0083; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0084).
  • The success of the archival law is judged too_early and its attribution insufficient_evidence, because no item shows use of e-government tools after the law began to apply; data on electronic archiving in practice after 1 June 2026 would settle this (MKD-EU-2025-001-0047; MKD-EU-2025-011-0043).
  • The figures on how many institutions use the document management system come from machine-translated national strategies capped at Medium confidence, so an English or independent count of users would strengthen the evidence (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0062; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0076).
  • The amendment of the archival law planned in 2023 and the general e-government framework are rated insufficient_evidence, so a source linking the 2023 plan to the 2025 law, or describing the framework, would settle their status (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0081; MKD-EU-2020-001-0122).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is closing the harmonisation gaps with the Gigabit Infrastructure Act in both laws and adopting and applying the by-laws; the ePrivacy conflict is left to its own issue under the taxonomy.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its electronic communications law with the European Electronic Communications Code and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act, and ties adoption of an aligned law to a Reform Agenda payment (MKD-EU-2024-007-0006; MKD-EU-2025-001-0022). A new Law on Electronic Communications was adopted in June 2025 and amended in December 2025, with application from 1 June 2026 and by-laws due within 15 months (MKD-EU-2025-011-0015; MKD-EU-2026-002-0002; MKD-GOV-2025-008-0032). Both measures are validated as adopted, not as applied. The Commission found the Reform Agenda step not achieved in 2025 and 2026 while the country considers it achieved, a confirmed conflict (MKD-EU-2025-011-0021; MKD-EU-2026-002-0001; MKD-EU-2026-002-0014). Separately, the Regional Roaming Agreement is judged to have worked, on Commission statements without price data (MKD-EU-2022-001-0134). What remains is closing the gaps with the Gigabit Infrastructure Act in two laws and adopting the by-laws. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

From 2020 to 2022 the Commission repeated that the Law on Electronic Communications needed further alignment with the EU acquis (MKD-EU-2020-001-0115; MKD-EU-2021-001-0097; MKD-EU-2022-001-0101). From 2022 its recommendations named the Electronic Communications Code and the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive, and in 2023 it found no progress (MKD-EU-2022-001-0087; MKD-EU-2023-001-0136). In 2024 the Reform Agenda made adoption of a new law aligned with the Gigabit Infrastructure Act a payment condition (MKD-EU-2024-007-0006). After the 2025 law, the Commission found significant harmonisation gaps (MKD-EU-2025-011-0018), and in May 2026, after the December amendments, it found alignment only partially achieved and asked for amendments to both the electronic communications and construction laws (MKD-EU-2026-002-0006; MKD-EU-2026-002-0015).

Conflicting evidence
  • North Macedonia's reported view in the screening report is that it is fully aligned with the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive, while the Commission's 2024 report says it is yet to align with that directive.
  • On the same Reform Agenda step on the Law on Electronic Communications in the same 2025 assessment, the beneficiary considers it fully achieved and the Commission considers it not achieved.
  • On the same Reform Agenda step in the same 2026 assessment, after the December 2025 amendments, the beneficiary considers it achieved and the Commission considers it not achieved.
  • The regulator's 2025 work report dates the start of the roam like at home regime to 1 June 2021, while the Commission dates the regional roaming-free zone to 1 July 2021.
  • North Macedonia stated in the screening published in February 2025 that the Law for Electronic Communications is fully aligned with the ePrivacy Directive, while the Commission's 2024 Report states that further efforts are needed for alignment with that Directive.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The Commission's May 2026 assessment considers the Reform Agenda step not achieved and the beneficiary considers it achieved, as it did in 2025, so the two sides conflict and the Commission's finding is the requirement compared here. Responding interventions carry proposed statuses that the reviewers check at G6: the 2025 law and December amendments adopted, the by-laws and 2026 draft amendments only proposed, and the law applicable only from 1 June 2026, with no evidence on the outcome of the grace period ending 30 June 2026. What remains is closing the harmonisation gaps with the Gigabit Infrastructure Act in both laws and adopting and applying the by-laws; the ePrivacy conflict is left to its own issue under the taxonomy.

Direction of travel: Commission wording that the law needs further alignment repeated from 2020 to 2022, and the matching sub-area wording in 2023 was no progress, but the wording then changed: the 2025 assessment found significant gaps after the new law, and the 2026 assessment found alignment partially achieved after the December 2025 amendments. The chapter-wide limited progress of 2024 is context only and was not decisive. Sources conflict on the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive: the Commission said in 2024 that the country was yet to align, while the country's reported view in the screening is full alignment, and this is not resolved here.

Priority: Adoption of an aligned law is a Reform Agenda step with a payment provision, and alignment with the Code recurs in the Commission's chapter recommendations from 2022 to 2025. It is central to the digital infrastructure theme because other reforms in the area rest on this legal framework. The roaming and net neutrality parts of the issue are largely positive and do not drive this rating.

Tractability: The mechanisms are legal alignment and implementing rules, led by one ministry with the regulator and parliament, and a new law and amendments were adopted in 2025, which favours progress. Against that, the Commission assessed the Reform Agenda step as not achieved in both 2025 and 2026, with gaps remaining in two laws, and the by-laws are described as technically demanding and were not yet due. Adoption has been quick but alignment has twice fallen short, which does not support High.

Open questions
  • The outcome of the Reform Agenda grace period ending 30 June 2026 is not in the evidence (MKD-EU-2026-002-0017), so a later Commission assessment of the step is needed to settle whether alignment was reached.
  • Whether the 2025 law actually began to apply on 1 June 2026 and whether its by-laws were adopted is not shown, since the dates rest on the legal text in machine translation capped at Medium confidence (MKD-GOV-2025-008-0029; MKD-GOV-2025-008-0032); regulator or Commission reports after June 2026 would settle it.
  • Two confirmed conflicts remain unresolved: on the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive between the Commission and the country's screening view (MKD-EU-2024-001-0082; MKD-EU-2025-004-0015), and on the start date of roam like at home (MKD-GOV-2026-003-0033; MKD-EU-2021-001-0086); a Commission statement on the current alignment and an authoritative date source would settle them.
  • The roaming results rest on Commission statements, and later reductions towards 2028 are judged too_early (MKD-EU-2023-002-0026), so actual roaming price data for North Macedonia are needed.

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is independence shown in appointments and practice, more competition in a concentrated mobile market, and resolving the financing provisions for the Operational and Technical Agency, on which the Commission and the country disagree and which concern that agency and not the regulator itself.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to strengthen the independence and capacity of the electronic communications regulator and to improve competition in the telecom sector (MKD-EU-2025-001-0023; MKD-EU-2025-001-0133; MKD-EU-2020-001-0117). Parliament adopted a new Law on Electronic Communications in June 2025, which states that the Agency is independent, but that is a legal provision and no item confirms its application (MKD-GOV-2025-008-0005; MKD-EU-2025-014-0006). The Commission reports that parliament dismissed all five members of the regulator's commission in September 2024 (MKD-EU-2024-001-0087). On competition, machine-translated regulator reporting states that a spectrum tender received a single compliant bid, with the award decision postponed to 12 January 2026, and the Commission says a new operator took part in a tender (MKD-GOV-2026-003-0012; MKD-GOV-2026-003-0014; MKD-EU-2025-001-0144). Success and attribution for that tender are insufficient_evidence, and the mobile market remains concentrated (MKD-GOV-2026-003-0006). The validated assessment is that the gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is High and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's concern about the regulator's independence recurs in nearly unchanged terms from 2020 to 2025: concerns over appointments in 2020 and 2021, concerns over independence in 2022, calls to ensure full independence in 2023 and 2024, and a call to bolster independence in 2025 (MKD-EU-2020-001-0114; MKD-EU-2021-001-0096; MKD-EU-2022-001-0100; MKD-EU-2023-001-0150; MKD-EU-2024-001-0086; MKD-EU-2025-001-0133). The key recommendation on the regulator's independence and capacity appears in every report from 2021 to 2025 (MKD-EU-2021-001-0084; MKD-EU-2025-001-0023). On competition, the wording moves from no relevant developments in 2020 and 2021, to a market mainly shared by two operators in 2023, to a new operator taking part in a tender in 2025 (MKD-EU-2020-001-0116; MKD-EU-2023-001-0140; MKD-EU-2025-001-0144). In 2025 and 2026 the Commission adds points on the new law, including concerns about its provisions on financing the Operational and Technical Agency (MKD-EU-2025-014-0006; MKD-EU-2026-002-0009; MKD-EU-2026-002-0012).

Country response
  • Law on Electronic Communications 2025 · adopted
  • 5G spectrum assignment · in practice
  • Public tender for radio frequency bands 700 MHz, 1800 MHz and 3.x GHz · proposed
  • Third mobile network operator · proposed
Implementation and outcome
  • Public tender for radio frequency bands 700 MHz, 1800 MHz and 3.x GHz: Only one bid arrived by the deadline; the record found that it met the tender conditions. · success insufficient evidence, attribution insufficient evidence
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The latest Commission items still ask for the regulator's independence to be ensured and bolstered, and the 2025 law's statement that the Agency is independent is a legal provision, not evidence of practice. The compared statuses are proposals for G6: the law is adopted, while the third operator and the frequency tender are only proposed, and the latest evidence on the tender is a sole bidder with a decision deadline of 12 January 2026, in machine-translated regulator reporting. What remains is independence shown in appointments and practice, more competition in a concentrated mobile market, and resolving the financing provisions for the Operational and Technical Agency, on which the Commission and the country disagree and which concern that agency and not the regulator itself.

Direction of travel: Commission concern about the regulator's independence recurs in nearly unchanged terms in each report from 2020 to 2025, with no recorded improvement, so the default applies; in September 2024 parliament dismissed all five commission members, which the source reports without saying what it meant for independence. The chapter scale was not decisive. The competition part has moved a little, from no relevant developments in 2020 and 2021 to a market still shared by two operators in 2023 and a new operator taking part in a frequency tender in 2025, so the two parts of this issue do not move together.

Priority: Strengthening the independence and capacity of this regulator is a key Commission recommendation repeated in every report from 2021 to 2025, and an independent regulator is central to the digital infrastructure theme. It is not itself a Reform Agenda step, and the recommendation is shared with the media regulators, which are outside this issue. The rating rests on the independence part; the competition part is supported by repeated but less prominent findings.

Tractability: The two parts differ. Independence looks hard, because it depends on appointments by parliament and exposure to political interests, and six years of reports record no progress, while competition looks more realistic because a tender has reached a compliant bid. That tender rests on one bidder and was held up by elections and a missing opinion from the anti-corruption commission, as machine-translated regulator reporting states, so Medium is a blend that would not hold if the issue were split.

Open questions
  • No item shows whether the regulator's independence has improved in appointments or in practice, so evidence on appointments to the new commission and on how the 2025 law is applied would settle this (MKD-EU-2024-001-0087; MKD-GOV-2025-008-0005).
  • The outcome of the spectrum tender is unknown, with success and attribution rated insufficient_evidence on machine-translated regulator reporting capped at Medium confidence, so an award decision and later market share data would settle whether competition improved (MKD-GOV-2026-003-0012; MKD-GOV-2026-003-0014).
  • The Commission and North Macedonia disagree on whether the law's provisions on financing the Operational and Technical Agency are consistent with the EU telecoms code, and the evidence does not resolve this; a later Commission assessment or an amendment to the law would settle it (MKD-EU-2026-002-0009; MKD-EU-2026-002-0010).
  • The planned third mobile network operator rests on a machine-translated strategy and no item shows it introduced, so a regulatory decision or licence would settle its status (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0113).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is fixed broadband for small firms and rural areas, very low take-up of the fastest connections, and completing the 5G roll-out named in the Reform Agenda.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission has repeatedly called for wider broadband access, and the Reform Agenda ties a payment to 5G roll-out and a 5G security by-law (MKD-EU-2021-001-0044; MKD-EU-2024-007-0008). The Commission reports continued 5G expansion, and a machine-translated national source gives 96.99% population coverage (MKD-EU-2025-001-0143; MKD-GOV-2025-011-0023); 5G spectrum assignment and roll-out are validated as in_practice. The national broadband plan is validated as implemented, but its success is insufficient_evidence, and the national optical network is only proposed. The Commission reports household internet access rising to 90.8% in 2024 (MKD-EU-2025-001-0083), yet in 2025 it found that smaller companies and rural areas still face significant obstacles (MKD-EU-2025-001-0086), and take-up of the fastest connections remains very low (MKD-EU-2024-008-0025). Sources conflict on fixed coverage against the EU average. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is High and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's wording has been largely stable. From 2021 to 2023 it repeated that there is a particular need to increase access to broadband and that smaller companies still face obstacles to fixed broadband (MKD-EU-2021-001-0044; MKD-EU-2022-001-0055; MKD-EU-2023-001-0072). From 2024 it added fast internet for small businesses and non-urban areas and named rural areas alongside smaller companies (MKD-EU-2024-009-0008; MKD-EU-2024-001-0053). The 2024 Reform Agenda added a payment condition on 5G roll-out (MKD-EU-2024-007-0008). In 2025 the wording hardened to significant obstacles for smaller companies and rural areas (MKD-EU-2025-001-0086), while the 2026 assessment repeated the earlier sentence (MKD-EU-2026-003-0005).

Implementation and outcome
  • National Operational Broadband Plan 2019-2029: In line with the 2019-2023 national broadband plan targets, the 5G signal was expanded to Skopje. · success insufficient evidence, attribution Low
  • Public tender for radio frequency bands 700 MHz, 1800 MHz and 3.x GHz: Only one bid arrived by the deadline; the record found that it met the tender conditions. · success insufficient evidence, attribution insufficient evidence
Conflicting evidence
  • The ICT strategy says fixed broadband coverage of 77% of households is in line with an EU average of 78%, while the Commission's 2025 report says fixed broadband was available to 79.6% of households at the end of 2023, below an EU average of 93.1%.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: Latest EU items still ask for more access for smaller companies and rural areas, while the compared statuses, which are proposals for G6, show 5G roll-out in practice but the national optical network only proposed. Sources conflict on the size of the gap: the ICT strategy gives 77% fixed coverage against an EU average of 78%, the Commission gives 79.6% against 93.1%, and the strategy elsewhere gives 77% as very high capacity coverage after stating 69%, so the comparison with the EU cannot be relied on until the measures are checked. What remains is fixed broadband for small firms and rural areas, very low take-up of the fastest connections, and completing the 5G roll-out named in the Reform Agenda.

Direction of travel: The Commission's sentence that smaller companies still face obstacles repeats from 2021 to 2026 with the same figures, so the default applies, though repeats are not independent evidence, and in 2025 the wording hardened to significant obstacles for smaller companies and rural areas. National averages did rise, with home internet access at 90.8% in 2024, 5G coverage at 76% in 2023 and 97% in a machine-translated 2025 national source, and some progress on ICT infrastructure in matching sub-area wording in 2025, while differences between earlier household figures reflect different measures, not conflict. No series tracks the rural and small-business gap itself, so the averages do not show that the unevenness has narrowed, and the chapter scale was not decisive.

Priority: Roll-out of 5G network and services is named in a Reform Agenda step, and the Commission repeats the particular need to increase access to broadband in its assessments from 2021 to 2026, which makes it central to the digital infrastructure theme. The payment condition covers the 5G part, not the rural and small-business part, which appears in repeated assessments and not in the chapter's key recommendations. The large volume of items on this issue, much of it repeated wording and national statistics, did not raise the rating.

Tractability: Past progress is clear on 5G and on general access, where operators have invested and the Commission records continued expansion. The harder part depends on resources and on others: rural and low-demand areas lack commercial interest, the national network is at feasibility stage on a timetable to 2030 with mixed financing, and the government's own strategy, in machine translation, names lack of finance and high prices as challenges. Delivery therefore needs the ministry, the public broadcasting enterprise, operators and outside funders.

Open questions
  • The size of the gap with the EU is unsettled because the ICT strategy and the Commission give conflicting fixed coverage figures and EU averages (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0035; MKD-EU-2025-001-0084); checking the definitions behind each measure would settle it.
  • No series tracks the rural and small-business gap itself, as the 2023 rural figure is a single point (MKD-EU-2024-009-0010), so repeated coverage and take-up data by area and firm size are needed.
  • The outcome of the 2025 spectrum tender rests only on machine-translated regulator reporting capped at Medium confidence, and its success and attribution are insufficient_evidence (MKD-GOV-2026-003-0012); a published award decision would settle it.
  • Whether the national broadband plan caused the 5G expansion is insufficient_evidence (MKD-EU-2023-001-0125), so evidence on use and on the plan's own contribution, as distinct from operator investment, is needed.

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is to complete the digitalisation of institutional, municipal property and intellectual property registers and to raise the quality and use of population register data.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to complete the digitalisation of institutions' registers and data exchange, to improve the quality of population register data, and to digitalise intellectual property registration further (MKD-EU-2025-001-0004; MKD-EU-2023-001-0155; MKD-EU-2025-003-0165). The Central Population Register is assessed as in practice: the Commission reported it operational in 2020 and used to cross-check the 2021 census (MKD-EU-2020-001-0016; MKD-EU-2022-001-0017). The Commission nonetheless found its use still limited in 2024, and the government's machine-translated 2025 strategy also describes it as underused and in need of a larger data set (MKD-EU-2024-001-0026; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0067; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0141). The platform for digitalising registers, the Register of Registers and the digital register of charges are assessed only as proposed, and the 2023 strategy's baseline was no digital registers in 2022 (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0025; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0233; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0159; MKD-GOV-2023-002-0069). The Commission still finds municipal property registers analogue (MKD-EU-2024-001-0047). No outcome has been assessed. The gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is High and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's focus has moved from the population register to registers in general. In 2021 it asked for population register data to be fully uploaded and checked and used to cross-check census data, and in 2022 and 2023 it asked for better data quality, continuously verified against other registers (MKD-EU-2021-001-0106; MKD-EU-2022-001-0112; MKD-EU-2023-001-0155). From 2023 a key recommendation asks the country to complete the digitalisation of institutions' registers and data exchange as part of fully implementing the law on general administrative procedures, repeated almost word for word in 2024 and 2025 (MKD-EU-2023-001-0002; MKD-EU-2024-001-0002; MKD-EU-2025-001-0004). The 2025 report notes efforts but keeps the recommendation (MKD-EU-2025-001-0003). The 2025 screening report adds intellectual property registration (MKD-EU-2025-003-0164; MKD-EU-2025-003-0165).

Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Conflicting evidence
  • The 2023 report says eIDAS alignment was further delayed, while the 2023 public administration reform strategy says the 2019 law on electronic documents, identification and trust services is aligned with European legislation on digitalisation.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The population register is proposed as in practice, but the register platform, the Register of Registers and the wider e-services reform are all proposed only, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is to complete the digitalisation of institutional, municipal property and intellectual property registers and to raise the quality and use of population register data. The fully digital National Real Estate Register and the Commission's analogue property registers are a noted difference of register and level, not a conflict, and the machine-translated strategy on low use is capped at Medium confidence.

Direction of travel: The Commission repeated the need to improve population register data in 2021, 2022 and 2023, and the same recommendation to complete the digitalisation of institutions' registers in 2023, 2024 and 2025, with use of the register still limited in 2024. The 2025 mention of efforts does not change the recommendation, so the default of persistent applies. The Chapter 10 scale is context only and was not decisive.

Priority: The Commission's main findings gave the same key recommendation to complete register digitalisation in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and base registers are central to the digital government theme. The recommendation is one clause of a wider one on administrative procedures and is shared with the data exchange and e-services issues, which reviewers may weigh. The Reform Agenda payment step on a register of charges is flagged as doubtful for this theme and was not relied on.

Tractability: The operating population register shows that delivery is possible, and a register platform was begun with EU support. Against that, completion needs many institutions and municipalities to act, and the strategy's baseline of no digital registers in 2022 shows how much remains. The two strategy items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

Open questions
  • No later source confirms that the register digitalisation platform came into use in 2023 as planned, and a count of digitalised registers against the strategy's baseline and targets would settle progress (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0025; MKD-GOV-2023-002-0069).
  • The 2023 report says eIDAS alignment was further delayed while the 2023 strategy states that the 2019 digital laws are aligned with European legislation, a confirmed conflict that a Commission alignment assessment of the law would settle (MKD-EU-2023-001-0138; MKD-GOV-2023-002-0016).
  • The fully digital National Real Estate Register rests only on the country's own account, while the Commission finds municipal property registers analogue, so independent evidence on use of each register is missing (MKD-EU-2023-003-0085; MKD-EU-2023-003-0086).
  • Much of the evidence on register plans and on the underuse of the population register comes from machine-translated government strategies, capped at Medium confidence, which an official English version or independent usage data would strengthen (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0067; MKD-GOV-2023-002-0077).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is full alignment with the General Data Protection Regulation, a law transposing the Law Enforcement Directive, safeguards for transfers, harmonised sector laws and confirmed ePrivacy alignment.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align fully with the General Data Protection Regulation, to adopt a law transposing the Law Enforcement Directive, to ensure safeguards for international transfers and to harmonise sector laws (MKD-EU-2023-001-0027; MKD-EU-2023-001-0030; MKD-EU-2023-001-0031; MKD-EU-2025-001-0066). The 2020 Law on Personal Data Protection has applied in full since August 2021, and the Agency reports supervisions and new rulebooks (MKD-EU-2022-001-0021; MKD-GOV-2025-010-0085). A draft law transposing the Law Enforcement Directive was withdrawn in September 2022, and the Agency reports that neither that transposition nor its own draft amendments had started moving in 2025, in machine-translated reporting (MKD-GOV-2026-002-0035; MKD-GOV-2026-002-0037). In 2025 Parliament amended the law to allow transfers to NATO countries without prior consultation of the Agency, and the Commission found no progress and an insufficient framework (MKD-EU-2025-001-0065; MKD-EU-2025-001-0063; MKD-EU-2025-001-0062). The validated assessment is that the gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is High (an analyst override) and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

In 2020 the Commission's wording centres on the Law Enforcement Directive, recording no concrete progress on alignment (MKD-EU-2020-001-0036). From 2023 the requirement broadens: the screening report calls the framework partially aligned and asks for the recast of the law to be completed and a new law on the Law Enforcement Directive, and the 2023 report adds transfers, the Agency's independence and the harmonisation of sector laws (MKD-EU-2023-003-0073; MKD-EU-2023-003-0074; MKD-EU-2023-003-0075; MKD-EU-2023-001-0028; MKD-EU-2023-001-0031). In 2024 and 2025 the Commission records no progress and states that full alignment remains pending, and it adds ePrivacy alignment (MKD-EU-2024-001-0039; MKD-EU-2024-001-0102; MKD-EU-2025-001-0064; MKD-EU-2025-001-0148). In 2025 it also calls the framework insufficient and notes the absence of safeguards for transferred data (MKD-EU-2025-001-0062; MKD-EU-2025-001-0066).

Implementation and outcome
  • Law on financial companies: Recent changes to the Law on financial companies led to more complaints (to the data protection agency). · success insufficient evidence, attribution Medium
Conflicting evidence
  • In 2025 the State Audit Office says personal data protection in AI projects is regulated by legislation aligned with European standards, especially the GDPR, while the Commission says adoption of legislation to fully align with the GDPR is still pending.
  • The State Audit Office's June 2025 report states that national data protection legislation is aligned with EU legislation, while the Commission's 2025 Report states that adoption of legislation to fully align with the General Data Protection Regulation and the Law Enforcement Directive is still pending.
  • The Agency's 2025-2030 strategy describes a robust and comprehensive legal framework that aligns closely with the acquis, while the Commission's 2025 Report states that the legal framework for the protection of personal data is insufficient.
  • North Macedonia stated in the screening published in February 2025 that the Law for Electronic Communications is fully aligned with the ePrivacy Directive, while the Commission's 2024 Report states that further efforts are needed for alignment with that Directive.
  • The State Audit Office report dates the Law on Personal Data Protection to 2018, while the Commission's 2020 Report states that the new law was adopted in February 2020.
  • The ITU profile of February 2022 lists the Law on the Security of Network and Information Systems as an existing enabler, while the Commission's 2022 report says the draft of that law has not yet been adopted.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The 2020 law is proposed as in practice, with the Commission confirming full application from August 2021, while the amendments and the Law Enforcement Directive law are proposed only, the earlier draft was withdrawn in 2022, and all these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is full alignment with the General Data Protection Regulation, a law transposing the Law Enforcement Directive, safeguards for transfers, harmonised sector laws and confirmed ePrivacy alignment. Sources conflict, since the State Audit Office and the Agency's strategy describe the law as aligned while the Commission calls the framework insufficient, and the country claims full ePrivacy alignment while the Commission seeks further efforts; this judgement does not rely on Article 122 of the unofficial translation (MKD-GOV-2020-001-0043), which may be mistranslated and, read literally, would suspend core chapters until accession.

Direction of travel: The Commission found no concrete progress on the Law Enforcement Directive in 2020, partial alignment and a need for full alignment in 2023, and pending alignment in 2024 and 2025, so the requirement has not changed across three or more reports. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2024 and 2025 covers more than this issue and was not decisive. The 2025 transfer amendment without equivalent safeguards is a further concern but a single event.

Priority: Full alignment with the data protection rules is central to the data theme and is repeated by the Commission in 2023, 2024 and 2025, but none of the 2020 to 2025 reports names it in the key recommendations, and it is in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition. The 2024 and 2025 main findings record no progress, but that is a finding and not a key recommendation, so this is a central requirement with thin support under the test. National and agency items were not counted.

Tractability: Texts already exist: the Agency drafted amendments in April 2022 and a Law Enforcement Directive draft reached Parliament with, as the Agency reports, a positive informal Commission opinion. Yet the Government withdrew that draft in 2022, neither process moved in 2025, and sector laws need several ministries. The Agency's annual report items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

Open questions
  • Sources conflict on alignment: the State Audit Office and the Agency's strategy describe the legislation as aligned with EU law, while the Commission calls the framework insufficient and full alignment pending, and only a Commission assessment of a new or amended law would settle this (MKD-GOV-2025-011-0154; MKD-GOV-2024-006-0005; MKD-EU-2025-001-0064; MKD-EU-2025-001-0062).
  • North Macedonia states that its electronic communications law is fully aligned with the ePrivacy Directive, while the Commission seeks further efforts and could not yet fully evaluate it, so a completed Commission evaluation would settle this conflict (MKD-EU-2025-004-0023; MKD-EU-2024-001-0102; MKD-EU-2025-004-0071).
  • Article 122 of the unofficial translation of the 2020 law reads as suspending core chapters until accession, which contradicts the other evidence of application and may be a translation fault, so a check against the Macedonian text would settle it (MKD-GOV-2020-001-0043).
  • Much of the evidence on what the Agency has done comes from its own machine-translated reports, capped at Medium confidence or lower, and the effect of the Law on financial companies is rated insufficient_evidence for success, so independent evidence on supervision results and complaint trends would strengthen the record (MKD-GOV-2026-002-0037; MKD-EU-2023-001-0206).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is the outstanding NIS2 provisions and Cybersecurity Act certification alignment (last raised before the law passed), the 15 by-laws legally due within six months but not shown as adopted, the entity lists, the disclosure and crisis frameworks, working coordination, and application to the sectors the law defers until accession.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its network and information security law with the NIS2 Directive and the Cybersecurity Act, to adopt and implement a cybersecurity strategy, and to improve coordination, and the Reform Agenda ties payments to the law and strategy, an operational competent authority and the NIS2 disclosure and crisis frameworks (MKD-EU-2024-001-0095; MKD-EU-2025-004-0106; MKD-EU-2023-001-0146; MKD-EU-2024-007-0002; MKD-EU-2024-007-0004; MKD-EU-2024-007-0005). After a 2019 draft stalled, the Government adopted the Cyber Security Strategy 2025-2028 in January 2025 and Parliament adopted the law in June 2025, both assessed as adopted (MKD-EU-2021-001-0095; MKD-EU-2025-011-0008; MKD-EU-2025-011-0002). The Commission found the law sufficient for the Reform Agenda step but not fully aligned with the acquis (MKD-EU-2025-011-0007; MKD-EU-2025-011-0012). The 15 by-laws, entity lists, disclosure and crisis frameworks and working coordination are not shown in place, and the State Audit Office found the National Cyber Security Council met only once (MKD-EU-2025-011-0004; MKD-GOV-2024-008-0038). No outcome has been assessed. The gap is assessed as partly_addressed. Priority is High, direction of travel is improving and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's wording has moved from adoption to completeness of alignment. In 2021 it records no progress on the 2019 draft law and calls for more effort on a fragmented strategy (MKD-EU-2021-001-0095; MKD-EU-2021-001-0089). From 2022 to 2024 it repeatedly asks North Macedonia to adopt the law, aligned with NIS and then NIS2, and a new cybersecurity strategy, adding in 2023 a call for better coordination and a stronger National Cybersecurity Council (MKD-EU-2022-001-0087; MKD-EU-2023-001-0148; MKD-EU-2023-001-0128; MKD-EU-2023-001-0146; MKD-EU-2024-001-0095). The 2024 Reform Agenda turns these into payment conditions (MKD-EU-2024-007-0002). In 2025, after adoption, the Commission records some progress but asks the country to continue aligning with NIS2 and the Cybersecurity Act (MKD-EU-2025-001-0020; MKD-EU-2025-001-0022; MKD-EU-2025-004-0106).

Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Conflicting evidence
  • The ITU profile of February 2022 lists the Law on the Security of Network and Information Systems as an existing enabler, while the Commission's 2022 report says the draft of that law has not yet been adopted.
  • The Commission says the National Cyber Security Council was established in July 2020, while the State Audit Office says it was formed in 2019.
  • The Government's action plan is titled as covering 2025-2027, while the Commission describes the accompanying action plan as covering 2025-2028.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The Commission found the 2025 law sufficient for the Reform Agenda step, which required alignment of primary legislation only, yet says it does not fully align with the acquis and still asks the country to continue aligning; the law, strategy and competent authority are proposed as adopted and the by-laws and disclosure and crisis frameworks as proposed, and these statuses are themselves proposals for review. What remains is the outstanding NIS2 provisions and Cybersecurity Act certification alignment (last raised before the law passed), the 15 by-laws legally due within six months but not shown as adopted, the entity lists, the disclosure and crisis frameworks, working coordination, and application to the sectors the law defers until accession. The law's text is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and the regulator's one-line statement that the strategy is applied is government reporting without specifics, so neither is treated as closure.

Direction of travel: Commission items moved from no further progress on the 2019 draft law in 2021, through repeated calls to adopt the law and strategy in 2022, 2023 and 2024, to adoption of the strategy in January 2025 and the law in June 2025, which the 2025 report counts as some progress. The chapter scale (limited progress 2021 to 2024, some progress 2025) is context only and was not decisive, and the improvement lies in the legal and strategic framework, since no item shows better coordination after the 2023 call, the 2024 audit finding of a Council that met once and the 2025 strategy's own description of coordination as critical. A February 2022 ITU item lists the law as existing while the Commission's 2022 report says it was still a draft, and later Commission and audit items support the draft reading; the differing dates for the Council (2019 or 2020) and the action plan's end (2027 or 2028) do not affect this value.

Priority: The law and strategy, an operational competent authority and the NIS2 frameworks are each Reform Agenda payment steps, and NIS2 or cybersecurity legislation recurs in the Commission's key recommendations from 2022 to 2025. The issue is the legal base on which the rest of the cybersecurity theme rests. The rating rests on these EU requirements and not on the large number of national plan and audit items.

Tractability: Much of what remains is drafting that the Ministry controls, and adoption followed within a year of the Reform Agenda step, which favours progress; against this, the first draft law stalled from 2019 to 2025, the Council barely functioned and no item shows the by-laws adopted after their deadline. Coordination needs many bodies, the strategy itself names political support and budget as key risks, and one reporting obligation to ENISA cannot be met outside the EU. Tractability is therefore higher for legal alignment than for coordination.

Open questions
  • Whether the 15 by-laws, the entity lists and the response team and network required by the 2025 law were adopted or set up by their deadlines is not shown, and official gazette entries or ministry reports would settle it (MKD-GOV-2025-007-0054; MKD-GOV-2025-007-0055; MKD-GOV-2025-007-0058).
  • The regulator states that the strategy is applied, but this is government reporting without specifics, and the half-yearly implementation reports the strategy promises would show what has been delivered (MKD-GOV-2026-003-0021; MKD-GOV-2025-005-0096).
  • Confirmed conflicts remain on whether the law existed in February 2022, on whether the Council was formed in 2019 or July 2020, and on whether the action plan runs to 2027 or 2028, and the official gazette and Government decisions would settle them (MKD-IO-2022-002-0058; MKD-EU-2022-001-0098; MKD-EU-2021-001-0036; MKD-GOV-2024-008-0093; MKD-GOV-2025-006-0001; MKD-EU-2025-011-0010).
  • The law's text and the audit findings are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and no evidence shows the competent authority staffed or performing supervisory checks, which later Commission Reform Agenda assessments would show (MKD-GOV-2025-007-0016; MKD-EU-2024-007-0004).

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is staffed and trained response teams working to the Reform Agenda standard, security officers and tested plans in institutions, and secure government infrastructure in actual use.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks state institutions to strengthen their cyber infrastructure and expertise and the national Computer Incident Response Centre to strengthen its staffing and operational capacity significantly, and the Reform Agenda ties payments to operational response teams, a staffed competent authority and a secure government network (MKD-EU-2025-001-0141; MKD-EU-2025-001-0142; MKD-EU-2024-007-0003; MKD-EU-2024-007-0004; MKD-EU-2024-007-0007). North Macedonia adopted a cyber security strategy and action plan in January 2025 and a law on network and information security in June 2025, which establishes the national and government response teams (MKD-GOV-2025-007-0025). The State Audit Office reports, in machine-translated findings, that only 3 of 11 MKD-CIRT posts were filled and that 67% of surveyed institutions had no response team, and the disaster recovery centre is used by 3 of about 140 bodies (MKD-GOV-2024-008-0054; MKD-GOV-2024-008-0068; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0043). In April 2026 the Commission still reports major deficiencies (MKD-EU-2026-003-0009). The validated assessment is that the gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is High and tractability is Low.

EU requirement

From 2020 to 2023 the Commission frames cybersecurity mainly at regional level, as a priority for capacity building and resilience against hybrid threats (MKD-EU-2020-002-0019; MKD-EU-2021-002-0006; MKD-EU-2022-002-0021). From 2023 its country wording is essentially unchanged: state institutions need stronger cyber capacity, infrastructure and expertise, and the national response centre needs more staff (MKD-EU-2023-001-0147; MKD-EU-2024-001-0096; MKD-EU-2024-001-0097; MKD-EU-2025-001-0141). The 2025 wording sharpens this to significant strengthening of the centre (MKD-EU-2025-001-0142). In October 2024 the Reform Agenda adds concrete payment conditions on response teams, the competent authority and a secure network (MKD-EU-2024-007-0003; MKD-EU-2024-007-0004; MKD-EU-2024-007-0007). The Commission's reform programme assessments move from large deficiencies in 2025 to major deficiencies in 2026 (MKD-EU-2025-012-0009; MKD-EU-2026-003-0008).

Country response

  • Law on Electronic Management and Electronic Services · implemented
  • Law on Security of Network and Information Systems 2025 · adopted

  • Reform 2.2.2.1 Secure Digital infrastructures roll-out · proposed

Implementation and outcome
  • Government Conclusion of the 131st session on mandatory online cyber security training: More than 19,500 of 129,374 public employees attended cybersecurity training by December 2023, which the audit calls insufficient. · success mixed, attribution Medium
  • Information with proposed measures to improve information system security 2023: 13% of surveyed institutions took no action on the proposed security measures. · success mixed, attribution Low
Conflicting evidence
  • MKD-CIRT records 1,443 incident reports for 2020, while the State Audit Office chart gives 1,441 for the same year.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The latest EU items, of November 2025 and April 2026, still call for significant strengthening and report major deficiencies, while responses are proposed as adopted on paper (the law, strategy and action plan, the national and government response teams) or only planned (government data centre, secure network, security operations centre), and the disaster recovery centre is used by 3 of about 140 bodies; these statuses are themselves proposals for review. What remains is staffed and trained response teams working to the Reform Agenda standard, security officers and tested plans in institutions, and secure government infrastructure in actual use. The Reform Agenda's 2024 baseline of CERTs not operational sits against statements that MKD-CIRT is in place, possibly because the baseline means NIS2 readiness, and the audit evidence behind this finding is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence, with percentages from a survey of 18 institutions.

Direction of travel: The Commission's wording is essentially unchanged across three reports, that state institutions need stronger capacity and infrastructure and the national centre more staff (2023, 2024, 2025), and its reform programme assessments repeat large or major deficiencies in 2025 and 2026, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Incident counts cannot show a trend in capacity, because reporting was not mandatory and the figures are not comparable (1,441 or 1,443 for 2020, 2,804 for 2022, about 170 in 2023 on an unstated definition). The World Bank's advanced rating and the audit's finding of poor protection are a noted difference and not a conflict, since an index of national commitments and a test of practice measure different things, and the 2024 index itself lists technical and capacity measures as areas for growth.

Priority: Operational national and government CERTs, a staffed competent authority and a secure government network are Reform Agenda payment steps, and the Commission has repeated the need for capacity in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports. The Commission's reform programme assessments also name these deficiencies, and without operating capacity the legal framework has little effect, so the issue is central to the theme. The rating does not rest on the volume of audit and action plan items.

Tractability: Progress needs people the state has struggled to hire and keep (IT posts about half filled, 3 of 11 MKD-CIRT posts filled, a shortage the strategy says extends across the region), action across about 140 bodies, and budgets the strategy itself calls at risk, while the main infrastructure is at pre-feasibility stage and looks to outside funding. Past progress is weak, as most surveyed institutions had no response team five years after the previous strategy called for them, and the new 40% salary supplement is adopted with no item yet showing its effect. Strengthening MKD-CIRT alone would be more achievable than system-wide capacity, and the audit and strategy items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

Open questions
  • No item shows the national or government response teams operating to the Reform Agenda standard, and the Reform Agenda's 2024 baseline of not operational sits against statements that MKD-CIRT is in place, so a Commission payment assessment after June 2026 would settle their status (MKD-GOV-2024-002-0004; MKD-EU-2025-004-0093; MKD-GOV-2025-007-0057).
  • Incident figures do not show a trend in capacity, since sources give conflicting counts for 2020 (1,443 and 1,441) and later figures use different definitions, so consistent mandatory incident reporting under the new law would be needed (MKD-GOV-2022-003-0006; MKD-GOV-2024-008-0055; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0048).
  • The audit evidence on staffing and protection is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence, and based on a survey of 18 institutions, so an updated audit or staffing data would test whether capacity has changed (MKD-GOV-2024-008-0043; MKD-GOV-2024-008-0068).
  • The new 40% salary supplement for cyber security staff is adopted but no item shows its effect on hiring or retention, so later vacancy data for MKD-CIRT and institutions would settle this (MKD-GOV-2025-007-0048; MKD-GOV-2022-004-0009).

Security of 5G networks not ensured

Priority HighDirection persistentGap partly addressedTractability Medium

Assessment: The Commission asks North Macedonia to implement the EU 5G Cybersecurity Toolbox, including supplier risk assessment and restrictions on high-risk suppliers, and the Reform Agenda requires a fully implemented 5G security by-law by December 2027.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to implement the EU 5G Cybersecurity Toolbox, including supplier risk assessment and restrictions on high-risk suppliers, and the Reform Agenda requires a fully implemented 5G security by-law by December 2027 (MKD-EU-2025-001-0145; MKD-EU-2024-007-0008; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0065). April 2021 amendments gave the regulator prior security approval of 5G equipment, and the Commission reported the regulator adopted by-laws in 2022 (MKD-EU-2021-001-0093; MKD-EU-2022-001-0097), but the screening report says not all the amendments were fully implemented (MKD-EU-2025-004-0047). The 2025 Law on Electronic Communications, validated as adopted, empowers the regulator to assess suppliers and restrict high-risk ones, according to a machine-translated text (MKD-GOV-2025-008-0022). The 5G security by-law and the supplier risk assessment remain proposed, and no item shows an assessment carried out. No outcome is recorded. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is High and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission has named the 5G toolbox in successive recommendations from 2022 to 2025, and the core requirement has not changed (MKD-EU-2022-001-0087; MKD-EU-2023-001-0121; MKD-EU-2024-001-0015; MKD-EU-2025-001-0022). In 2024 the Reform Agenda turned it into a payment condition linked to a 5G security by-law and 5G roll-out (MKD-EU-2024-007-0008). In 2025 the wording became more specific, asking the country to continue implementing the toolbox, including assessing suppliers' risk profiles and restricting or excluding high-risk suppliers (MKD-EU-2025-004-0073; MKD-EU-2025-001-0145). The Commission's 2025 enlargement communication also presents secure 5G infrastructure under the toolbox as a regional priority (MKD-EU-2025-002-0011).

Country response
  • Amendments to the Law on Electronic Communications (April 2021) · reversed
  • By-laws implementing the April 2021 amendments to the Law on Electronic Communications · adopted
  • Law on Electronic Communications 2025 · adopted
  • Reform 2.2.2.1 Secure Digital infrastructures roll-out · proposed
  • 5G spectrum assignment · in practice
  • 5G roll-out · in practice
  • 5G security bylaw · proposed
  • Risk profile assessment of network equipment suppliers, manufacturers and operators in annual supervision · proposed
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The latest EU items ask the country to continue implementing the toolbox, including assessing suppliers and restricting high-risk ones, and the Reform Agenda requires the security by-law fully implemented by December 2027; the 2025 law is proposed as adopted, the by-law and supplier assessment as proposed, and the 2021 amendments as reversed because the new law replaces them, all of which are proposals for review. What remains is adopting and applying the by-law and actually carrying out supplier risk assessments and any restrictions, since the law gives the power (machine translated, capped at Medium) but no item shows it used. The Reform Agenda's statement that the step is largely achieved sits against its own partial compliance baseline and the Commission's later wording, and it appears to rest mainly on spectrum and legislation, so it is not treated as closure; the Commission's finding that this law's reform step was not achieved concerns the Code and the Gigabit Act and not the toolbox, and the law allows 15 months for by-laws, so the finding does not decide this gap.

Direction of travel: The Commission has named the 5G toolbox in its recommendations in four successive reports (2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, two of these items being classified under the framework issue), and its November 2025 wording still asks the country to continue, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Legal steps did occur (2021 amendments, 2022 by-laws, the June 2025 law with supplier risk provisions), but the screening report says not all the 2021 amendments had been implemented. A reviewer could read the 2025 law as the start of improvement, but it began to apply only in June 2026 and no later EU item assesses it.

Priority: Toolbox compliance is a Reform Agenda step and has been named in the Commission's key recommendations in four successive reports, and the enlargement communication presents it as a basis of secure digital infrastructure. The issue is narrow, one clause among several in the chapter's key recommendation, so centrality is the weakest part of this rating and a reviewer could reasonably set Medium. The small number of items did not lower the rating, as volume is not a criterion.

Tractability: Few actors are needed, mainly the regulator and the Ministry working with operators, the law already provides the power and by-laws under the 2021 amendments were reported adopted by the following year, which all favour progress. However, not all the 2021 amendments were implemented four years on, a supplier assessment planned from 2023 is not shown as done, and operators complained of having no consultation in 2021. The evidence does not show what restrictions would cost operators, so the rating is not set higher.

Open questions
  • Whether the regulator has carried out any supplier risk assessment or restriction is not shown, although one was planned from 2023 (MKD-EU-2025-004-0048); regulator supervision reports or a Commission assessment would settle it.
  • The supplier assessment power rests on a machine-translated legal text capped at Medium confidence (MKD-GOV-2025-008-0022), so the official text or an English Commission summary is needed.
  • The Reform Agenda says the step is largely achieved while its own baseline records partial compliance (MKD-GOV-2024-001-0067; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0066); a Commission assessment of the 5G toolbox step itself would settle how far it has been met.
  • No EU item assesses the 2025 law's application since June 2026, so later Commission reporting is needed to judge whether the direction of travel is changing.
Evidence

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is full alignment of the partially harmonised provisions, adoption of the 14 by-laws, which no item shows as adopted, and actual application.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its law on electronic identification and trust services with the revised EU Digital Identity Regulation, including a national Digital Identity Wallet, and the Reform Agenda ties a payment to an updated law (MKD-EU-2024-001-0030; MKD-EU-2024-007-0009). Parliament adopted amendments transposing eIDAS 2.0 on 27 June 2025, and the Commission considered the Reform Agenda step achieved while finding the law not fully aligned (MKD-EU-2025-011-0027; MKD-EU-2025-011-0031; MKD-EU-2025-011-0033). The amendments are validated as adopted; a machine-translated law text says they apply only from 1 June 2027 (MKD-GOV-2025-009-0041). The 14 by-laws and the wallet remain proposed, with some by-laws tied to December 2027 (MKD-EU-2025-011-0029). The 2019 framework is validated as in_practice, with narrow use. No outcome is recorded. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is High.

EU requirement

The Commission's wording has moved from basic alignment to the revised regulation. In 2022 it said North Macedonia had yet to align with the eIDAS Regulation, and in 2023 that alignment was further delayed (MKD-EU-2022-001-0103; MKD-EU-2023-001-0138). In 2024 it treated the law as harmonised with the 2014 regulation and asked for alignment with the revised 2024 regulation, including a Digital Identity Wallet, which the Reform Agenda made a payment condition (MKD-EU-2024-001-0029; MKD-EU-2024-001-0030; MKD-EU-2024-007-0009). In 2025 it recorded some progress through the eIDAS 2.0 amendments but said further efforts are required for full alignment (MKD-EU-2025-001-0001; MKD-EU-2025-001-0148).

Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Conflicting evidence
  • The 2022 report says national legislation has yet to align with eIDAS, while the screening report says the by-laws of the first half of 2020 established a legal environment harmonised with eIDAS.
  • The 2023 report says eIDAS alignment was further delayed, while the 2023 screening report says the legal environment has been harmonised with eIDAS since the first half of 2020.
  • The 2023 report says eIDAS alignment was further delayed, while the 2023 public administration reform strategy says the 2019 law on electronic documents, identification and trust services is aligned with European legislation on digitalisation.
  • The 2023 report says eIDAS alignment was further delayed, while the 2024 report says national legislation is harmonised with the 2014 eIDAS Regulation, and the list of amendments to the law in MKD-GOV-2025-009-0003 shows none between the two reports.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The law was amended in June 2025 and the Commission counted the step as achieved for Reform Agenda purposes, while saying the law does not fully align and asking for further efforts in its 2025 report; the intervention statuses used here are themselves proposals. What remains is full alignment of the partially harmonised provisions, adoption of the 14 by-laws, which no item shows as adopted, and actual application. The machine-translated law text, capped at Medium confidence, says the amendments apply only from 1 June 2027.

Direction of travel: The Commission moved from 'yet to align' (2022) and 'further delayed' (2023) to treating the law as harmonised with the 2014 regulation and asking for the 2024 revision (2024), then to amendments transposing eIDAS 2.0, with 'some progress' for e-government and further efforts required (2025). Sources conflict on whether alignment with the 2014 regulation already existed in 2020 (screening report and 2023 strategy against the 2022 and 2023 reports), which affects the start point but not the trend. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive; the judgement rests on the issue's own items.

Priority: The updated law is a Reform Agenda payment condition, and eIDAS alignment was raised by the Commission in each report from 2022 to 2025. It is the legal base of the electronic identification theme. The rating rests on these requirements and not on the number of items, most of which are provisions of one law.

Tractability: The remaining work is mainly legal drafting led by one ministry, with a gap analysis by SIGMA and a by-law roadmap already available, and the ministry met the June 2025 law deadline. Earlier delays in 2022 and 2023 and the staged by-laws, some tied to the wallet in December 2027, are the main limits.

Open questions
  • Sources conflict on whether the law was already aligned with the 2014 regulation before 2024, with the screening report and a government strategy against the Commission's 2022 and 2023 reports (MKD-EU-2023-003-0041; MKD-GOV-2023-002-0016; MKD-EU-2022-001-0103; MKD-EU-2023-001-0138); a Commission statement on the earlier alignment status would settle it.
  • No source up to the freeze date reports any of the 14 by-laws as adopted (MKD-EU-2025-011-0029), so official gazette records or a later Commission assessment are needed.
  • The 1 June 2027 application date rests on a machine-translated law text capped at Medium confidence (MKD-GOV-2025-009-0041), so the official text or an English Commission source is needed to confirm it.
  • No outcome evidence shows use of electronic identification or trust services by citizens, so usage data are needed to judge any result.

View detail
Assessment in brief

Under the Reform Agenda, the EU asks North Macedonia to join the EU Third Countries trusted list, make qualified trust services available, implement a Digital Identity Wallet and sign the Western Balkans mutual recognition agreement on trust services, and the Commission repeatedly finds the existing e-identification and e-signature tools not user friendly or free for citizens (MKD-EU-2024-007-0010; MKD-EU-2024-007-0014; MKD-EU-2025-001-0050). The 2019 law is in practice, two providers accredited in 2021 offer advanced and qualified signatures, and the Ministry of Digital Transformation has supervised them (MKD-EU-2026-002-0021; MKD-EU-2026-002-0022; MKD-EU-2026-002-0025). This provider outcome is assessed as a mixed success with Medium attribution. Electronic identity is in practice but little used, and the machine-translated audit found that high-level eID did not raise use (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0049; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0102; MKD-EU-2023-003-0042). The country requested trusted list inclusion on 30 October 2025, but the Commission considers the step not achieved, and the wallet and cross-border recognition remain proposed (MKD-EU-2026-002-0026; MKD-EU-2026-002-0029; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0074). The gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is High and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The requirement has grown from usage to recognition. In 2021 the Commission noted only that electronic signature use had increased modestly (MKD-EU-2021-001-0013). In 2024 the Reform Agenda set payment conditions to join the trusted list, issue qualified certificates and implement a wallet and the regional agreement, and the annual report asked for alignment with the revised eIDAS Regulation and described the tools as cumbersome, not free and not user friendly (MKD-EU-2024-007-0010; MKD-EU-2024-007-0014; MKD-EU-2024-001-0030; MKD-EU-2024-001-0031). The 2025 report says the tools are "still" not user friendly or free (MKD-EU-2025-001-0050; MKD-EU-2025-001-0147). In May 2026 the Commission specified the outstanding trusted list tasks and set a grace period to 31 December 2026 (MKD-EU-2026-002-0028; MKD-EU-2026-002-0030).

Implementation and outcome
  • Law on Electronic Documents, Electronic Identification and Trust Services: Under the 2019 eIDAS 1 framework, two trust service providers, Telekom and KIBS, were accredited in 2021 in Slovenia and the Czech Republic. · success mixed, attribution Medium
Conflicting evidence
  • North Macedonia reports having completed all preparatory activities for the trusted list, while the Commission says it still needs to finalise its self-assessment and publish its national trusted list in the required format.
  • On the same trusted list step in the same assessment, the beneficiary considers it achieved and the Commission considers it not achieved.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: Two providers offer advanced and qualified signature services, as the Commission reports and as the Reform Agenda step asks, but the same step is not achieved, the tools remain not free or user friendly, and the wallet and mutual recognition are still proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. The two sides conflict: North Macedonia reports the trusted list preparation complete and considers the step achieved, while the Commission says the self-assessment and published list are outstanding. What remains is inclusion in the trusted list (grace period to 31 December 2026), usable and free tools in common use, the wallet and cross-border recognition.

Direction of travel: The Commission said in 2024 that the tools were cumbersome and neither free nor user friendly, and in 2025 that they were still not, while its 2021 report recorded only a modest rise in electronic signature use. In 2026 it found the trusted list step not achieved despite the request of 30 October 2025, so steps were taken without a changed result. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive, and the 2024 audit evidence that high-level eID did not raise use is machine translated and capped at Medium.

Priority: Joining the trusted list and implementing the wallet are Reform Agenda steps, the first with a stated payment provision, and the Commission repeated its concern about the tools in 2024 and 2025. Recognition and use are central to the electronic identification theme.

Tractability: The outstanding trusted list tasks are specific and technical, and two providers have passed ministry checks, which favours progress. Use and usability need many institutions and users, the wallet depends on regional partners and the mutual recognition agreement, and the list depends on Commission assessment. The audit found failed procurement of institutional seal certificates (machine translated, capped at Medium), which is a warning on delivery.

Open questions
  • North Macedonia reports all trusted list preparations complete and considers the step achieved, while the Commission says the self-assessment and published list are outstanding and the step not achieved, a confirmed conflict that the Commission's decision by the end of the grace period would settle (MKD-EU-2026-002-0018; MKD-EU-2026-002-0024; MKD-EU-2026-002-0028; MKD-EU-2026-002-0029).
  • The audit could not confirm use of the 150,000 digital identities announced through the Mastercard arrangement or who received 12,000 qualified signatures, in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, and certificate issuance and usage data would settle it (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0100; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0101).
  • There are no current figures on how many citizens and businesses use eID and qualified signatures, and the latest benchmark score of 23% dates from 2022, so a newer benchmark or portal usage data would show whether use has changed (MKD-EU-2023-003-0042).
  • It is not shown whether the failed procurement of institutional seal certificates, which left seals expired from May 2023, has been resolved, which a later audit or ministry report would confirm (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0135; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0111).

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to fully implement the law on general administrative procedures by completing data exchange, and a Reform Agenda payment condition asks for more data exchange between institutions and documents obtained ex officio (MKD-EU-2025-001-0004; MKD-EU-2024-007-0016; MKD-GOV-2024-002-0018). The interoperability platform is in practice, and the Commission reports that customs exchanges data regularly through it (MKD-EU-2025-001-0166). Government figures, machine translated, show connections rising from 39 institutions in 2021 to 58 or 63 in 2025 and transactions reaching 8 million in 2024, with the Commission noting more connections and transactions (MKD-GOV-2022-004-0030; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0064; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0184; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0185; MKD-EU-2024-001-0028). The Commission still finds only a few institutions using it, and the government's 2021 conclusions on connecting about 1,300 institutions are assessed as failed, with Low attribution, after the audit found only six new requests (MKD-GOV-2022-004-0049; MKD-GOV-2022-004-0051). The planned upgrade remains proposed (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0183). The gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is High and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The diagnosis has hardly changed, while the requirement has become firmer. In 2020 the Commission found that many institutions did not use the system despite having the equipment, and asked for political will and funding (MKD-EU-2020-001-0121; MKD-EU-2020-001-0020). In 2021 and 2022 it asked for administrative data sharing to be reinforced and simplified, citing missing communications software and lack of will (MKD-EU-2021-001-0007; MKD-EU-2022-001-0008; MKD-EU-2022-001-0110). From 2023 a key recommendation asks the country to complete data exchange under the law on general administrative procedures, repeated in 2024 and 2025, and in 2024 the Reform Agenda tied ex officio data exchange to a payment condition (MKD-EU-2023-001-0002; MKD-EU-2024-001-0002; MKD-EU-2025-001-0004; MKD-EU-2024-007-0016). Specific demands also appeared for asset declaration checks and inspections (MKD-EU-2024-001-0037; MKD-EU-2025-003-0009).

Implementation and outcome
  • Government conclusions of June and September 2021 on connecting to the interoperability platform: After the government conclusions, the ministry received only six new connection requests. · success failed, attribution Low
Conflicting evidence
  • North Macedonia tells the 2023 screening that the once-only principle is applied, while its 2024 Reform Agenda says institutions still do not gather evidence ex officio as the law prescribes.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The platform operates and some institutions, such as customs, exchange data regularly, but the 2025 Commission recommendation still asks to complete data exchange and the responding upgrades and reforms are mainly proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. There is a confirmed contradiction: the country told the 2023 screening that the once-only principle is applied, while its 2024 Reform Agenda says institutions still do not gather evidence ex officio. What remains is regular use of the platform by the institutions obliged to use it, so that evidence is obtained ex officio as the law prescribes.

Direction of travel: Commission wording that few institutions use the platform runs from 2020 through 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, which sets the persistent default; the 2025 report records only efforts and repeats the requirement. Connection and transaction figures rose (39 institutions in 2021 to 58 or 63 in 2025; 1.5 million transactions in 2022 to 8 million in 2024), and the Commission confirms the increases in 2023 and 2024, but the counts come from government documents, machine translated and capped at Medium, and most institutions remain outside. The 2020 Commission 'slight increase' and the audit's falling traffic are a noted difference of measure and period, and the chapter scale was context only and not decisive.

Priority: Data exchange and ex officio evidence sit in a Reform Agenda payment condition, and completing data exchange is a repeated recommendation on public administration reform in 2023, 2024 and 2025, in the main findings in the last two. It is central to the interoperability and data themes. The large number of items, mostly from one national audit, played no part in this rating.

Tractability: The platform exists and the government controls it, and use has risen somewhat, which favours progress. Against that, the audit found about 1,300 obliged institutions with no costed plan, IT pay at less than half the private sector and no coordinating body, findings the 2025 strategy partly repeats (all machine translated, capped at Medium), and the Commission cites missing software and lack of will. ITU's account of a ministers' council is a noted difference over a different body, leaving how far coordination worked in practice uncertain.

Open questions
  • North Macedonia told the 2023 screening that the once-only principle is applied, while its 2024 Reform Agenda says institutions still do not gather evidence ex officio, a confirmed conflict that data on ex officio requests made through the platform would settle (MKD-EU-2023-003-0029; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0097).
  • Connection and transaction figures come from machine-translated government documents capped at Medium confidence and differ by measure and period, including a fall from about 3.6 million transactions in 2021 to 1.5 million in 2022, so a consistent independent series would settle the trend (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0060; MKD-GOV-2022-004-0083; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0185).
  • The State Audit Office evidence behind the failed outcome is filed under the government family and machine translated, so the reviewers' confirmation of its independence and an English or verified text would firm up that judgement (MKD-GOV-2022-004-0049).
  • ITU describes a ministers' council while the audit found no body coordinating systems used by several institutions, a noted difference over different bodies that leaves open how far coordination worked in practice, which evidence of that council's decisions on the platform would settle (MKD-IO-2022-002-0066; MKD-GOV-2022-004-0017; MKD-GOV-2022-004-0065).

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to keep consolidating and upgrading its customs IT systems in line with the Union Customs Code work programme and the electronic customs strategic plan, to upgrade its transit system to Phase 6 and to recruit IT staff, and states that alignment on accession is critical to EU financial interests and security (MKD-EU-2025-001-0033; MKD-EU-2025-001-0034; MKD-EU-2025-001-0167; MKD-EU-2025-002-0010). After delays reported in 2023 and 2024, the Commission states that the New Computerised Transit System Phase 5 was completed and launched in January 2025, and notes good progress (MKD-EU-2024-001-0108; MKD-EU-2025-001-0031; MKD-EU-2025-001-0191). Phase 6, the export system and the import control system remain Reform Agenda steps due between 2026 and 2027 (MKD-GOV-2024-001-0117; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0123; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0125). The screening report rates alignment between low and partial, with remaining systems costed at about EUR 34.5 million (MKD-EU-2025-004-0155; MKD-EU-2025-004-0161). No usage data exist for Phase 5. The validated judgements are priority High, direction of travel improving, unresolved gap partly_addressed and tractability High.

EU requirement

The core recommendation has barely changed: from 2021 the Commission asks the country to consolidate and apply its customs IT systems in line with the strategic plan modules and ensure their upgrade, and from 2024 it adds the Union Customs Code work programme and continued legal alignment (MKD-EU-2021-001-0116; MKD-EU-2022-001-0124; MKD-EU-2023-001-0173; MKD-EU-2024-001-0019; MKD-EU-2025-001-0033). The specific ask moved with events: implement Phase 5 in 2023 and 2024, then upgrade to Phase 6 in November 2025 (MKD-EU-2023-001-0172; MKD-EU-2024-001-0018; MKD-EU-2025-001-0034). In 2024 the Reform Agenda set payment conditions for Phase 6, the export system and the import control system (MKD-EU-2024-007-0019; MKD-EU-2024-007-0020; MKD-EU-2024-007-0021), and staff recruitment became a recurring ask (MKD-EU-2024-001-0109; MKD-EU-2025-001-0167).
