Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: NCTS Phase 5 is live, but the 2025 screening rates alignment between low and partial, and Phase 6, the export system and ICS2 are proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is development of the remaining systems under the strategic plan, costed at about EUR 34.5 million, with full alignment planned for 2026 to 2030.

Direction of travel: NCTS Phase 5 preparation started by 2021, delays were reported in 2023 and 2024, and the system launched in January 2025, with the Commission noting 'good progress' on IT systems in 2025. The Commission's recommendation to consolidate systems repeats each year, but the stated result changed. The sub-area wording matches this issue, yet the chapter scale was context only and not decisive.

Priority: E-customs steps appear in the Reform Agenda with a stated payment provision for Phase 6, and the customs IT recommendation recurs from 2021 to 2025, in the main findings in 2024 and 2025. The Commission calls alignment on accession critical to EU financial interests and security, so the issue is central to Chapter 29. Some Reform Agenda items carry a theme_doubtful flag because their wording stresses efficiency, not connection to the EU.

Tractability: One capable agency leads, and it has delivered NCTS Phase 5 after delay and kept Phase 4 running satisfactorily. The limits are IT staffing, the planned 15 experts not yet shown as hired, cost, and an EU-driven timetable to 2030.

Open questions
  • No source gives usage or performance data for Phase 5 since its launch, so transit declaration and processing statistics would be needed to show it working in practice (MKD-EU-2025-001-0031).
  • The Reform Agenda's own text gives a 2 to 4 per cent time reduction for Phase 6 while the payment condition gives 2 to 5 per cent, and the signed Reform Agenda annex would settle which applies (MKD-GOV-2024-001-0117; MKD-EU-2024-007-0019; MKD-GOV-2024-002-0023).
  • The plan to hire 15 more IT experts and the 2024 upgrade of the economic operators module are not shown as done, and customs staffing figures or a later Commission report would settle this (MKD-EU-2025-004-0162; MKD-EU-2025-004-0151).
  • The draft Law on Single Window for Trade, needed for the new national single window, is not reported as adopted, and its publication would settle whether that system can proceed (MKD-IO-2024-001-0108).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is a much wider set of fully transactional, commonly requested services that people actually use, on an agreed count, and equal access, where the Commission's statement that the portal caters for special needs conflicts with the audit's finding (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to offer many more fully digitalised services on its national e-services portal and to treat the digitalisation of public services as a priority, and a Reform Agenda payment condition requires a 50 per cent increase in the offer of e-services (MKD-EU-2023-003-0037; MKD-EU-2025-004-0103; MKD-EU-2024-007-0015). The Commission states that the portal was upgraded, its offer widened with services most demanded by citizens, and some certificates put online (MKD-EU-2025-001-0135; MKD-EU-2025-001-0136). The State Audit Office, in machine translation, found only 0.556 requests per registered user and about 140 laws not aligned with the digitalisation package (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0194; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0002), and the 2025 strategy reports about 13 of 100 adults registered (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0075). In April 2026 the Commission found digital government quite underdeveloped, with most e-services rarely used (MKD-EU-2026-003-0007). There is no outcome evidence. The validated judgements are priority High, direction of travel persistent, unresolved gap partly_addressed and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's message has stayed essentially the same from 2020 to 2026. It first asked institutions to commit more to the portal and to encourage its use (MKD-EU-2020-001-0015; MKD-EU-2021-001-0011). From 2022 it asked for a wider offer of services and noted that fully electronic services had barely grown (MKD-EU-2022-001-0045; MKD-EU-2022-001-0046; MKD-EU-2023-003-0106). In 2023 and 2024 it asked for the 135 new services to be completed and found the most common services, such as personal documents, still not online (MKD-EU-2023-001-0011; MKD-EU-2024-001-0023; MKD-EU-2024-001-0090). From 2024 the Reform Agenda added the 50 per cent target, and in 2025 the screening asked for digitalisation to be treated as a priority (MKD-EU-2024-007-0015; MKD-EU-2025-004-0103). In 2026 the Commission still describes rare use and few fully transactional services (MKD-EU-2026-003-0007).

  • Legal revision for electronic evidence and life-event services (3.2.2.6) · proposed
  • Mandatory integration of e-services on the portal (A 3.2.1.3) · proposed
  • Memoranda of understanding with Montenegro on judicial reform and digitalisation of public services · adopted
  • Revision of the price of e-services (A 3.2.2.8) · proposed
  • Digital connection as a basic right · proposed
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Conflicting evidence
  • For the same Reform Agenda target on e-services in October 2024, the Agenda gives a 2024 baseline of 264 while the Commission assessment gives a current figure of 392.
  • The Reform Agenda gives 264 e-services as the 2024 baseline, while the Commission report gives 124 services accessible online by September 2024.
  • Commission documents of June and October 2024 give 246 services available online and 124 services accessible online by September 2024.
  • The Commission states in 2024 that most administrative services are offered online and offline, while the State Audit Office in 2024 records 1,120 services available only in person.
  • North Macedonia told the 2023 screening that the platform allows access to people with disabilities, while the State Audit Office finds that visually impaired persons cannot use the portal e-services.
  • The Commission states in 2024 that the portal caters to people with special needs, while the State Audit Office concludes in 2024 that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services.
  • The 2023 report says eIDAS alignment was further delayed, while the 2023 public administration reform strategy says the 2019 law on electronic documents, identification and trust services is aligned with European legislation on digitalisation.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The portal is proposed as in practice and its upgrade as implemented, while the Reform Agenda reform is proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals, and the upgrade status sits uneasily with the Commission's 2024 note that the 135 services were not yet configured. Progress against the 50% target cannot be fixed, because the 264 baseline conflicts with the Commission's 392 and 124 figures, and 246 also conflicts with 124, so sources are cited both ways. What remains is a much wider set of fully transactional, commonly requested services that people actually use, on an agreed count, and equal access, where the Commission's statement that the portal caters for special needs conflicts with the audit's finding (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services.

Direction of travel: From 2020 to 2026 the Commission repeats the same shortfall: too few fully transactional services, low use and below-expectation results, ending with 'quite underdeveloped' in 2026, and the world index rank falls from 72 to 80 to 84 (the last from a machine-translated strategy table, capped at Medium confidence). The 2025 report does record a real change, with most-demanded services and some certificates now online, so the case for 'improving' is open but rests on one report that the 2026 finding does not bear out. The Chapter 10 scale (Some, Limited, Limited, Some progress in 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025) is context only and was not decisive, and service counts were not used for trend because their definitions differ.

Priority: The e-services increase is a Reform Agenda payment condition, and widening the portal's services is a recommendation repeated across three or more reports, including 'treat as a priority' in the 2025 screening. It is central to the digital government theme and Chapter 10. The rating rests on these, not on the large number of national audit and strategy items.

Tractability: A single platform, EU funding and a dated payment step favour progress, and the Commission reports new services in 2025. Against that, the Commission's own wording shows the 135-service upgrade slipping for years and fragmented ownership, and the State Audit Office (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) reports about 140 laws unaligned and 101 of 242 posts unfilled, which means many institutions must act.

Open questions
  • Sources conflict on the number of services, with the Reform Agenda baseline of 264 against Commission figures of 392, 246 and 124 in 2024, so progress against the 50 per cent target cannot be measured until an agreed count and definition is published (MKD-GOV-2024-001-0092; MKD-EU-2024-008-0015; MKD-EU-2024-009-0014; MKD-EU-2024-001-0072).
  • The Commission states that the portal caters to people with special needs, while the State Audit Office, in machine translation capped at Medium confidence, finds that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services, and an independent accessibility test of the portal would settle this conflict (MKD-EU-2024-001-0020; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0136; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0026).
  • The Commission states that most administrative services are offered online and offline, while the State Audit Office records 1,120 services available only in person, and a complete service catalogue showing the channel for each service would settle this conflict (MKD-EU-2024-001-0088; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0055).
  • Use figures come mainly from machine-translated national audit and strategy texts and no recent usage series exists, so regular portal statistics on transactions per service would be needed to show whether the 2025 upgrade changed use (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0006; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0075; MKD-EU-2025-001-0135).

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is alignment with the AI Act and the enforcement structures it needs, none of which yet exists.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission invites North Macedonia to align fully with the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and to put in place the necessary enforcement structures (MKD-EU-2025-001-0149). The State Audit Office reports that a working group formed in 2021 met only once and that no national AI strategy or legislation for public sector AI projects has been adopted (MKD-GOV-2025-011-0008; MKD-GOV-2025-011-0009; MKD-GOV-2025-011-0089). The 2025 digital strategy lists drafting an AI strategy and legislation aligned with the AI Act as planned actions, assessed as proposed (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0206; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0207). The audit reports that the ADA digital assistant is not functioning after about EUR 150 thousand was spent, and the strategy route and ADA are each assessed as failed (MKD-GOV-2025-011-0049). The Commission welcomed the signed AI Factory Antenna grant, but no activity under it is reported (MKD-EU-2026-005-0001). Much of the national evidence is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence. The gap is assessed as open. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is new (as an EU requirement) and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The requirement is recent, so there is no repeated Commission wording to compare. The first Commission item appears in the November 2025 report, which invites North Macedonia to "fully align" with the AI Act and to ensure the necessary enforcement structures (MKD-EU-2025-001-0149). The only later Commission item, from April 2026, does not mention the AI Act: it welcomes the AI Factory Antenna grant and encourages outreach to neighbouring countries, a regional ecosystem of experts and users, and use of the European Digital Innovation Hubs (MKD-EU-2026-005-0002). The requirement is therefore new as an EU ask, although national sources show that the gap itself is older (MKD-GOV-2024-001-0024; MKD-GOV-2025-011-0009).

Implementation and outcome
  • AI pilot in the 112 emergency service: In implementation, the 112 pilot shows AI can help emergency operators respond faster and more efficiently. · success insufficient evidence, attribution insufficient evidence
  • AI pilot in the 112 emergency service: Despite the Crisis Management Centre's efforts, the 112 AI pilot was not fully implemented. · success failed, attribution Medium
  • National strategy for AI: Since the working group was formed in 2021 it has met only once, and the national AI strategy has not been prepared. · success failed, attribution Medium
  • ADA digital assistant: Two years on, the ADA digital assistant, on which about EUR 150,000 was spent, is not functioning. · success failed, attribution Medium
Conflicting evidence
  • In 2025 the State Audit Office says personal data protection in AI projects is regulated by legislation aligned with European standards, especially the GDPR, while the Commission says adoption of legislation to fully align with the GDPR is still pending.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: Against the single EU alignment ask of 2025, the responding AI legislation and AI strategy are still proposed, and the adopted ICT strategy and signed Antenna grant do not supply alignment or enforcement; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is alignment with the AI Act and the enforcement structures it needs, none of which yet exists. National sources confirm the absence (machine-translated audit, capped at Medium), and the audit's statement that data protection law is aligned with the GDPR conflicts with the Commission's statement that full alignment is pending, which is left unresolved.

Direction of travel: The EU requirement first appears in 2025 (AI Act alignment and enforcement structures) and the only later EU item, in 2026, concerns the AI Factory Antenna, so there is no repeated EU wording to compare; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Separately, national sources show the gap is older than the EU ask: a 2024 government plan mentions AI as a future need, and the 2025 audit traces a stalled strategy to a 2021 working group, but these are one-year snapshots rather than a trend. The value therefore means new as an EU requirement, not new as a national gap.

Priority: The rating rests only on the EU layer: one body-text invitation in the 2025 report to align fully with the AI Act, plus a 2026 readout that encourages outreach and does not mention the Act. It is not a benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, is absent from the 2025 Chapter 10 key recommendations and is not repeated, so it cannot be High; Medium reflects a requirement central to the AI theme with thin support. The much larger national audit, strategy and research evidence (over 200 of 229 items, mostly from a few documents) describes the gap but was given no weight here.

Tractability: Drafting is within government control, with the EU Act as a template and AI legislation already listed in an adopted action plan, but enforcement structures need a designated authority, specialist staff and funding, across several bodies. The record is weak: one working group meeting since 2021, a digital assistant no longer functioning and no line of accountability between the ministry and the innovation fund, though a data protection law gives some base and an EU-funded Antenna grant is signed. This leans on machine-translated national evidence (capped at Medium), and the audit's finding that no public sector project has been implemented sits against its report of the Buki platform at a state university, a difference of scope it does not explain.

Open questions
  • The State Audit Office says data protection in AI projects is governed by law aligned with the GDPR, while the Commission says full GDPR alignment is still pending, and this confirmed conflict is left unresolved pending a comparison of the law against the GDPR (MKD-GOV-2025-011-0156; MKD-EU-2025-001-0064).
  • The success of the AI pilot in the 112 emergency service is insufficient_evidence, and measured data on response times or call handling would be needed to judge it (MKD-GOV-2025-011-0165; MKD-EU-2024-001-0093).
  • Key evidence comes from the machine-translated State Audit Office report and digital strategy, capped at Medium confidence, so checking the Macedonian originals or finding independent English sources would strengthen the assessment (MKD-GOV-2025-011-0089; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0207).
  • The audit finds that no public sector AI project has been implemented while also reporting the Buki platform at a state university, and a clarification of scope from the audit office would settle whether these differ only in scope (MKD-GOV-2025-011-0093; MKD-GOV-2025-011-0067).

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission has asked every year from 2020 to 2026 for the Public Revenue Office to extend or keep expanding e-services for taxpayers, alongside better business processes and compliance risk management (MKD-EU-2020-001-0140; MKD-EU-2025-001-0151; MKD-EU-2026-003-0012). The Commission reports that the Office issues pre-filled annual returns through its electronic personal tax platform and names the e-Tax system and the e-VAT application as working e-services; all three are assessed as in practice (MKD-EU-2020-001-0143; MKD-EU-2025-004-0122; MKD-EU-2022-006-0026). The Commission states that e-Tax simplified tax reporting, assessed as worked with Medium attribution though no measure is given; for e-VAT, success and attribution are insufficient_evidence (MKD-EU-2022-006-0026; MKD-EU-2023-006-0028). The electronic tax administration and e-invoicing remain at the planning and draft legislation stage, in machine-translated plan items capped at Medium confidence (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0201; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0237; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0202). The validated assessment is partly_addressed, with priority Medium, direction of travel persistent and tractability High.

EU requirement

The request has changed very little. From 2020 to 2022 the Commission asked the country to develop a new integrated IT tax model or system, improve risk management and further extend e-services for taxpayers (MKD-EU-2020-001-0140; MKD-EU-2021-001-0112; MKD-EU-2022-001-0115). In 2023 it said the Public Revenue Office still had to replace its fragmented IT system with an integrated one and continue to expand e-services (MKD-EU-2023-001-0163). From 2024 the annual reports speak of continuing the process of expansion of e-services and no longer name the integrated IT system in that sentence, although the February 2025 screening report still asks for it (MKD-EU-2024-001-0104; MKD-EU-2025-001-0151; MKD-EU-2026-003-0012; MKD-EU-2025-004-0121). The 2021 report recorded some progress through upgraded e-tax services (MKD-EU-2021-001-0110).

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The Commission still asks in 2026 for expansion, while e-Tax, e-VAT and pre-filled returns are proposed as in practice and the electronic tax administration only as proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals, and the Macedonian-language plan items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence. What remains is a wider range of taxpayer e-services, with the electronic tax administration still at project documentation and draft legislation stage.

Direction of travel: The Commission's recommendation to keep extending taxpayer e-services recurs every year from 2020 to 2026 with almost no change, moving only from 'further extend' to 'continue the process of expansion', so the default applies; this is one repeated view, not independent evidence. The Chapter 16 'Some progress' wording of 2021 is context only and was not decisive.

Priority: The recommendation is repeated across more than three reports, but taxpayer e-services are one clause beside business processes, the integrated IT system and compliance risk, so the issue is not central to Chapter 16 or the theme. The Reform Agenda's e-services step names the fiscal sector only as an example, and this was not read as a payment condition on this issue.

Tractability: One agency leads, working platforms exist, and upgrades are reported by the Commission, so progress depends little on other actors or the EU. A caution is that the source does not say how far further e-services depend on the integrated IT system, which has been outstanding since 2020.

Open questions
  • No usage figures are given for the e-Tax system, the e-VAT application or pre-filled returns, so data on the number and share of filings made online would be needed to judge results beyond the Commission's statements (MKD-EU-2022-006-0026; MKD-EU-2025-004-0122).
  • The Commission's statement that e-Tax simplified tax reporting gives no measure and the 2023 wording repeats 2022, so evidence such as filing time or compliance cost data would be needed to confirm the result independently (MKD-EU-2022-006-0026; MKD-EU-2023-006-0028).
  • Sources differ on whether an integrated tax information system exists to be expanded or has still to be built, with the Commission asking in 2025 for a new system and an international report referring to expanding the existing one, and a clear statement from the Public Revenue Office or the Commission would settle it (MKD-EU-2025-004-0121; MKD-IO-2024-001-0095).
  • Progress on the electronic tax administration and e-invoicing is known only from machine-translated plan rows, and evidence of the project documentation, the law and the systems being delivered would be needed (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0201; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0237; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0202).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is raising e-market use from 350 to the required 800 awards in 2026, wider take-up of e-catalogues, and the data analysis the Commission asked for in 2023.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to complete its e-procurement platform, build the confidence of contracting authorities to use the e-market for low-value contracts, and develop the red flag system and data analysis to report on possible corruption or bid-rigging (MKD-EU-2020-001-0093; MKD-EU-2023-003-0137; MKD-EU-2023-003-0123). The Commission states that the electronic procurement system works efficiently and that its use is obligatory, and the system is assessed as in_practice (MKD-EU-2024-001-0055; MKD-EU-2025-001-0092; MKD-EU-2023-003-0112). The e-market was launched in 2022, and the Commission reports 70 awards through it in 2022 and 258 in 2023 (MKD-EU-2022-001-0056; MKD-EU-2023-001-0075; MKD-EU-2024-001-0056). The Commission credits e-appeals and the electronic system with a high level of transparency, assessed as worked, though not with a fall in corruption (MKD-EU-2023-003-0121). What remains is raising e-market use to the 800 awards set as a Reform Agenda payment condition for 2026, wider use of e-catalogues and stronger data analysis (MKD-EU-2024-007-0001; MKD-EU-2023-003-0114). The gap is assessed as partly_addressed. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is improving and tractability is High.

EU requirement

The Commission's wording has moved from building the platform to getting it used. In 2020 it asks for the e-procurement platform to be completed and the portal upgraded with new modules, and in 2021 for adoption of the bylaw on the low-value e-marketplace (MKD-EU-2020-001-0093; MKD-EU-2020-001-0094; MKD-EU-2021-001-0045). In 2023 the focus turns to use: the Commission finds poor use of the e-market, little interest from procuring entities and e-catalogues only just starting, and asks for further development of the red flag system and data analysis (MKD-EU-2023-003-0137; MKD-EU-2023-001-0074; MKD-EU-2023-003-0114; MKD-EU-2023-003-0123). From 2024 the requirement becomes a quantified payment condition of at least 800 e-market awards in 2026, while the Commission repeats that the core system functions efficiently (MKD-EU-2024-007-0001; MKD-EU-2025-001-0092).

Country response

  • Electronic System for Public Procurement (ESPP) · in practice

  • ESPP electronic archive and e-complaints modules · in practice
  • e-appeals function of the ESPP · in practice
  • Red flag system in the ESPP · in practice
  • ESPP COVID-19 markers and data feed · implemented
  • SAC processing system · insufficient evidence
  • Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) · proposed
  • Integrated tax information system (ITIS) · proposed

Implementation and outcome
  • Red flag system in the ESPP: Use of 'red flags' in the e-procurement portal contributed to stronger administrative control by the Public Procurement Bureau. · success worked, attribution Medium
  • e-appeals function of the ESPP: The remedy system has benefited significantly from the introduction of e-appeals. · success worked, attribution Medium
  • e-appeals function of the ESPP: Introducing e-appeals made the submission and conduct of appeals efficient and transparent. · success worked, attribution High
  • e-appeals function of the ESPP: North Macedonia achieved high transparency in public procurement through its electronic procurement and e-appeals system. · success worked, attribution Medium
  • Electronic System for Public Procurement (ESPP): North Macedonia achieved high transparency in public procurement through its electronic procurement and e-appeals system. · success worked, attribution Medium
Conflicting evidence
  • The Commission 2020 report says the e-appeals section was still being developed, while North Macedonia reports that e-appeals became fully operational on 1 April 2019.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The system is working and the e-market and red-flag modules are proposed as in practice, with the low-value bylaw at insufficient evidence; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is raising e-market use from 350 to the required 800 awards in 2026, wider take-up of e-catalogues, and the data analysis the Commission asked for in 2023.

Direction of travel: The e-market moved from development in 2021 to launch in 2022, and awards rose from 70 in 2022 to 258 in 2023 (259 in the Reform Agenda, a minor difference of count), with 350 small-value transactions in 2024, though that item does not name the e-market. The Commission's finding of poor use in 2023 is not repeated later, and no later item shows change on e-catalogues or red-flag analysis. The Chapter 5 'Limited progress' wording of 2022 and 2025 is context only and was not decisive.

Priority: E-market use is a Reform Agenda payment condition, which meets one limb of the High test, but the Commission finds the core system functions efficiently and the shortfall concerns low-value contracts and add-on modules. It is therefore not central to Chapter 5 or the theme, and the proposal rests on that reading of centrality.

Tractability: One bureau runs a platform that is already obligatory for all contracting authorities, awards rose about fivefold in two years, and a payment is attached to the target. The main limit is the confidence of contracting authorities, and the target is still more than double the 2024 count.

Open questions
  • The Commission's 2020 report says the e-appeals section was still being developed, while North Macedonia reports it fully operational from 1 April 2019, and this confirmed conflict remains unresolved pending a dated record from the Bureau or the State Appeals Commission (MKD-EU-2020-001-0096; MKD-EU-2023-003-0115).
  • The 2024 figure of 350 small-value transactions does not name the e-market, so e-market award data for 2024 to 2026 would be needed to judge progress towards the 800 target (MKD-EU-2025-001-0091).
  • Whether the bylaw on the low-value e-marketplace was ever adopted is insufficient_evidence, and the official gazette or a Bureau statement would settle it (MKD-EU-2021-001-0046).
  • No evidence after 2023 shows how e-catalogues or the red flag system are used, and usage figures or Commission findings on data analysis would be needed (MKD-EU-2023-003-0122; MKD-EU-2023-003-0114).

Current direction of travel
persistent Validated
Current priority
Medium Validated

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is full online information and procedures under the Services Directive, especially on licences, and a transparent electronic register of all regulated professions.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to upgrade its point of single contact so that service providers have full online information and procedures under the Services Directive, especially on licences, and to set up a transparent electronic register of all regulated professions (MKD-EU-2024-001-0071; MKD-EU-2025-001-0113; MKD-EU-2025-001-0206). The Commission reports that the point of single contact was upgraded and reached 312 online services by September 2025, and the platform is assessed as implemented, not in practice, as no source gives evidence of use (MKD-EU-2025-001-0111; MKD-EU-2025-001-0112). The Commission still finds it not fully in line with the acquis, and states that the list and register of regulated professions are yet to be put in place (MKD-EU-2025-003-0124; MKD-EU-2025-003-0120). Whether the new Central Register portal has simplified procedures is insufficient_evidence (MKD-EU-2025-003-0122). The gap is assessed as partly_addressed. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is persistent and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's wording has changed little in substance. On the register of regulated professions, it asks in 2020 and 2021 for data validation to be finalised, notes in 2022 that a transparent list is missing, and from 2024 states that the list and register are "yet to be put in place", adding in November 2025 a call for a transparent electronic register of all regulated professions (MKD-EU-2020-001-0171; MKD-EU-2021-001-0074; MKD-EU-2022-001-0077; MKD-EU-2024-001-0073; MKD-EU-2025-001-0206). On the point of single contact, it moves from asking for one to be established in 2021 to asking, in nearly identical words in 2023, 2024 and 2025, for www.uslugi.gov.mk to be upgraded to meet the Services Directive, with the November 2025 report adding licences and business procedures (MKD-EU-2021-001-0124; MKD-EU-2023-001-0103; MKD-EU-2024-001-0071; MKD-EU-2025-003-0123; MKD-EU-2025-001-0113).

Country response
  • Law on Central Registry · adopted
  • Law no. 215/2021 One Stop Shop · adopted
  • Point of Single Contact · implemented
  • 2024-2025 action plan on the Services Directive · insufficient evidence
  • New portal of the Central Register · implemented
  • Upgrade of the e-services portal for issuing licences to business activities · insufficient evidence
  • Central Register as Point of Single Contact · implemented
Implementation and outcome
  • New portal of the Central Register: The new Central Register portal has simplified procedures for businesses. · success insufficient evidence, attribution insufficient evidence
Conflicting evidence
  • The Reform Agenda gives 264 e-services as the 2024 baseline, while the Commission report gives 124 services accessible online by September 2024.
  • Commission documents of June and October 2024 give 246 services available online and 124 services accessible online by September 2024.
  • In the same screening report North Macedonia says the Central Register operates as the Point of Single Contact, while the Commission identifies the Point of Single Contact as www.uslugi.gov.mk.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: A contact point platform exists and is proposed as implemented, but the Commission finds it not fully in line with the acquis and the list and register still absent; these statuses are themselves proposals. Sources conflict on which body is the contact point (Central Register or uslugi.gov.mk), and the 238 (2023) and 124 (2024) service counts are not explained. What remains is full online information and procedures under the Services Directive, especially on licences, and a transparent electronic register of all regulated professions.

Direction of travel: The requirement that the point of single contact be upgraded to meet the Services Directive is unchanged in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and the register of regulated professions moves from unfinished data validation (2020, 2021) to 'yet to be put in place' (2024, 2025). The contact point itself did advance, from early stage in 2021 to a platform with 312 online services in 2025, so the two limbs of this issue point different ways. No Chapter 3 scale rating is linked to the issue, and the scale would be context only.

Priority: The point of single contact was a key recommendation only in 2021, 2022 and 2023, with the 2021 item flagged as doubtful for the theme, and later Commission items on it and the 2025 item on the register of professions are in body text, so the requirement is repeated. It is a sector portal under the Services Directive and is not central to the digital government theme, which is the same reading applied to taxpayer e-services (RI-TEC-005) and e-procurement (RI-TEC-006). Its importance to Chapter 3 is not the test for a technology issue, and no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition names it.

Tractability: The platform is in place and service numbers have been added, which favours progress on the contact point. Against that, sectoral laws must be aligned, the responsible body is unclear between sources, and a register of all professions needs input from many regulators.

Open questions
  • In the same screening report the country says the Central Register is the point of single contact while the Commission names www.uslugi.gov.mk, and this confirmed conflict needs a statement of the legal designation to settle it (MKD-EU-2025-003-0121; MKD-EU-2025-003-0123).
  • Sources give conflicting counts of online services for 2024 (264, 246 and 124) and the fall from 238 in 2023 is unexplained, so a consistent series with stated definitions would be needed (MKD-GOV-2024-001-0092; MKD-EU-2024-009-0014; MKD-EU-2024-001-0072; MKD-EU-2023-001-0104).
  • Whether the 2024-2025 action plan on the Services Directive and the business licence portal upgrade were completed is insufficient_evidence, and government reports on these measures would settle it (MKD-EU-2023-001-0102; MKD-EU-2021-001-0073).
  • No source reports how far service providers actually use the online services, so usage data for the portal would be needed to judge results.

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is interoperability with Health Insurance Fund data, an end to paper referrals, and alignment with the eHealth acquis.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to make eHealth data interoperable with Health Insurance Fund data, to improve the eHealth appointment system and to align its legislation with the EU acquis on eHealth (MKD-EU-2025-001-0018; MKD-EU-2025-001-0213; MKD-EU-2025-003-0183). The country runs the Moj Termin eHealth system, which the Commission says was introduced in 2013 and helped to significantly reduce waiting times, and it launched the MyHealth mobile application in 2023 and later added new modules (MKD-EU-2022-006-0041; MKD-EU-2023-001-0208; MKD-EU-2025-001-0123). The Commission's statement on waiting times is judged as worked with Medium attribution, but it gives no figures. The Commission also finds that referrals were still on paper in 2024 and that the system is not yet interoperable with Health Insurance Fund data (MKD-EU-2024-001-0077; MKD-EU-2025-001-0124). Planned connections to the population register and the digital wallet remain proposed (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0235; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0236). The validated assessment is that the gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is Medium and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

In 2022 and 2023 the Commission's wording is identical: Moj Termin should be extended to primary care doctors (MKD-EU-2022-006-0042; MKD-EU-2023-006-0040). In 2024 the focus shifts to the system's shortcomings, as the Commission finds that referrals are still done on paper and that the application is not interoperable with Health Insurance Fund data (MKD-EU-2024-001-0077). The 2025 screening report adds a new element, stating that national legislation is not aligned with the EU acquis on eHealth (MKD-EU-2025-003-0174; MKD-EU-2025-003-0176; MKD-EU-2025-003-0183). In November 2025 interoperability with Health Insurance Fund data is raised to a key recommendation, and the Commission adds that the appointment system needs to be improved (MKD-EU-2025-001-0018; MKD-EU-2025-001-0124; MKD-EU-2025-001-0213).

Country response
9 interventions and their validated implementation status
  • Law on Personal Data Protection 2020 · in practice
  • Law on Health Care · adopted
  • Law on Healthcare Records · adopted
  • Reform 2.2.2.3 Widen the offer of public e-services · proposed
  • Moj Termin eHealth system · in practice
  • MojTermin connection with the digital wallet (A 3.2.8.5) · proposed
  • MojTermin connection with the population register (A 3.2.8.1) · proposed
  • MyHealth mobile application · implemented
  • Platform for appointments and traceability of health data (ERP measure 4) · insufficient evidence
Implementation and outcome
  • Moj Termin eHealth system: The MojTermin system improved patient management, patient experience and follow up through dashboards, a booking system and e-services. · success mixed, attribution Low
  • Moj Termin eHealth system: The Moj Termin eHealth system, introduced in 2013, helped to significantly reduce waiting times. · success worked, attribution Medium
  • Moj Termin eHealth system: The Moj Termin eHealth system, introduced in 2013, helped to significantly reduce waiting times. · success worked, attribution Medium
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The 2025 report still asks for interoperability, and the responding steps are proposed (population register and wallet connections) or at insufficient evidence (platform for traceability), none naming Health Insurance Fund data; these statuses are themselves proposals and the plan items are machine translated, capped at Medium confidence. The paper-referral finding and the screening's account of a tool holding referrals are a noted difference, not a conflict, since storing data and issuing on paper can both be true, but practice needs checking. What remains is interoperability with Health Insurance Fund data, an end to paper referrals, and alignment with the eHealth acquis.

Direction of travel: Commission wording on extending Moj Termin is the same in 2022 and 2023, and non-interoperability with Health Insurance Fund data recurs in 2024 and 2025, with non-alignment of legislation added in the 2025 screening. Functional upgrades in 2023 and 2025 are real but have not changed the stated shortfall. The default for three unchanged reports is not strictly triggered, and no Chapter 28 scale rating was decisive.

Priority: The Commission's requirement is repeated in 2024 and 2025 and raised to a recommendation in 2025, but it is a narrow part of Chapter 28 and only recently prominent. The Reform Agenda's e-services step names the health sector as an example, and this was not read as a payment condition on this issue.

Tractability: A central tool and one lead ministry exist and upgrades are reported, but interoperability needs the Health Insurance Fund as well, and alignment with the acquis needs legislation. National plan and World Bank items add that the platform needs upgrading and users need digital literacy; the plan item is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence.

Open questions
  • The Commission's 2024 finding that referrals are on paper sits beside the screening report's account of a central tool that stores referrals; this is a noted difference rather than a confirmed conflict, and evidence on how referrals are issued in practice would settle it (MKD-EU-2024-001-0077; MKD-EU-2025-003-0176).
  • The platform for appointments and traceability of health data is rated insufficient_evidence because no item after 2023 says what became of it, so a later government or Commission account would settle its status (MKD-EU-2022-006-0043; MKD-EU-2023-006-0041).
  • The reported reduction in waiting times rests on Commission statements with no figures, and ITU's statement on improved patient management is flagged as a possible misread, so waiting-time data from the health system would settle the size of the effect (MKD-EU-2022-006-0041; MKD-IO-2022-002-0074).
  • The planned connections of Moj Termin to other systems come from a machine-translated national strategy capped at Medium confidence, and none names Health Insurance Fund data, so a plan or report covering that link would settle whether the core requirement is being addressed (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0235; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0236; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0156).

Current direction of travel
persistent Validated
Current priority
Medium Validated

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is digital communication with courts generally, videoconferencing for hearings, and connections between other justice institutions, including the Ministry of Justice and the prosecution.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission has asked North Macedonia to digitalise its justice system, including digital communication with courts, videoconferencing for hearings and connections between justice IT systems (MKD-EU-2020-001-0030; MKD-EU-2024-001-0035; MKD-EU-2025-001-0058). The Commission's 2026 Rule of Law report describes the digital interconnection of the Administrative Court, the Higher Administrative Court and other public bodies as a key advancement that enables electronic exchange of data and documents (MKD-EU-2026-006-0002). Its implementation status is validated as implemented, but this rests on one statement with no usage data, and no outcome is recorded, so no result can be claimed. The Luris software, which North Macedonia said in 2023 needed connecting between the Ministry of Justice and the Public Prosecutor's Office, is at insufficient_evidence (MKD-EU-2023-003-0130). The validated unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium, a tentative rating.

EU requirement

The Commission's wording has narrowed over time. In 2020 it said that IT connections needed to be prioritised, including full digitalisation of cases and summoning, with training for judges and judicial staff (MKD-EU-2020-001-0030). In 2023 it said that digitalisation, including interoperability between IT systems, and coordination between the relevant authorities needed to improve (MKD-EU-2023-003-0089). In 2024 and 2025 it used identical wording, calling for more efforts to digitalise the justice system, in particular communication with courts and videoconferencing for court hearings (MKD-EU-2024-001-0035; MKD-EU-2025-001-0058). No Commission item from 2021 or 2022 is in the evidence.

Country response
  • Digital interconnection between the Administrative Court, the Higher Administrative Court and other public bodies · implemented
  • Luris software · insufficient evidence
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The administrative courts' interconnection is proposed as implemented and the Commission calls it a key advancement, but no status is recorded for the judicial IT strategies and council, and Luris is at insufficient evidence; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is digital communication with courts generally, videoconferencing for hearings, and connections between other justice institutions, including the Ministry of Justice and the prosecution.

Direction of travel: Commission calls for digital court communication and connected IT recur in 2020, 2023, 2024 and 2025, with identical wording in the last two, and the single 2026 item on the administrative courts cannot alone show a change of direction. Support is thin (eight items, none for 2021 or 2022, most flagged theme_doubtful), and no chapter scale was decisive.

Priority: The recommendation is repeated, including in the 2024 and 2025 reports, within the important Chapter 23 area, but digital communication is a supporting part of judicial reform and no benchmark or payment condition on it appears in the input. Evidence is thin and most items are flagged theme_doubtful.

Tractability: One interconnection shows that progress is possible, but several independent justice institutions must act together, and the Commission points to weak coordination. The evidence on actors and resources is thin, so this rating is tentative.

Open questions
  • Whether the administrative courts' interconnection is used and has improved coordination is not settled, because the only evidence is one statement without usage data (MKD-EU-2026-006-0002); system usage figures or case processing data would settle it.
  • Whether the Luris software works and was connected between the Ministry of Justice and the Public Prosecutor's Office is at insufficient_evidence (MKD-EU-2023-003-0130); a later Commission or government statement on its status would settle it.
  • Progress on digital communication with courts generally and on videoconferencing for hearings is not shown by any intervention item, so government or Commission reporting on these specific measures is needed.
  • The evidence base is thin, with eight items, none for 2021 or 2022 and most flagged theme_doubtful, so further Commission or justice sector sources would strengthen the direction of travel judgement.
Evidence

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is updating the plan's targets, settling the aid rules and financing the backhaul network; the reported non-use of the Western Balkans Investment Framework for infrastructure sits beside technical assistance from it for a feasibility study, which appears to be a difference between study and construction but should be checked.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its national broadband targets with the Digital Decade, to align further with EU rules on aid for broadband deployment, and to strengthen the capacity of the public broadcasting enterprise mandated to build optical infrastructure (MKD-EU-2025-004-0011; MKD-EU-2025-003-0192; MKD-EU-2025-001-0132). The National Operational Broadband Plan remains in force, but the Commission reported its implementation slowed in 2021 and further delayed in 2022 (MKD-EU-2025-001-0130; MKD-EU-2021-001-0087; MKD-EU-2022-001-0090). The country states that its targets will be aligned with the Digital Compass and that a mapping study is in preparation (MKD-EU-2025-004-0018; MKD-EU-2025-004-0026). A feasibility study for a national transport optical network has started, but no network is built (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0039; MKD-GOV-2024-003-0003). The Broadband Competence Office, in machine translation, reports that none of the three measures towards the 100 Mbps target was implemented (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0038). The validated judgements are priority Medium, direction of travel persistent, unresolved gap partly_addressed and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

In 2020 the Commission recorded some progress, citing ICT strategy preparations and the new Broadband Competence Office (MKD-EU-2020-001-0103). In 2022 and 2023 its assessments found a strategic approach to broadband access lacking, the 2023 one adding national strategic investment and the targets of the National Broadband Plan (MKD-EU-2022-006-0040; MKD-EU-2023-006-0038). The 2025 screening made the requirement more specific: align the targets with the Digital Decade and align further on State aid for broadband, while noting that the Western Balkans Investment Framework and the Connecting Europe Facility had not been used for infrastructure (MKD-EU-2025-004-0011; MKD-EU-2025-003-0192; MKD-EU-2025-004-0025). In November 2025 the Commission added the need to strengthen the public broadcasting enterprise (MKD-EU-2025-001-0132). No 2026 Commission item addresses the framework.

Country response
20 interventions and their validated implementation status
  • Law on Electronic Communications 2025 · adopted
  • National long-term ICT Strategy (unadopted drafts) · insufficient evidence
  • ICT Development Strategy SMART/MK: 2030 · adopted
  • National Cybersecurity Strategy 2018-2022 · reversed
  • National Operational Broadband Plan 2019-2029 · implemented
  • National Broadband Competence Office · in practice

  • Accelerated integration: EU Broadband Competence Offices network · proposed
  • 5G roll-out · in practice

  • Guidelines for submitting data for newly built electronic communications network and accompanying assets · adopted
  • Web GIS Collector · insufficient evidence
  • National transport optical network · proposed
  • Alignment of national broadband targets with the Digital Compass · proposed
  • Feasibility study for mapping existing and planned broadband coverage · proposed
  • Mandate of the public broadcasting enterprise to build optical infrastructure and provide broadband access · adopted
  • Market monitoring and trend analysis mechanisms · proposed

  • State aid for backhaul optical infrastructure and NGA networks in white and grey zones · proposed
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Conflicting evidence
  • Two 2022 sources give different periods for the same plan: ITU names the National Operational Broadband Plan as 2019-2029 and the Commission names the national broadband operational plan as 2019-2023.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The latest EU items ask for targets aligned with the Digital Decade, further alignment on aid for broadband and stronger capacity at the public broadcasting enterprise. The compared statuses are proposals for G6: the ICT strategy with its 2030 goals is adopted, but its alignment with the Digital Decade is the government's own statement in machine translation, and target alignment, State aid and the national network are only proposed, while none of the three plan measures towards the 100 Mbps target has been implemented. What remains is updating the plan's targets, settling the aid rules and financing the backhaul network; the reported non-use of the Western Balkans Investment Framework for infrastructure sits beside technical assistance from it for a feasibility study, which appears to be a difference between study and construction but should be checked.

Direction of travel: The plan's implementation slowed in 2021 and was further delayed in 2022, a strategic approach to broadband was found lacking in 2022 and 2023, the plan was said only to remain valid in 2024 and 2025, and the 2025 screening asks for its targets to be aligned with the Digital Decade; the 2020 chapter-wide some progress is context and was not decisive. Newer Reform Agenda investment and a feasibility study are plans and do not yet show change, so this is not improving, and no 2026 Commission item addresses the framework. Sources conflict on the plan's period, with ITU and the 2025 report giving 2019-2029 and the 2022 and 2024 reports giving 2019-2023, which affects how far the delays can be measured against targets.

Priority: The requirement is repeated by the EU, in the 2022 and 2023 assessments and the 2025 screening, but it is not named in a benchmark, a Reform Agenda payment step or the chapter's key recommendations. The Reform Agenda plan does call the broadband network the most important digital project, but as an investment, so the issue matters for the theme with thinner support than the legal and regulator issues.

Tractability: Updating targets is within the government's control and a mapping study is the stated first step, but financing the network depends on outside funders, State aid alignment and a public enterprise whose capacity the Commission says needs strengthening. Past progress is weak: the plan was delayed in 2021 and 2022, and the national broadband competence office, reported in machine translation, finds none of three measures implemented. The financing figures come from a table flagged as possibly misread, so they support only the general point that funding is mixed.

Open questions
  • Sources conflict on the plan's period, with ITU and the 2025 report giving 2019 to 2029 and the 2021, 2022 and 2024 reports giving 2019 to 2023, and the adopted plan text would settle how delays should be measured against its targets (MKD-IO-2022-002-0019; MKD-EU-2021-001-0087; MKD-EU-2022-001-0090; MKD-EU-2024-001-0083; MKD-EU-2025-001-0130).
  • The claim that the 2030 ICT strategy goals are aligned with the Digital Decade, and the Office's finding on the three unimplemented measures, rest on machine-translated government text capped at Medium confidence, so official English versions or the Office's report itself would be needed (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0017; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0004; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0038).
  • The reported non-use of the Western Balkans Investment Framework sits beside its technical assistance for the network feasibility study, which appears to separate study from construction but should be checked against funding records (MKD-EU-2025-004-0025; MKD-GOV-2024-003-0002).
  • The financing figures for the network come from a table flagged as possibly misread, so a confirmed financing plan is needed before the funding gap can be assessed (MKD-GOV-2024-003-0003).

RI-TEC-016 · Technology & AIValidated

Open data and re-use of public sector information incomplete

Priority MediumDirection persistentGap partly addressedTractability High

Assessment: The Commission asks that all institutions regularly provide and update data, that proactive disclosure of datasets be encouraged, and that North Macedonia step up alignment with the Open Data Directive.

2025 report: 0 items2026 update: Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package
2025 → 2026 comparison
Latest evidence
2025-10-20, Стратегија за развој на ИКТ СМАРТ/МК 2030 (ICT Development Strategy SMART/MK 2030) MKD-GOV-2025-004-0234
2025 position

The 2025 report has no in-scope item on this issue; the alpha position rests on other sources (see the evidence below).

2026 update

Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package

What changed

Not yet assessed. Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package

Current direction of travel
persistent Validated
Current priority
Medium Validated

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is alignment with the Open Data Directive and regular publication by institutions on a functioning portal.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks that all institutions regularly provide and update data, that proactive disclosure of datasets be encouraged, and that North Macedonia step up alignment with the Open Data Directive (MKD-EU-2020-001-0013; MKD-EU-2022-001-0011; MKD-EU-2025-004-0109). The Law on the Use of Public Sector Data is adopted, and the government reports 580 datasets from 74 institutions on the open data portal by December 2022 (MKD-EU-2025-004-0086; MKD-GOV-2023-002-0011). Amendments to align the law with the Directive have been with a working group since 2023 and are assessed as proposed (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0012; MKD-EU-2025-004-0084; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0198). The Commission stated in 2020 that access to public information improved thanks to the transparency strategy that set up the portal, assessed as a mixed success with Medium attribution, because the State Audit Office reports that the portal has not functioned since early 2025 owing to procurement problems, in machine-translated text (MKD-EU-2020-001-0012; MKD-GOV-2025-011-0030). The portal's status is therefore unclear. The gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, the priority is Medium and tractability is High.

EU requirement

The requirement has moved from practice to legal alignment. In 2020 the Commission recorded some progress on transparency, including an operational open government data portal, and asked all institutions to provide and update data regularly so the system works smoothly (MKD-EU-2020-001-0001; MKD-EU-2020-001-0013). In 2022 it asked for proactive disclosure of information and datasets to be further encouraged (MKD-EU-2022-001-0011). In 2025 the screening reports state that the Law on the Use of Public Sector Data is partially aligned with the Open Data Directive, ask the country to invest further efforts in aligning with it, and ask it to monitor other EU data legislation (MKD-EU-2025-004-0082; MKD-EU-2025-004-0109; MKD-EU-2025-005-0013). The matter does not appear among the Commission's main findings.

Country response

Implementation and outcome
  • 2019-2021 Transparency Strategy: Access to public information improved thanks to the 2019-2021 transparency strategy, which includes an open government data portal. · success mixed, attribution Medium
Conflicting evidence
  • The SMART/MK strategy of October 2025 states that the country is not aligned with the Open Data Directive, while the Commission's screening report published in February 2025 states that the Law on the Use of Public Sector Data is partially aligned with it.
  • The ITU profile of February 2022 lists the Law on the Security of Network and Information Systems as an existing enabler, while the Commission's 2022 report says the draft of that law has not yet been adopted.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: A Law on the Use of Public Sector Data is adopted and 580 datasets were reported by 2022, but the amendments and the Directive alignment action are proposed only, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is alignment with the Open Data Directive and regular publication by institutions on a functioning portal. Sources conflict, since the October 2025 strategy says the country is not aligned while the screening report's country presentation says partially aligned, so both are the country's own statements (the conflict register attributes the second to the Commission), and the Commission's own finding is only that further efforts are needed; the machine-translated items are capped at Medium confidence.

Direction of travel: Commission items ask for regular data updates in 2020 and more proactive disclosure in 2022, while amendments for Open Data Directive alignment were in preparation in 2023 and still with a working group in 2025; the 2020 sub-area rating of some progress concerns transparency more widely and, like the chapter scale, was not decisive. The State Audit Office reports that the portal has not functioned since early 2025, in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, and the country's published screening presentation describes the portal favourably without addressing this. That outage rests on one source with no later status, so it does not yet support worsening, though confirmation would.

Priority: The Commission raises the matter in 2020, 2022 and 2025, but not in its main findings, so it is a repeated requirement that is not central. Most items here come from one national audit and one national strategy, and that volume was not treated as importance.

Tractability: One ministry leads, the portal and 74 publishing institutions already existed by 2022, and the stated cause of the outage is a procurement problem rather than a structural one. Progress does not depend on the EU, although the amendments have been slow since 2023. This view leans on machine-translated items capped at Medium confidence, and government reporting on datasets does not itself show success.

Open questions
  • The country's February 2025 presentation describes the portal as in line with best practice while the State Audit Office says it has not functioned since early 2025, in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, and a later source on whether the portal was restored would settle both its status and whether the 2020 result has lasted (MKD-EU-2025-004-0083; MKD-GOV-2025-011-0030).
  • The October 2025 strategy states that the country is not aligned with the Open Data Directive while the February 2025 screening report states that the law is partially aligned, a confirmed conflict that a Commission table of concordance or alignment assessment would settle (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0087; MKD-EU-2025-004-0086).
  • The ITU profile of 2022 lists the network and information security law as an existing enabler while the Commission's 2022 report says the draft had not been adopted, a confirmed conflict that dated legislative records would settle (MKD-IO-2022-002-0058; MKD-EU-2022-001-0098).
  • There are no data on use of the portal or on how regularly institutions update their datasets after 2022, which portal statistics or an Open Data Maturity assessment would provide (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0011; MKD-GOV-2025-011-0040).

Data protection authority lacks independence and resources

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is autonomy in hiring and spending, and funding and staff that match the Agency's tasks.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission has found since 2021 that North Macedonia's Personal Data Protection Agency depends on government for staff and funds, and in 2025 said its capacities need to improve (MKD-EU-2021-001-0032; MKD-EU-2024-001-0040; MKD-EU-2025-001-0211). The Agency drafted amendments to secure its autonomy in April 2022, but its own machine-translated report says adoption had still not started in 2025 (MKD-GOV-2026-002-0032; MKD-GOV-2026-002-0037). The Commission reports staff falling from 21 to 20, and the Agency reports 18 at the end of 2024 and 17 at the end of 2025 (MKD-EU-2023-001-0036; MKD-EU-2024-001-0041; MKD-GOV-2025-010-0011; MKD-GOV-2026-002-0016). The Commission also found no director appointed from January 2025 (MKD-EU-2025-001-0204). The 2020 data protection law is validated as in_practice, with weak application, and no outcome is recorded. What remains is autonomy in hiring and spending, and resources matching the Agency's tasks. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is worsening. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's concern has stayed the same in substance but its findings have become more severe. In 2021 it described the Agency's dependence on the Ministry of Finance and another ministry for recruitment and organisation (MKD-EU-2021-001-0032). In 2022 and 2023 it said understaffing seriously harmed implementation, and in 2023 it called for alignment on the Agency's independence and noted that it is not financially autonomous (MKD-EU-2022-001-0023; MKD-EU-2023-001-0028; MKD-EU-2023-001-0037). In 2024 it said the Agency lacks independence to hire staff and spend its budget (MKD-EU-2024-001-0040). In 2025 it added that no director had been appointed and called for improved capacities, while a general communication asked for sustained resources and stronger independence (MKD-EU-2025-001-0204; MKD-EU-2025-001-0211; MKD-EU-2025-002-0002).

Country response
  • Law on Personal Data Protection 2020 · in practice
  • Draft Law amending the Law on Personal Data Protection · proposed
  • Law transposing the EU Law Enforcement Directive (planned) · proposed
  • Strategy for the Implementation of the Right to Personal Data Protection 2025-2030 · implemented
  • Agency observer status at the European Data Protection Board · implemented
  • National Programme for the Adoption of the Acquis · implemented
  • Personal Data Protection Agency oversight of security services under the Law on Interception of Communications · implemented
  • TAIEX support for the Strategy · implemented
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The amendments meant to secure the Agency's autonomy are proposed only, and the 2025-2030 strategy's proposed status of implemented means only that work has begun, with the Commission finding it was held back; these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is autonomy in hiring and spending, and funding and staff that match the Agency's tasks. Statements that the Agency is independent describe its legal status, while the Commission and the Agency's own reports describe its operating dependence, so this is a noted difference and not a conflict.

Direction of travel: The Commission moved from dependence on ministries in 2021 and understaffing in 2022 and 2023 to staff falling further in 2024 and no director in 2025, with reported staff of 21, then 20, then 18 at the end of 2024 and 17 at the end of 2025. The last two counts are the Agency's own, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, but they run the same way as the Commission's findings. The Agency reports a director from 5 December 2025, which is a later date than the Commission's finding, not a conflict, and the chapter scale was not decisive.

Priority: The Commission has raised the Agency's dependence and capacity from 2021 to 2025 and an independent authority is central to the data theme, but the requirement appears only in body text, in 2023 and 2025 and in the 2025 communication in general terms. It is in no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, and the main findings do not mention it, so it is a central requirement with thin support, on the same footing as RI-TEC-019.

Tractability: Only a few domestic actors are needed, a draft has existed since April 2022 and the budget is small. Past progress is poor, however: the draft has not moved, the Ministry of Finance repeatedly refused funds or returned the employment plan, and the director post took most of 2025 to fill. The Agency's reports are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and they are a party's account of its own constraints.

Open questions
  • The latest staffing, budget and funding refusals rest on the Agency's own machine-translated reports capped at Medium confidence, some at Low (MKD-GOV-2025-010-0012; MKD-GOV-2026-002-0016; MKD-GOV-2026-002-0017); Commission or Ministry of Finance figures would settle them.
  • Whether the director reported by the Agency from December 2025 has improved its functioning is not shown, so later Commission assessments of the Agency's operation are needed.
  • How far the 2025 to 2030 data protection strategy has been carried out is unclear, since the Commission says implementation was held back (MKD-EU-2025-001-0069); a progress report against the strategy's actions would settle it.
  • No outcome evidence shows whether the Agency's supervision improves compliance (MKD-GOV-2026-002-0040), so data on compliance rates over time are needed.

RI-TEC-019 · Technology & AIValidated

Data protection authority not consulted and its advice not followed

Priority MediumDirection worseningGap openTractability Medium

Assessment: In every report from 2020 to 2025 the Commission finds that the Personal Data Protection Agency is not systematically consulted on sectoral and implementing laws and that its recommendations are not fully followed, and in 2023 and 2024 that Parliament does not follow up its reports.

2025 report: 4 items2026 update: Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package
2025 → 2026 comparison
Latest evidence
2026-04-06, Годишен извештај за 2025 година (Personal Data Protection Agency annual report 2025) MKD-GOV-2026-002-0109
2025 position

  • Parliament amended the data protection law to allow personal data transfers to NATO countries, without consulting the data protection agency. MKD-EU-2025-001-0065
  • The government removed the data protection agency from the bodies that must be consulted before sectoral laws and regulations are adopted. MKD-EU-2025-001-0068
  • The factors listed held back implementation of the Personal Data Protection Strategy 2025-2030. MKD-EU-2025-001-0069
  • There was no progress on coordination, communication and responsiveness to data protection agency recommendations. MKD-EU-2025-001-0070

What changed

Current direction of travel
worsening Validated
Current priority
Medium Validated

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is systematic consultation of the Agency on sector and implementing laws, follow-up of its recommendations and follow-up of its reports in Parliament.

View detail
Assessment in brief

In every report from 2020 to 2025 the Commission finds that the Personal Data Protection Agency is not systematically consulted on sectoral and implementing laws and that its recommendations are not fully followed, and in 2023 and 2024 that Parliament does not follow up its reports (MKD-EU-2020-001-0049; MKD-EU-2022-001-0028; MKD-EU-2023-001-0041; MKD-EU-2024-001-0045). In 2025 the Commission reported, as a concerning development, that the government removed the Agency from the list of bodies that must be consulted, and that Parliament amended the data protection law to allow transfers to NATO countries without consulting it (MKD-EU-2025-001-0068; MKD-EU-2025-001-0065). The Agency's own report, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, confirms the deletion in the Government's Rules of Procedure of 31 December 2024 (MKD-GOV-2025-010-0035). The Commission found no progress on responsiveness to the Agency's recommendations in 2025 (MKD-EU-2025-001-0070). No intervention is recorded as responding to the issue. The validated assessment is open, with priority Medium, direction of travel worsening and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

The finding was stable in substance from 2020 to 2024, with small shifts in wording. In 2020 and 2021 the Commission said recommendations were not fully implemented and not all laws were submitted before adoption, noting some progress in 2021 (MKD-EU-2020-001-0049; MKD-EU-2021-001-0031). From 2022 it said the Agency was not systematically consulted on sectoral or implementing legislation and its advice not always taken on board, and the 2023 screening report called for more systematic consultation (MKD-EU-2022-001-0028; MKD-EU-2023-003-0077; MKD-EU-2023-001-0032; MKD-EU-2024-001-0043). In 2023 and 2024 it added the lack of parliamentary follow-up and weak responsiveness (MKD-EU-2023-001-0041; MKD-EU-2024-001-0044; MKD-EU-2024-001-0045). In 2025 the wording changed: the Commission reported the Agency's removal from the mandatory consultation list and no progress on responsiveness (MKD-EU-2025-001-0068; MKD-EU-2025-001-0070).

Country response
  • Law on Personal Data Protection (amendment on transfers to NATO countries) · adopted
  • Strategy for the Implementation of the Right to Personal Data Protection 2025-2030 · implemented
  • Amendments to the Electoral Code on biometric voter identification · adopted
  • 'StopKorona' contact tracing application · insufficient evidence
  • Removal of the PDPA from the mandatory consultation list · implemented
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Conflicting evidence
  • For 2022 the Commission's 2023 Report gives reprimands in 10 cases, while the country presentation in the 2023 screening report gives reprimands in 4 cases for the same period.
  • For 2021 the Commission's 2023 Report gives reprimands in 17 cases, while the country presentation in the 2023 screening report gives reprimands in 4 cases.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: No intervention is recorded as responding to this issue, and the one recent measure, the removal from the consultation list, has a proposed status of implemented and runs the opposite way; these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is systematic consultation of the Agency on sector and implementing laws, follow-up of its recommendations and follow-up of its reports in Parliament.

Direction of travel: The Commission's finding was essentially unchanged from 2020 to 2024, with some progress noted in 2021, and then changed in 2025, when the Government removed the Agency from the mandatory consultation list and Parliament amended the law without consulting it. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2025 matches this issue and the chapter scale was not decisive. The Agency's report confirms the deletion in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, and its count of opinions (5 for 2024, 15 for 2025) does not show that consultation improved.

Priority: The finding recurs in every report from 2020 to 2025 and the Commission called the 2025 removal concerning, but the 2023 list of areas requiring alignment does not include it and it is not in the main findings. It is a repeated requirement that supports the authority's role rather than being central to the theme, and reviewers may weigh the 2025 reversal differently.

Tractability: Restoring the consultation duty is a change to the Government's own Rules of Procedure, which the Agency identifies precisely and which depends on no one outside the country. Getting ministries to follow advice and Parliament to act on reports is harder, and the Government removed the duty recently. The Agency's items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

Open questions
  • The Agency's counts of opinions given on draft laws, 5 in 2024 and 15 in 2025, come from machine-translated reports and do not show whether consultation improved, so data on the share of relevant draft laws sent to the Agency would settle this (MKD-GOV-2025-010-0036; MKD-GOV-2026-002-0064).
  • No source shows whether ministries now act on the Agency's recommendations or whether Parliament has debated its reports, and records of that follow-up would be needed to judge these parts of the requirement (MKD-EU-2024-001-0044; MKD-EU-2024-001-0045).
  • Two confirmed conflicts on the number of reprimands stand unresolved, with the Commission's 2023 report giving 10 cases for 2022 and 17 for 2021 against 4 in each year in the country's screening presentation, and the Agency's own annual figures would settle them (MKD-EU-2023-001-0038; MKD-EU-2023-003-0072; MKD-EU-2023-003-0068).
  • Whether the Government will restore the consultation duty in Article 24 of its Rules of Procedure, as the Agency proposes in a machine-translated report, is not known, and an amendment to the Rules would show it (MKD-GOV-2026-002-0063).
Evidence

45 in-scope items from 11 sources; 21 machine translated. Evidence limit: relies partly on machine translation
