Full brief: issue_brief_RI-TEC-019.md

RI-TEC-020 · Technology & AIValidated

Weak compliance with data protection rules

Priority MediumDirection persistentGap openTractability Low

Assessment: The Commission finds that, in general, data controllers do not implement the Law on Personal Data Protection, calls for awareness raising in all sectors, and reports in 2025 that breaches are becoming more frequent, some go unreported and state bodies show low awareness.

2025 report: 2 items2026 update: Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package
2025 → 2026 comparison
Latest evidence
2026-04-06, Годишен извештај за 2025 година (Personal Data Protection Agency annual report 2025) MKD-GOV-2026-002-0108
2025 position

2 items from the Commission's 2025 report on North Macedonia.

  • Data breaches are becoming more frequent and some are not reported as the law requires. MKD-EU-2025-001-0071
  • State administrative bodies still show low awareness of data protection and insufficient IT protection of personal data. MKD-EU-2025-001-0072
2025 report quotes (2)

“Data breaches are increasingly frequent, and some are not reported in line with the legal requirements.”

MKD-EU-2025-001-0071 · European Commission, North Macedonia 2025 Report, SWD(2025) 753 final, 2025, p. 38 · evidence confidence High

“There is still a low awareness of data protection and insufficient IT protection of personal data in the state administrative bodies.”

MKD-EU-2025-001-0072 · European Commission, North Macedonia 2025 Report, SWD(2025) 753 final, 2025, p. 38 · evidence confidence High

2026 update

Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package

What changed

Not yet assessed. Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package

Current direction of travel
persistent Validated
Current priority
Medium Validated

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is for controllers, including public bodies, to apply the law, report breaches and face effective sanctions.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission finds that, in general, data controllers do not implement the Law on Personal Data Protection, calls for awareness raising in all sectors, and reports in 2025 that breaches are becoming more frequent, some go unreported and state bodies show low awareness (MKD-EU-2023-001-0033; MKD-EU-2023-001-0044; MKD-EU-2025-001-0071; MKD-EU-2025-001-0072). The law is assessed as in_practice, and the Agency reports 196 supervisions in 2025, with 121 decisions ordering violations to be removed (MKD-GOV-2026-002-0040; MKD-GOV-2026-002-0053). The Agency adopted a new rulebook on security of processing and took over an e-classroom platform, but the data protection officer network and the sanction amendments remain proposed (MKD-GOV-2025-010-0085; MKD-GOV-2025-010-0077; MKD-GOV-2024-006-0056; MKD-GOV-2024-006-0024). Success on awareness and on the e-classroom is insufficient_evidence, and no independent evidence shows changed behaviour. The Agency reports its Misdemeanour Commission disrupted by staff departures (MKD-GOV-2026-002-0060). Much Agency evidence is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence. The gap is assessed as open. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is persistent and tractability is Low.

EU requirement

The Commission's concern has stayed the same while its findings have become broader. In 2020 it notes that misdemeanour fines for data protection breaches remain low (MKD-EU-2020-001-0173; MKD-EU-2020-001-0047). In 2023 it states more generally that controllers do not implement the law and that there is a strong need for awareness raising and a culture of data protection in all sectors (MKD-EU-2023-001-0033; MKD-EU-2023-001-0044). By November 2025 it adds that breaches are increasingly frequent, some are not reported as the law requires, and state administrative bodies still show low awareness and insufficient IT protection of personal data (MKD-EU-2025-001-0071; MKD-EU-2025-001-0072). Compliance has not been a named key recommendation in these reports.

Country response
20 interventions and their validated implementation status
  • Law on Personal Data Protection 2020 · in practice
  • Strategy for the Implementation of the Right to Personal Data Protection 2025-2030 · implemented
  • Law on financial companies · adopted
  • Central Population Register · in practice
  • Interoperability platform (MIM) · in practice
  • Rulebook on Security of Personal Data Processing · adopted
  • Rulebook on carrying out supervision (amendment) · adopted
  • Rulebook on notifying personal data breaches (supplement) · adopted
  • Communication Strategy 2026-2030 · proposed
  • Communication Strategy 2027-2032 · proposed
  • E-classroom web platform · implemented
  • Interoperability platform for data protection officers · proposed
  • Network of data protection officers · proposed
  • Agency memoranda of cooperation · implemented
  • Amendment of sectoral legislation on misdemeanour sanctions · proposed
  • Documents on certification and codes of conduct · proposed
  • National Programme for the Adoption of the Acquis · implemented
  • Personal Data Protection Agency oversight of security services under the Law on Interception of Communications · implemented
  • Supervisory activities on the position of data protection officers · proposed
  • TAIEX support for the Strategy · implemented
Implementation and outcome
  • Law on financial companies: Recent changes to the Law on financial companies led to more complaints (to the data protection agency). · success insufficient evidence, attribution Medium
  • Law on Personal Data Protection 2020: The Agency states that awareness of controllers and citizens has significantly increased through implementation of the Law on Personal Data Protection. · success insufficient evidence, attribution insufficient evidence
  • E-classroom web platform: A continuous rise is recorded in the number of e-classroom users completing the data protection quizzes. · success insufficient evidence, attribution insufficient evidence
Conflicting evidence
  • For 2022 the Commission's 2023 Report gives reprimands in 10 cases, while the country presentation in the 2023 screening report gives reprimands in 4 cases for the same period.
  • For 2021 the Commission's 2023 Report gives reprimands in 17 cases, while the country presentation in the 2023 screening report gives reprimands in 4 cases.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The security rulebook has been adopted and the e-classroom is proposed as implemented, but the data protection officer network and the sanction amendments are proposed only, no independent evidence shows changed behaviour, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is for controllers, including public bodies, to apply the law, report breaches and face effective sanctions. Reprimand counts conflict between the Commission's report (10 for 2022, 17 for 2021) and the country presentation (4 for each), and low notification numbers (19 for 2022, 11 for 2025) are read by the Agency as under-reporting, so they do not conflict with the Commission's finding of more frequent breaches.

Direction of travel: The Commission called fines low in 2020, found in general that controllers do not implement the law in 2023, and in 2025 found low awareness and more frequent breaches, some unreported; the 2022 statement of progress on compliance sits in the paragraph on one body's supervision, so it is not a general trend. The Agency's statements of significant progress concern its own application of the framework, a noted difference from the Commission's sub-area rating, and supervision counts measure enforcement rather than compliance. The chapter scale was not decisive, and the machine-translated Agency findings are capped at Medium confidence.

Priority: Compliance is central to whether the law has effect, but the Commission's direct findings on it are thin, mainly 2023 and 2025, and it is not a named key recommendation. The large volume of items comes from the Agency's own reports and was not treated as importance.

Tractability: Progress needs behaviour to change across very many public and private controllers, and it depends on an Agency whose supervision and misdemeanour capacity is shrinking. The evidence shows awareness work and enforcement activity, but no sustained improvement in compliance. The Agency's items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

Open questions
  • For 2021 and 2022 the Commission's report gives 17 and 10 reprimands while the country presentation gives 4 for each year, and this confirmed conflict needs the Agency's annual reports for those years to settle it (MKD-EU-2023-001-0038; MKD-EU-2023-003-0068; MKD-EU-2023-003-0072).
  • Success of the law on awareness and of the e-classroom is insufficient_evidence because the only evidence is the Agency's own reporting, so independent awareness surveys or user figures would be needed (MKD-GOV-2024-006-0003; MKD-GOV-2026-002-0104).
  • No evidence measures compliance among controllers over time, and repeated supervision findings on comparable controllers, or independent audits, would show whether behaviour is changing (MKD-GOV-2026-002-0045; MKD-GOV-2026-002-0043).
  • Whether the sectoral amendments on misdemeanour sanctions and the data protection officer network have been delivered is not shown, and later Agency or Commission reports would settle it (MKD-GOV-2024-006-0024; MKD-GOV-2024-006-0056).

RI-TEC-027 · Technology & AIValidated

Interoperability framework not aligned with EU

Priority MediumDirection persistentGap openTractability High

Assessment: The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its national interoperability framework and legislation with the European Interoperability Framework and the Interoperable Europe Act.

2025 report: 2 items2026 update: Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package
2025 → 2026 comparison
Latest evidence
2025-11-04, North Macedonia 2025 Report, SWD(2025) 753 final MKD-EU-2025-001-0137

  • The country should continue aligning with the European Interoperability Framework and the Interoperable Europe Act. MKD-EU-2025-001-0049
  • North Macedonia should continue aligning with the European Interoperability Framework and the Interoperable Europe Act. MKD-EU-2025-001-0137

“Efforts need to continue to align with the European Interoperability Framework and the Interoperable Europe Act.”

“North Macedonia should continue its efforts to align with the European Interoperability Framework, and the Interoperable Europe Act.”

MKD-EU-2025-001-0137 · European Commission, North Macedonia 2025 Report, SWD(2025) 753 final, 2025, p. 74 · evidence confidence High

2026 update

Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package

What changed

Not yet assessed. Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package

Current direction of travel
persistent Validated
Current priority
Medium Validated

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is a national framework shown to be aligned with the current European framework and with the Interoperable Europe Act.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align its national interoperability framework and legislation with the European Interoperability Framework and the Interoperable Europe Act (MKD-EU-2024-001-0091; MKD-EU-2025-001-0137). North Macedonia stated at the 2023 screening that its framework was aligned with European Interoperability Framework 2.0 and that it planned further alignment with the updated version, and its 2025 digital strategy, in machine translation, says care will be taken to align (MKD-EU-2023-003-0012; MKD-EU-2023-003-0009; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0140). The State Audit Office found in 2022 that no study supported the ministry's claim to follow that framework (MKD-GOV-2022-004-0069). The alignment itself is rated proposed, and no aligned text is shown. The Commission links outdated legislation with under-use of the interoperability platform as an obstacle to digital services (MKD-EU-2023-001-0014). The validated assessment is that the gap is open, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is Medium and tractability is High.

EU requirement

The requirement has barely changed. In July 2023 the screening report asks North Macedonia to align with the latest European Interoperability Framework and to seek alignment with the proposed Interoperable Europe Act (MKD-EU-2023-003-0013; MKD-EU-2023-003-0015). The 2023 and 2024 reports repeat in identical words that the country should align with both the framework, latest revised in 2017, and the Interoperable Europe Act, and the 2024 report specifies national legislation (MKD-EU-2023-001-0015; MKD-EU-2024-001-0027; MKD-EU-2024-001-0091). In 2025 the wording becomes a call to continue efforts to align with both, which reports no result (MKD-EU-2025-001-0049; MKD-EU-2025-001-0137).

Country response
  • Interoperability platform (MIM) · in practice
  • Alignment with the European Interoperability Framework · proposed
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The only responding intervention, alignment with the framework, has proposed status at the freeze, and this status is itself a proposal, so no aligned text is shown. Items are in tension and this is not recorded in the contradictions file: the 2023 screening says the framework is aligned with framework 2.0, while the 2023 report asks for alignment with the 2017 revision and the audit (machine translated, capped at Medium) found no study confirming alignment. What remains is a national framework shown to be aligned with the current European framework and with the Interoperable Europe Act.

Direction of travel: The Commission repeated the recommendation to align with the European Interoperability Framework and the Interoperable Europe Act in near-identical terms in 2023, 2024 and 2025, which sets the persistent default under the rules. The 2025 wording ('efforts need to continue') reports no result. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive.

Priority: This is a repeated EU requirement across three reports, but no item places it in a benchmark, a Reform Agenda payment condition or the main findings list of a report. It supports the interoperability theme, yet the Commission itself treats use of the platform as the wider obstacle.

Tractability: The mechanism is legal and framework alignment, which one ministry can lead without depending on others. The caution is the record: the recommendation has not moved in three years and the plan is still only stated in a government strategy.

Open questions
  • The 2023 screening states that the national framework is aligned with European Interoperability Framework 2.0, while the Commission asks for alignment with the latest framework and the audit found no alignment study; this tension is not recorded as a confirmed conflict, and a Commission assessment of the national framework text would settle it (MKD-EU-2023-003-0012; MKD-EU-2023-001-0015; MKD-GOV-2022-004-0069).
  • The only evidence of current national plans is a machine-translated strategy capped at Medium confidence, so a draft or adopted legal text aligning the framework would settle whether work has started (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0140).
  • The Commission treats under-use of the interoperability platform as part of the obstacle, so evidence on whether alignment changes how many institutions exchange data would show whether alignment matters in practice (MKD-EU-2023-001-0014).

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is a functional criminal records system with ECRIS analysis done, the technical adaptations for the Visa Information System, an IT structure compatible with Eurodac on accession, and the funding for them.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission's 2023 screening report sets out what North Macedonia needs to connect to EU justice and home affairs systems: an analysis of the means to implement ECRIS, significant technical adaptations and funding for the Visa Information System, and an IT structure compatible with Eurodac by accession (MKD-EU-2023-003-0091; MKD-EU-2023-003-0095; MKD-EU-2023-003-0096). It found no functional system yet to share criminal records (MKD-EU-2023-003-0090). Frontex prepared a Masterplan for interoperable IT systems, but it is validated only as proposed, as no source shows the systems being built (MKD-EU-2022-001-0044; MKD-EU-2024-001-0049). The Commission reports that the roll-out of CT SIENA increased opportunities for counter-terrorism exchange, judged to have worked, but this narrow outcome says nothing about readiness for EU large-scale systems (MKD-EU-2020-001-0060). The country's request for Eurodac access before accession has no basis in EU law (MKD-EU-2023-003-0103). The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is insufficient_evidence. Priority is Medium and tractability is Low.

EU requirement

No change can be traced. The requirements on ECRIS, the Visa Information System and Eurodac come essentially from one 2023 screening report, so there is no earlier or later Commission wording on the same points to compare (MKD-EU-2023-003-0091; MKD-EU-2023-003-0095; MKD-EU-2023-003-0096). The same report also asks for adequate funding of the border sector, including IT systems in line with EU standards (MKD-EU-2023-003-0099). Commission items from 2021, 2022 and 2024 describe the Frontex biometric plan rather than restating a requirement, so they do not show whether the requirement has moved (MKD-EU-2021-001-0122; MKD-EU-2022-001-0044; MKD-EU-2024-001-0049).

Country response
  • Frontex Masterplan for IT systems for mixed migration flows · proposed
  • Biometric registration system that follows the Eurodac model · insufficient evidence
  • CT SIENA · implemented
  • secure communication link for information exchange (SIENA) · implemented
  • Alignment with the entry-exit system and ETIAS · proposed
  • Request for information exchange and access to Eurodac before accession (accelerated integration) · proposed
Implementation and outcome
  • CT SIENA: Rolling out CT SIENA increased opportunities for direct and secure counter-terrorism information exchange. · success worked, attribution High
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: Responding interventions are proposed or lack a clear status, and these statuses are themselves proposals; part of the requirement falls due only at accession, and Eurodac access before accession has no legal basis, so 'open' does not by itself mean late. What remains is a functional criminal records system with ECRIS analysis done, the technical adaptations for the Visa Information System, an IT structure compatible with Eurodac on accession, and the funding for them.

Direction of travel: The requirements on ECRIS, the Visa Information System and Eurodac come essentially from one 2023 screening report, so there is no repeated or changed wording to compare. The 2021, 2022 and 2024 items concern a Frontex biometric plan and do not show whether readiness moved. The chapter scale was context only and not decisive.

Priority: The systems matter for Chapter 24, but support is thin: one screening report states the requirements and no item shows a benchmark, Reform Agenda condition or repeated key recommendation. This is central with thin support.

Tractability: Progress depends on the EU: the Commission says EU law gives candidates no Eurodac access, and the country reports it cannot build to Eurodac without the technical specifications and struggles to secure funding. The Frontex plan offers a route for border systems, but no item shows it being carried out.

Open questions
  • Whether readiness has improved since 2023 is insufficient_evidence, because no later Commission item repeats the screening requirements; a later Commission assessment of ECRIS, Visa Information System and Eurodac readiness would settle it.
  • The status of the planned biometric registration system following the Eurodac model is insufficient_evidence, as the only item dates from 2021 (MKD-EU-2021-001-0122); a later Commission or Frontex report would settle it.
  • No source shows whether the Frontex Masterplan is being carried out or funded (MKD-EU-2024-001-0049), so implementation and budget reporting on the planned systems is needed.
  • Whether a functional criminal records system and the ECRIS analysis now exist is not shown after 2023 (MKD-EU-2023-003-0090), so Ministry of Justice or Commission reporting is needed.
Evidence

Not ready to connect to other EU sectoral information systems

Assessment: The Commission asks North Macedonia to prepare several sectoral systems to connect with EU information systems, notably the civil protection system CECIS, the Business Registers Interconnection System (BRIS), EU taxation IT systems and the own resources reporting system.

What changed

Not yet assessed. Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package

Current direction of travel
persistent Validated
Current priority
Medium Validated

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is connection to those systems, noting that BRIS and the Internal Market Information System also depend on EU decisions or accession.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to prepare several sectoral systems to connect with EU information systems, notably the civil protection system CECIS, the Business Registers Interconnection System (BRIS), EU taxation IT systems and the own resources reporting system (MKD-EU-2025-005-0019; MKD-EU-2025-003-0150; MKD-EU-2025-001-0026; MKD-EU-2025-001-0190). The Commission reported steps towards the CECIS connection from 2020 to 2022 but no progress in 2023, and says in 2025 that the link is still not made, while the country plans it by 2027 (MKD-EU-2020-001-0157; MKD-EU-2022-001-0127; MKD-EU-2023-001-0181; MKD-EU-2025-001-0177; MKD-EU-2025-005-0018). Some areas show more: the Commission states that alignment with the EU Digital COVID Certificate was completed in 2021 and that the country has achieved high-level integration of EU food safety IT tools (MKD-EU-2021-002-0002; MKD-EU-2025-006-0003). Most other responses are proposed, and BRIS and the Internal Market Information System also depend on EU decisions or accession (MKD-EU-2025-003-0190; MKD-EU-2025-005-0003). The validated assessment is open, with priority Medium, direction of travel persistent and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

The requirement has grown by sector rather than changed in wording. The CECIS link has been raised since 2020, and the Commission moved from reporting steps towards it to no progress in 2023, an issue for immediate attention in 2024 and still needing to be done in 2025 (MKD-EU-2020-001-0157; MKD-EU-2023-001-0181; MKD-EU-2024-001-0110; MKD-EU-2025-005-0019). Business register readiness for BRIS appears from 2023 in the same words, and the 2025 screening report adds that alignment on structured, machine-readable data is needed (MKD-EU-2023-001-0109; MKD-EU-2024-001-0075; MKD-EU-2025-003-0150). Preparing for interoperability with EU taxation IT systems, and the own resources IT system and reporting access, entered in 2024 and are repeated in 2025, when the own resources items are described as still pending (MKD-EU-2024-001-0017; MKD-EU-2024-001-0111; MKD-EU-2025-001-0026; MKD-EU-2025-001-0190).

Country response
12 interventions and their validated implementation status
  • Electronic freight transport information system (eFTI) · proposed
  • Connection to the Common Emergency Communication and Information System (CECIS) · proposed
  • Alignment with the EU Digital COVID Certificate system · implemented
  • Internal Market Information System access · proposed
  • IT system for managing A and B accounts · proposed
  • Phytosanitary information system · implemented
  • SDMX-based architecture for data transmission to Eurostat · implemented
  • TRACES module for phytosanitary certification · proposed
  • Upgrade of the EMCS including the System for the Exchange of Excise Data (SEED) · proposed
  • Decision 2020/263 on computerising the movement and surveillance of excise goods · proposed
  • Interconnection with the Business Registers Interconnection System (BRIS) prior to accession · proposed
  • Transfer of vehicle registration data to the European Vehicle Register · proposed
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The latest Commission items still ask for the CECIS link, business register readiness, tax interoperability and the own resources system, and the responding interventions are nearly all proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. North Macedonia states it is technically ready for BRIS, but the Commission says machine-readable data alignment is still needed. What remains is connection to those systems, noting that BRIS and the Internal Market Information System also depend on EU decisions or accession.

Direction of travel: The sectors do not share one trend, so this rests on those with repeated wording: CECIS from 2020 to 2025 (with 'no progress' in 2023), the business registers link from 2023 to 2025, and EU tax systems and own resources in 2024 and 2025. Some areas are better, including the 2021 COVID certificate alignment and food safety tools in 2025, which the residual label hides. The chapter scales were context only and not decisive.

Priority: Each requirement is repeated, and tax interoperability reaches the main findings in 2024 and 2025 and CECIS is an issue for immediate attention in 2024, but none is central to the theme as a whole and the only Reform Agenda references are railway and freight outputs in the government's text. This is a residual group spanning several chapters, so the rating is an average that would differ by sector.

Tractability: The sectors differ: food safety shows active use of EU tools, the CECIS link looks technically limited yet has not been finished in over five years, and BRIS requires full company law alignment and access to groups open only to Member States and EEA countries. The rating is a mid-point, not a uniform finding.

Open questions
  • North Macedonia states it is technically ready to interconnect with BRIS, while the Commission says alignment on machine-readable data and with EU company law is still needed, and a Commission assessment of the register against those provisions would settle readiness (MKD-EU-2025-003-0138; MKD-EU-2025-003-0150; MKD-EU-2025-003-0145).
  • The country's use of SDMX for transmitting data to Eurostat and the synchronisation of its phytosanitary information system rest on its own presentation, and independent confirmation from the Commission would be needed to show use (MKD-EU-2023-003-0124; MKD-EU-2025-006-0007).
  • The priority and tractability ratings are averages over a residual group of sectors that differ, so sector-by-sector evidence, for example on the CECIS connection planned by 2027, would be needed to judge each link separately (MKD-EU-2025-005-0018; MKD-EU-2025-006-0004).
  • No item shows how the EU Digital COVID Certificate alignment was used after August 2021, so later evidence of use would be needed to say more than that alignment was completed (MKD-EU-2021-002-0002).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is actual use of these channels and SME adoption beyond basic technologies, as the Commission still reported low digitalisation in 2026.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission finds that digitalisation of the economy remains low and restrains the competitiveness of domestic companies, and it asks North Macedonia to support companies through the European Digital Innovation Hub and to take part actively in Digital Europe Programme calls (MKD-EU-2026-003-0003; MKD-EU-2025-001-0029; MKD-EU-2025-014-0005). The country signed an association agreement to the Digital Europe Programme in June 2023, and the Commission reports that the first European Digital Innovation Hub was set up (MKD-EU-2023-001-0143; MKD-EU-2025-001-0157). No item shows actual participation in calls. SME vouchers, a support portal and a grant mechanism appear only as plans in a machine-translated strategy (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0240; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0239; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0159). The Commission notes that SME digital adoption has accelerated but remains uneven and largely basic (MKD-EU-2025-001-0085). No outcome is linked to any intervention. The validated assessment is that the gap is partly_addressed, the direction of travel is persistent, priority is Medium and tractability is Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission's wording is close to unchanged. From 2020 to 2023 it states that digitalisation of the economy is advancing but remains low compared with the EU (MKD-EU-2020-001-0070; MKD-EU-2021-001-0039; MKD-EU-2022-001-0050; MKD-EU-2023-001-0068). In 2024 and 2025 the wording becomes advancing slowly, and economic governance documents link low digitalisation and weak innovation to weak business competitiveness (MKD-EU-2024-001-0050; MKD-EU-2025-001-0082; MKD-EU-2024-009-0003; MKD-EU-2025-012-0003). In 2025 the Commission adds more specific asks, on active participation in Digital Europe calls and support to companies through the European Digital Innovation Hub, and notes accelerated but uneven SME adoption (MKD-EU-2025-014-0005; MKD-EU-2025-001-0029; MKD-EU-2025-001-0085). In 2026 it still describes digitalisation as low (MKD-EU-2026-003-0003).

Country response
12 interventions and their validated implementation status
  • ICT Development Strategy SMART/MK: 2030 · adopted
  • Smart Specialisation Strategy S3-MK 2024-2027 · adopted
  • Association Agreement to the Digital Europe Programme · adopted
  • Digital Innovation Hubs (national) · proposed
  • Support and subsidy system for digital transformation of agriculture · proposed
  • Action Plan of the Industrial Strategy 2022-2023 (programme for digital and green transitions) · adopted
  • Competitiveness for Jobs and Economic Transformation (C-JET) grant · insufficient evidence
  • Financial support and grant mechanism for digital transformation · proposed
  • Digital service vouchers for SMEs (A 4.1.1.2) · proposed
  • Measure 4.1.3 Capacity to use the Digital Europe programme · proposed
  • Project to measure the digitalisation level of construction companies · proposed
  • Digital support portal for SMEs (A 4.1.1.1) · proposed
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The latest EU asks concern support to companies through the innovation hub and active use of Digital Europe calls; the hub is set up and the association agreement signed, while vouchers, the support portal and the grant mechanism are proposed, and these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is actual use of these channels and SME adoption beyond basic technologies, as the Commission still reported low digitalisation in 2026.

Direction of travel: The Commission's wording is close to unchanged across reports: advancing but low in 2020 to 2023, advancing slowly in 2024 and 2025, and low in 2026, with one 2025 note that SME adoption has accelerated but stays uneven and basic. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. The 54.5% website figure repeats across reports and was not treated as new evidence, and the 3% and 19.7% online sales figures use different populations, so they show no trend.

Priority: The finding is repeated in most years, largely in economic governance documents, but it has few specific recommendations; the only key recommendation found is the 2025 hub item, and no benchmark or payment condition names it in the input. It is therefore a repeated EU concern that is not central to accession steps.

Tractability: Government can fund and steer support, and EU programmes and a first hub already exist, but results depend on many small firms' demand, skills and finance. Past effort is small and not evaluated: EUR 0.5 million budgeted in 2023, and the strategy itself says there has been no support mechanism for projects of greater national importance; that source is machine translated and capped at Medium.

Open questions
  • No item shows North Macedonia taking part in Digital Europe Programme calls or how many companies the innovation hub has supported, so participation and hub activity data would settle whether these channels are used (MKD-EU-2025-014-0005; MKD-EU-2025-001-0157).
  • The online sales figures of 3% of SMEs and 19.7% of enterprises use different populations and the 54.5% website figure is repeated across reports, so a consistent time series on enterprise digital adoption would be needed to show any trend (MKD-IO-2022-002-0079; MKD-GOV-2024-010-0003; MKD-EU-2021-001-0043; MKD-EU-2023-001-0071).
  • The C-JET grant to assess SME digital needs is rated insufficient_evidence, so a World Bank report on its status and findings would settle it (MKD-IO-2024-001-0109).
  • The evidence on planned support schemes and on the absence of a support mechanism comes from a machine-translated strategy capped at Medium confidence, so programme documents or budget data showing schemes in operation would strengthen the record (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0084; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0240).

Digital single market rules not aligned

Assessment: The Commission asks North Macedonia to align with the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act, to align fully with electronic commerce rules and to harmonise its legislation with the Geo-blocking Regulation, and its screening report finds no alignment with the platform-to-business regulation.

Current direction of travel
persistent Validated
Current priority

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is the alignment itself for all these acts, plus full alignment on electronic commerce.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align with the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act, to align fully with electronic commerce rules and to harmonise its legislation with the Geo-blocking Regulation, and its screening report finds no alignment with the platform-to-business regulation (MKD-EU-2025-001-0138; MKD-EU-2025-004-0065; MKD-EU-2025-004-0029). The country states it plans to align with the platform-to-business and geo-blocking rules by 2027 and with the Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act by 2028, and it has asked to join the related EU expert groups, which the Commission will explore (MKD-EU-2025-004-0030; MKD-EU-2025-004-0032; MKD-EU-2025-004-0092; MKD-EU-2025-004-0101; MKD-EU-2025-004-0108). The only delivered step is training from European services on the Digital Services Act in June 2024 (MKD-EU-2024-001-0094). No draft law and no outcome evidence are reported. The validated judgements are priority Medium, direction of travel persistent, unresolved gap open and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

From 2021 to 2023 the Commission's concern was the slow pace of e-commerce (MKD-EU-2021-001-0108; MKD-EU-2022-006-0028; MKD-EU-2023-006-0029). From 2023 it asked for alignment with the Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act to be stepped up, first to give businesses predictability, then in 2024 alongside equal access to online services, and in November 2025 as something the country still needs to do (MKD-EU-2023-001-0139; MKD-EU-2024-001-0092; MKD-EU-2025-001-0138). The 2025 screening widened the requirement: it found legislation largely aligned with the e-Commerce Directive but not aligned with the platform-to-business or geo-blocking rules, and asked for full alignment on electronic commerce and geo-blocking (MKD-EU-2025-004-0027; MKD-EU-2025-004-0029; MKD-EU-2025-004-0031; MKD-EU-2025-004-0065).

Country response
11 interventions and their validated implementation status
  • Strategy for the Implementation of the Right to Personal Data Protection 2025-2030 · implemented
  • Accelerated integration: DMA, DSA, P2B and geo-blocking groups · proposed
  • Alignment with the Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act · proposed
  • Employment Action Plan 2021-2023 · insufficient evidence
  • Alignment with eIDAS 2.0, the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act · proposed
  • Alignment with the Geo-blocking Regulation (EU) 2018/302 · proposed
  • Alignment with the P2B Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 · proposed
  • Harmonisation of legislation in the context of digitisation processes · proposed
  • Towards a Feasible Implementation of the Digital Services Act in the Western Balkans (study) · implemented
  • Trainings from European services on the DSA · implemented
  • Transposition of acts resulting from the EU digital strategy · proposed
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The latest EU items still require alignment with the DSA, DMA and Geo-blocking Regulation, and the responding alignment measures are all proposed, with national targets of 2027 and 2028 and only training delivered; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is the alignment itself for all these acts, plus full alignment on electronic commerce. The country's report of being largely aligned with the e-Commerce Directive and the Commission's call to align fully differ in degree and speaker, and were not treated as closure.

Direction of travel: The ask to align with the Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act recurs with little change in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and e-commerce was described as slow in 2021, 2022 and 2023. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Growth figures for online transactions are country-reported, partly repeated and on differing bases, so they were not read as closing the issue.

Priority: The requirement is repeated in three reports and relates to binding acquis, but it sits in Chapter 10 body text, not in the 2024 or 2025 key recommendations, and is not named as a benchmark or payment condition in the input. It is therefore a repeated EU requirement that is not central under the criteria.

Tractability: The work is mainly legislative with EU texts as templates, a government timetable and a request for expert group participation, which depends partly on the Commission. No draft is reported and past progress is limited to training, and applying platform rules will need capacity that the input does not evidence.

Open questions
  • No draft law transposing any of these acts is reported, so a published draft or legislative programme entry would show whether the 2027 and 2028 targets are realistic (MKD-EU-2025-004-0028; MKD-EU-2025-004-0030).
  • The finding that legislation is largely aligned with the e-Commerce Directive and the call to align fully differ in degree and were not treated as closure, and a table of concordance for the e-commerce law would settle what is missing (MKD-EU-2025-004-0027; MKD-EU-2025-004-0065).
  • Growth figures for internet transactions are country-reported, partly repeated and on differing bases, so a consistent e-commerce statistical series would be needed to judge whether e-commerce is still slow (MKD-EU-2021-001-0107; MKD-EU-2022-006-0027).
  • The input does not show which authorities would apply platform rules or whether they have the capacity, and an institutional plan for enforcement would settle this (MKD-EU-2024-001-0094).

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is further alignment with Directive (EU) 2019/1151, including scrutiny of a company's object and verification of directors' appointment and disqualification.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission asks North Macedonia to align further with Directive (EU) 2019/1151 on the use of digital tools and processes in company law, including scrutiny of a company's object and verification of the appointment and disqualification of directors (MKD-EU-2025-003-0149; MKD-EU-2025-001-0015; MKD-EU-2025-001-0116). The country cites the Law on Trade Companies and the Law on Central Registry as regulating this area, both assessed as adopted (MKD-EU-2025-003-0187). The Commission states that company registration and filing can be carried out fully online through the Central Registry's one-stop shop, which is assessed as in_practice, and it finds a high level of alignment with disclosure requirements and digital tools (MKD-EU-2023-001-0108; MKD-EU-2025-001-0115; MKD-EU-2025-003-0142). No outcome has been assessed. What remains is the narrower set of legal amendments, with no draft reported. The gap is assessed as partly_addressed. Priority is Medium, direction of travel is persistent and tractability is High.

EU requirement

The Commission's wording is essentially unchanged. In 2021 and 2022 it states that further alignment is necessary with the 2019 acquis on digital tools and cross-border operations, and from 2023 to November 2025 the key recommendations ask for alignment on the use of digital tools and processes in company law, always bundled with cross-border operations and, in some years, shareholder engagement (MKD-EU-2021-001-0075; MKD-EU-2022-001-0078; MKD-EU-2023-001-0107; MKD-EU-2024-001-0010; MKD-EU-2025-001-0015). The ask becomes more specific from 2024, naming scrutiny of the company's object and checks on directors (MKD-EU-2024-001-0074; MKD-EU-2025-003-0149). The February 2025 screening report adds that alignment is already high, which narrows the remaining ask but does not show change over time (MKD-EU-2025-003-0142).

Country response
  • Law on Central Registry · adopted
  • Law on Trade Companies · adopted
  • Central Registry one-stop-shop online company registration · in practice
  • Online access to Central Registry company information · implemented
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Conflicting evidence
  • In 2025 North Macedonia states it is aligned with the acquis on the use of digital tools and processes in company law, while the Commission says further alignment on the use of digital tools and processes is necessary.
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: Fully online company registration is in practice and the Commission finds high alignment, on a status that is itself a proposal. What remains is further alignment with Directive (EU) 2019/1151, including scrutiny of a company's object and verification of directors' appointment and disqualification. The country's statement that it is aligned and the Commission's statement that further alignment is necessary are a confirmed contradiction, reported here and not resolved.

Direction of travel: The alignment ask on digital tools in company law recurs in near-identical wording in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, so the default applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. The 2025 screening finding of a high level of alignment shows the remaining ask is narrow, but it is not evidence of change over time.

Priority: It appears in the key recommendations of three reports, but always bundled with other company law items, and digital tools are a narrow strand on which the Commission already finds high alignment. It is therefore a repeated EU requirement that is not central to the chapter, and it is not a benchmark or payment condition in the input.

Tractability: The remaining points are specific legal amendments in a field with few actors and a working one-stop-shop registry, and they depend on no other institution's roll-out. The ask has nonetheless stood since 2021 with no reported draft, which is why the rating depends on the small scope and not on past momentum.

Open questions
  • North Macedonia states it is aligned with the acquis on digital tools in company law while the Commission says further alignment is necessary, and this confirmed conflict needs a provision-by-provision comparison with Directive (EU) 2019/1151 to settle it (MKD-EU-2025-003-0133; MKD-EU-2025-001-0116).
  • No source reports a draft amendment on object scrutiny or director checks, so a government legislative plan or draft law would show whether work has started (MKD-EU-2025-003-0149).
  • Free online access to basic company information rests on the country's own presentation, and an independent check of the registry would be needed to confirm it is in practice (MKD-EU-2025-003-0135).

RI-TEC-021 · Technology & AIValidated

Personal data protection in electoral processes weak

Priority LowDirection insufficient evidenceGap openTractability Medium

Assessment: The Commission states that data protection in the electoral sector needs improvement, that there is no assessment of whether the Electoral Code is harmonised with the data protection law, and that oversight of personal data used in election campaigns is inadequate.

2025 report: 0 items2026 update: Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package
2025 → 2026 comparison
Latest evidence
2023-11-08, North Macedonia 2023 Report, SWD(2023) 693 final MKD-EU-2023-001-0045
2025 position

The 2025 report has no in-scope item on this issue; the alpha position rests on other sources (see the evidence below).

2026 update

Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package

What changed

Not yet assessed. Awaiting 2026 Enlargement Package

Current direction of travel
insufficient evidence Validated
Current priority
Low Validated

Unresolved gap (open): What remains is an assessment of the Code against data protection law and proper oversight of personal data used in campaigns.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission states that data protection in the electoral sector needs improvement, that there is no assessment of whether the Electoral Code is harmonised with the data protection law, and that oversight of personal data used in election campaigns is inadequate (MKD-EU-2022-001-0029; MKD-EU-2023-003-0080; MKD-EU-2023-001-0045). Amendments supplementing the provisions on biometric voter identification were adopted in April 2021 (MKD-EU-2021-001-0004), and the Commission notes that the Electoral Code brought in biometric data without prior consultation of the Personal Data Protection Agency (MKD-EU-2022-001-0030; MKD-EU-2023-003-0081). The amendments are assessed as adopted, and no item shows biometric identification used at an election. The Commission reports that the State Election Commission addressed some irregularities identified in supervision (MKD-EU-2022-001-0031; MKD-EU-2023-003-0082), but this does not reach the assessment of the Code or campaign data oversight. No evidence after 2023 addresses the issue. The validated judgements are priority Low, direction of travel insufficient_evidence, unresolved gap open and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

The Commission first raised the issue in its 2022 report, stating that several improvements were needed in data protection in the electoral sector (MKD-EU-2022-001-0029). The 2023 screening report and the 2023 report repeated this in almost the same words and added specific points: no assessment of the Code against data protection law, the need to ensure respect for privacy, and inadequate oversight of campaign data (MKD-EU-2023-003-0079; MKD-EU-2023-003-0080; MKD-EU-2023-003-0083; MKD-EU-2023-001-0042; MKD-EU-2023-001-0045). The finding on the missing prior consultation appears in both years (MKD-EU-2022-001-0133; MKD-EU-2023-003-0129). No Commission item from 2024 or 2025 addresses the issue, so the requirement has not been restated since 2023.

Country response
  • Amendments to the Electoral Code on biometric voter identification · adopted
Implementation and outcome

No stated outcome is linked to an intervention under this issue, so no success judgement was made.

Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: The latest requirement, from 2023, is unmet on the record: no intervention is recorded as responding and the Electoral Code's biometric provisions have a proposed status of adopted, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is an assessment of the Code against data protection law and proper oversight of personal data used in campaigns. The State Election Commission addressed some irregularities, but that does not reach these two points, and this finding rests on evidence no newer than 2023.

Direction of travel: The Commission used the same wording in three documents, its 2022 and 2023 reports and the 2023 screening report, but no item after 2023 addresses the issue, so the record shows neither that it continues nor that it has eased. The three-report default for persistent was therefore not applied, because the repeats span only two years and the 2024 and 2025 reports are silent. The chapter scale was not decisive.

Priority: The Commission raised it only in 2022 and 2023, it is not in the main findings, and it is peripheral to the data theme.

Tractability: Few actors are needed and an assessment of the Code is a limited task, and the State Election Commission has already acted on some irregularities. Oversight of campaign data and any change to the Electoral Code are likely to be harder, and the evidence on this is thin.

Open questions
  • The direction of travel is insufficient_evidence because the 2024 and 2025 Commission reports are silent, and a later Commission or Personal Data Protection Agency assessment would show whether the problem continues or has eased (MKD-EU-2023-001-0042).
  • Whether any assessment of the Electoral Code against the data protection law has since been carried out is not known, and a published assessment or Agency opinion would settle it (MKD-EU-2023-003-0080).
  • The record does not show whether oversight of personal data in election campaigns has improved, and Agency supervision reports covering recent elections would be needed (MKD-EU-2023-001-0045; MKD-EU-2023-003-0082).

What changed

Current direction of travel
insufficient evidence Validated
Current priority
Low Validated

Unresolved gap (partly addressed): What remains is a wider range and use of sector and local services, including municipal ones, with published statistics on delivery.

View detail
Assessment in brief

The Commission's requirement here is general: it states that ongoing digitalisation, including expanding services in sectors such as energy regulation and veterinary services, is essential to maintain progress (MKD-EU-2025-004-0132). The Commission reports that the energy regulator, pharmaceutical chamber and pension insurance fund developed electronic services, and that the Cadastre Office's new digital services cut unresolved cases by 20% and the backlog by 10%; that result is assessed as worked with Medium attribution, for one period only (MKD-EU-2024-001-0113; MKD-EU-2025-001-0075; MKD-EU-2025-001-0076). The national audit, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, describes five One Stop Shops, some not used effectively outside Skopje, portals requiring separate profiles and no public use statistics (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0209; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0120; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0088; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0089). A civil society study finds slow progress in municipal e-services (MKD-CSO-2025-001-0003). The validated assessment is partly_addressed, with priority Low, direction of travel insufficient_evidence and tractability Medium.

EU requirement

There is no repeated Commission wording to trace for this issue. The Commission's items are isolated additions: in 2024 it noted that companies can be registered online within a single day and reported electronic services developed by three sector bodies, and in 2025 it noted the move to digital platforms for construction permits and stated that expanding services in sectors such as energy regulation and veterinary services is essential (MKD-EU-2024-008-0030; MKD-EU-2024-001-0113; MKD-EU-2025-004-0138; MKD-EU-2025-004-0132). In November 2025 it reported the Cadastre Office's new digital services (MKD-EU-2025-001-0075). None of these sets a specific requirement on sector or municipal services, and no Commission item on this issue is recorded for 2020 to 2023.

Implementation and outcome
  • New digital services of the Cadastre Office: The Cadastre Office's new digital services reduced unresolved cases by 20% compared with 2024 and the backlog of received cases by 10%. · success worked, attribution Medium
Rationale for the judgements

Unresolved gap: Sector services exist, and One Stop Shops are proposed as implemented, while the analysis on e-services there, the mobile offices and the employment plan are proposed or at insufficient evidence; these statuses are themselves proposals, and the national items are machine translated, capped at Medium confidence. The Commission's requirement is general, not specific. What remains is a wider range and use of sector and local services, including municipal ones, with published statistics on delivery.

Direction of travel: No repeated Commission wording or comparable series exists: EU items are isolated additions (2024, 2025), and the Chapter 10 scale is context only and was not decisive. The other signals are partial and mixed, since e-Rabota's share of employer registrations rose from 60% to 69% but fell from 67% to 62% for agencies in government reports, and a civil society study finds general slow progress at municipal level. Government and civil society items here are Low or Medium confidence, and the Macedonian ones are machine translated.

Priority: The Commission mentions sector services only briefly, and most of the concern is raised by the national audit (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence), national plans and civil society, so the issue meets the test of being mainly raised by others. The Reform Agenda target falls on the national portal under the G5 split, and item volume was not counted.

Tractability: Individual sector bodies can and do make progress, as e-Rabota and the Cadastre Office show. Across many institutions and municipalities, however, the audit and ICT strategy (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) describe parallel systems built without clear guidance, and no single actor has control.

Open questions
  • Use statistics for independent sector and municipal portals are not public, according to the machine-translated audit, so published data on services delivered and users would settle how far these services are used (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0089).
  • Government reports on e-Rabota point in different directions, with the employer share of registrations rising from 60% to 69% and the private agency share falling from 67% to 62%, and these Low or Medium confidence machine-translated figures would need independent confirmation to show a trend (MKD-GOV-2022-002-0010; MKD-GOV-2025-003-0009; MKD-GOV-2022-002-0011; MKD-GOV-2025-003-0010).
  • The evidence on municipal services rests on one Low confidence civil society study, and a systematic count of municipal e-services and their use would be needed to judge progress at local level (MKD-CSO-2025-001-0003).
  • The Cadastre Office result covers one period and the sentence does not state where the figures come from, so a further year of data from a stated source would show whether it holds (MKD-EU-2025-001-0076).
Evidence

RI-FMW-001 · Chapter 2 · open the issue cardValidated

Nationality discrimination in access to employment

Problem
The law governing access to the labour market does not give EU workers equal treatment with nationals, for example by treating them as any other foreigner or reserving private sector posts for nationals.
Why it matters
A key recommendation on non-discrimination against EU workers is repeated in the 2020 to 2025 reports, and equal access is central to the chapter. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found in the evidence.
Direction of travel
persistent. Sub-area wording on access to the labour market, which matches this issue, says no progress in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, and the 2025 report says there were no legislative developments. The 2025 screening finding of partial alignment is a first assessment of that kind and does not show a change.
Main evidence
  • The country should keep adapting its labour market access law to the acquis, notably on nationality non-discrimination against EU workers. MKD-EU-2020-001-0076
  • Continue adapting the legal framework to the EU acquis on labour-market access, especially non-discrimination of EU workers on grounds of nationality. MKD-EU-2021-001-0060
  • Continue adapting the legal framework on labour market access, especially non-discrimination of EU workers on grounds of nationality. MKD-EU-2022-001-0063
  • Continue adapting the legal framework on labour market access, especially non-discrimination of EU workers on grounds of nationality in all sectors. MKD-EU-2023-001-0090
  • North Macedonia should continue aligning labour-market access rules with the EU acquis, particularly non-discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers. MKD-EU-2024-001-0008
  • The country should continue aligning labour market access law with EU rules, particularly on non-discrimination against EU workers by nationality. MKD-EU-2025-001-0013
  • By accession, North Macedonia needs to ensure EU citizens can access its labour market without restrictions. MKD-EU-2025-003-0033

“continue to adapt the legal framework in line with the EU acquis on access to the labour market, in particular regarding non -discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers;”

“continue to adapt the legal framework in line with the EU acquis on access to the labour market, in particular regarding non -discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers;”

“continue to adapt the legal framework in line with the EU acquis on access to the labour market, in particular regarding non- discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers;”

“continue to adapt the legal framework to the EU acquis on access to the labour market, particularly to rules on non -discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers in all sectors;”

MKD-EU-2023-001-0090 · European Commission, North Macedonia 2023 Report, SWD(2023) 693 final, 2023, p. 80 · evidence confidence High

“continue to adapt the legal framework to the EU acquis on access to the labour market, particularly to rules on non -discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers in all sectors;”

MKD-EU-2024-001-0008 · European Commission, North Macedonia 2024 Report, SWD(2024) 693 final, 2024, p. 12 · evidence confidence High

“continue to align the legal framework to the EU acquis on access to the labour market, particularly to rules on non -discrimination on grounds of nationality against EU workers in all sectors;”

MKD-EU-2025-001-0013 · European Commission, North Macedonia 2025 Report, SWD(2025) 753 final, 2025, p. 11 · evidence confidence High

“It needs to ensure that by the time of accession, EU citizens can access its labour market without any restrictions.”

MKD-EU-2025-003-0033 · European Commission, Screening report North Macedonia, Cluster 2 - Internal Market, 2025, p. 26 · evidence confidence High

Unresolved gap
open. What remains is equal treatment of EU workers in the law on access to the labour market, including an end to posts in private companies reserved for nationals.

RI-FMW-004 · Chapter 2 · open the issue cardValidated

Legal and organisational framework for joining EURES

Problem
The country has not set up the legal and organisational arrangements needed to join the European network of employment services, such as a system for appointing EURES members and partners and access for private employment agencies.
Why it matters
Alignment with EURES is named in the key recommendation in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and EURES is one of the chapter's main strands. The recommendation is a composite one, so the repetition is of one sentence and not of independent findings.
Direction of travel
persistent. Sub-area wording on EURES, which matches this issue, says no developments or measures in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025, and the 2023 key recommendation still asks for alignment. The screening report's 'good level of preparation' sits in tension with these and with its own finding that no appointment system exists; it is the only rating of this kind, so I do not read it as improvement, and I report the tension rather than resolve it.
Main evidence
  • Strengthen the Employment Service Agency through training, and further align legislation and exchange good practice in line with EURES and ELA rules. MKD-EU-2023-001-0089
  • North Macedonia should strengthen the Employment Service Agency through training and further align legislation and good practice with EURES and ELA regulations. MKD-EU-2024-001-0007
  • The country should strengthen the Employment Service Agency through training and align legislation and good practice exchange with EURES and ELA regulations. MKD-EU-2025-001-0012
  • North Macedonia needs to establish a system for appointing EURES members and partners. MKD-EU-2025-003-0066
Quotes (4)

“strengthen the capacity of the Employment Service Agency, by continuing training activities, and further align legislation and exchange of good practices , in line with EURES and ELA regulations;”

“strengthen the capacity of the Employment Service Agency, by continuing to organise training activities, and further align legislation and the exchange of good practices, in line with EURES and ELA regulations;”

MKD-EU-2024-001-0007 · European Commission, North Macedonia 2024 Report, SWD(2024) 693 final, 2024, p. 12 · evidence confidence High

“strengthen the capacity of the Employment Service Agency, by continuing to organise training, and further align legislation and the exchange of good practices, in line with the European Employment Services (EURES) and European Labour Authority (ELA) regulations;”

MKD-EU-2025-001-0012 · European Commission, North Macedonia 2025 Report, SWD(2025) 753 final, 2025, p. 11 · evidence confidence High

“North Macedonia needs to establish a system for the appointment of EURES members and partners.”

MKD-EU-2025-003-0066 · European Commission, Screening report North Macedonia, Cluster 2 - Internal Market, 2025, p. 28 · evidence confidence High

Unresolved gap
partly addressed. What remains is a legal system for appointing EURES members and partners and access for private employment agencies.

RI-FMW-008 · Chapter 2 · open the issue cardValidated

Gaps in bilateral social security and healthcare agreements

Problem
Bilateral social security coordination and healthcare agreements do not yet cover all EU Member States or all branches, so workers moving before accession lack coordinated protection.
Why it matters
Concluding agreements is in the key recommendation in the 2021 to 2025 reports, and social security coordination is a main strand of the chapter. The Commission's good preparation rating lowers the urgency but not the repeated requirement, so reviewers may reasonably weigh centrality differently.
Direction of travel
persistent. The chapter scale was context only, and the 2025 'good level of preparation' for coordination is a single rating with nothing before it. No new agreements are recorded in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 or 2025, despite negotiations started in 2023.
Main evidence
  • Conclude further bilateral social security coordination agreements and identify administrative measures to introduce in preparation for accession. MKD-EU-2021-001-0061
  • Sign more social security coordination and health insurance agreements with EU Member States and identify administrative measures to prepare for accession. MKD-EU-2022-001-0064
  • Continue negotiating bilateral social security and healthcare insurance agreements with EU Member States and put in place administrative measures for accession. MKD-EU-2023-001-0091
  • North Macedonia should conclude bilateral social security and healthcare insurance agreements with EU Member States and prepare administrative measures for accession. MKD-EU-2024-001-0009
  • The country should conclude social security and healthcare agreements with Member States and prepare administratively for accession and electronic exchange of social security data. MKD-EU-2025-001-0014
  • Experience from bilateral agreements gives North Macedonia a good level of preparation on social security coordination. MKD-EU-2025-003-0090

“continue to negotiate and conclude bilateral agreements on social security coordination and healthcare insurance with EU Member States and put in place administrative measures to prepare for accession and for electronic exchange of social security data.”

RI-FMW-009 · Chapter 2 · open the issue cardValidated

National social security law not aligned with the coordination regulations

Problem
National pension, health and other social security laws are only partly aligned with the EU coordination regulations, for example through citizenship conditions, and the administrative measures for applying them at accession are not identified or in place.
Why it matters
Administrative measures for coordination are in the key recommendation in each report from 2020 to 2025, and alignment with the regulations is central to this strand of the chapter. The screening report requires alignment, including on nationality conditions, by accession.
Direction of travel
persistent. The chapter scale was context only, and the 2025 ratings have nothing earlier to compare with. The recommendation on administrative measures recurs from 2020 to 2025, and the shift from identifying measures to putting them in place reflects wording, not a reported step.
Main evidence
  • The country should identify which administrative measures for social security coordination must be introduced before accession. MKD-EU-2020-001-0077
  • Conclude further bilateral social security coordination agreements and identify administrative measures to introduce in preparation for accession. MKD-EU-2021-001-0061
  • Sign more social security coordination and health insurance agreements with EU Member States and identify administrative measures to prepare for accession. MKD-EU-2022-001-0064
  • Continue negotiating bilateral social security and healthcare insurance agreements with EU Member States and put in place administrative measures for accession. MKD-EU-2023-001-0091
  • North Macedonia should conclude bilateral social security and healthcare insurance agreements with EU Member States and prepare administrative measures for accession. MKD-EU-2024-001-0009
  • The country should conclude social security and healthcare agreements with Member States and prepare administratively for accession and electronic exchange of social security data. MKD-EU-2025-001-0014
  • By accession, the pension and disability and health insurance laws must be aligned, including on nationality conditions. MKD-EU-2025-003-0107

“take steps to conclude further bilateral agreements on social security coordination, and work on identifying which administrative mea sures should be introduced in preparation for future accession.”

“step up signature of agreements on social security coordination and health care insurance with EU Member States and identify administrative measures to be introduced in preparation for future accession.”

RI-TEC-002 · Technology & AI · open the issue cardValidated

Digital transformation strategy and governance weak

Problem
There is no adopted long-term strategy for digital transformation aligned with EU targets, or the ministry or agency responsible lacks the capacity, staff and inter-institutional coordination to lead and monitor it.
Why it matters
The ICT strategy was a Chapter 10 key recommendation in five successive reports, and the ministry capacity ask has recurred in four reports to 2025, on an issue central to the digital transformation theme. The key recommendation itself left the list after adoption in 2025 and the capacity ask sits in body text, so High rests on treating adoption as the start rather than the end of the requirement. National plans and audits were not counted towards this rating.
Direction of travel
persistent. The only movement is that the key recommendation to finalise and adopt the ICT strategy, unchanged from 2020 to 2024, ended in 2025 because the strategy was adopted, and adoption is not improvement in governance. The Commission's wording that the ministry needs stronger capacity is unchanged across 2022 to 2025, which sets the default to persistent, and the 2025 report adds a call for more IT staff.

RI-TEC-004 · Technology & AI · open the issue cardValidated

Core e-government building blocks missing

Problem
Shared systems that every institution needs to work digitally, such as a single document management system, legal and technical arrangements for electronic archiving, a digital mailbox and shared administrative information systems, are missing or little used.
Why it matters
The archiving law, the storage platform and the single document system are named Reform Agenda steps with payments attached, and these shared systems are central to the digital government theme. The rating rests on those EU conditions, not on the many national plan items.
Direction of travel
persistent. The change since the Commission's 2023 call for basic systems is the adoption of the electronic archiving law in 2025 and the Reform Agenda steps themselves, and adoption alone does not show improvement. The Commission's technical checks found the document system only partially operational, and use has barely moved, from 21 institutions in 2022 to 22 in 2025, on machine-translated national figures capped at Medium.

Electronic communications law not aligned with EU rules

Problem
The law on electronic communications is not fully aligned with the European Electronic Communications Code, the Gigabit Infrastructure Act and related rules on cost reduction, spectrum, roaming and open internet access.
Why it matters
Adoption of an aligned law is a Reform Agenda step with a payment provision, and alignment with the Code recurs in the Commission's chapter recommendations from 2022 to 2025. It is central to the digital infrastructure theme because other reforms in the area rest on this legal framework. The roaming and net neutrality parts of the issue are largely positive and do not drive this rating.
Direction of travel
improving. Commission wording that the law needs further alignment repeated from 2020 to 2022, and the matching sub-area wording in 2023 was no progress, but the wording then changed: the 2025 assessment found significant gaps after the new law, and the 2026 assessment found alignment partially achieved after the December 2025 amendments. The chapter-wide limited progress of 2024 is context only and was not decisive.

Electronic communications regulator independence and market oversight weak

Problem
The electronic communications regulator lacks guaranteed independence in appointments and funding and sufficient capacity, and competitive safeguards in a concentrated telecom market are not applied.
Why it matters
Strengthening the independence and capacity of this regulator is a key Commission recommendation repeated in every report from 2021 to 2025, and an independent regulator is central to the digital infrastructure theme. It is not itself a Reform Agenda step, and the recommendation is shared with the media regulators, which are outside this issue. The rating rests on the independence part; the competition part is supported by repeated but less prominent findings.
Direction of travel
persistent. Commission concern about the regulator's independence recurs in nearly unchanged terms in each report from 2020 to 2025, with no recorded improvement, so the default applies; in September 2024 parliament dismissed all five commission members, which the source reports without saying what it meant for independence. The chapter scale was not decisive.

RI-TEC-013 · Technology & AI · open the issue cardValidated

Broadband and high-capacity network coverage uneven

Problem
Small businesses and rural or non-urban areas face obstacles to fixed broadband, and high-capacity and 5G networks are still being rolled out.
Why it matters
Roll-out of 5G network and services is named in a Reform Agenda step, and the Commission repeats the particular need to increase access to broadband in its assessments from 2021 to 2026, which makes it central to the digital infrastructure theme. The payment condition covers the 5G part, not the rural and small-business part, which appears in repeated assessments and not in the chapter's key recommendations. The large volume of items on this issue, much of it repeated wording and national statistics, did not raise the rating.
Direction of travel
persistent. The Commission's sentence that smaller companies still face obstacles repeats from 2021 to 2026 with the same figures, so the default applies, though repeats are not independent evidence, and in 2025 the wording hardened to significant obstacles for smaller companies and rural areas. National averages did rise, with home internet access at 90.8% in 2024, 5G coverage at 76% in 2023 and 97% in a machine-translated 2025 national source, and some progress on ICT infrastructure in matching sub-area wording in 2025, while differences between earlier household figures reflect different measures, not conflict.

Base registers incomplete, unreliable or not digitalised

Problem
Key registers, above all the population register, hold data of poor quality or are little used, and many institutional, property and intellectual property registers are not yet digitalised or kept up to date.
Why it matters
The Commission's main findings gave the same key recommendation to complete register digitalisation in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and base registers are central to the digital government theme. The recommendation is one clause of a wider one on administrative procedures and is shared with the data exchange and e-services issues, which reviewers may weigh. The Reform Agenda payment step on a register of charges is flagged as doubtful for this theme and was not relied on.
Direction of travel
persistent. The Commission repeated the need to improve population register data in 2021, 2022 and 2023, and the same recommendation to complete the digitalisation of institutions' registers in 2023, 2024 and 2025, with use of the register still limited in 2024. The 2025 mention of efforts does not change the recommendation, so the default of persistent applies.

RI-TEC-017 · Technology & AI · open the issue cardValidated Set by the analyst at G6 Flagged for re-review

Personal data protection law not aligned with EU rules

Problem
The personal data protection framework is not fully aligned with the General Data Protection Regulation, the Law Enforcement Directive and the ePrivacy Directive, rules on international transfers are missing, and sector laws are not harmonised.
Why it matters
Full alignment with the data protection rules is central to the data theme and is repeated by the Commission in 2023, 2024 and 2025, but none of the 2020 to 2025 reports names it in the key recommendations, and it is in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition. The 2024 and 2025 main findings record no progress, but that is a finding and not a key recommendation, so this is a central requirement with thin support under the test. National and agency items were not counted. (set by the analyst at G6)
Direction of travel
persistent. The Commission found no concrete progress on the Law Enforcement Directive in 2020, partial alignment and a need for full alignment in 2023, and pending alignment in 2024 and 2025, so the requirement has not changed across three or more reports. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2024 and 2025 covers more than this issue and was not decisive.

Cybersecurity legal and strategic framework incomplete

Problem
Network and information security law is not fully aligned with the NIS2 Directive and the Cybersecurity Act, the national cybersecurity strategy is late or fragmented in implementation, and responsibilities are split without effective coordination.
Why it matters
The law and strategy, an operational competent authority and the NIS2 frameworks are each Reform Agenda payment steps, and NIS2 or cybersecurity legislation recurs in the Commission's key recommendations from 2022 to 2025. The issue is the legal base on which the rest of the cybersecurity theme rests. The rating rests on these EU requirements and not on the large number of national plan and audit items.
Direction of travel
improving. Commission items moved from no further progress on the 2019 draft law in 2021, through repeated calls to adopt the law and strategy in 2022, 2023 and 2024, to adoption of the strategy in January 2025 and the law in June 2025, which the 2025 report counts as some progress. The chapter scale (limited progress 2021 to 2024, some progress 2025) is context only and was not decisive, and the improvement lies in the legal and strategic framework, since no item shows better coordination after the 2023 call, the 2024 audit finding of a Council that met once and the 2025 strategy's own description of coordination as critical.

  • Payment condition: the NIS2 competent authority is operational, staffed and supervising, and the list of entities in scope is finalised. MKD-EU-2024-007-0004

  • From a 'not compliant' baseline (2024), EUR 4,281,623.70 is tied to adopting and implementing a cybersecurity framework aligned with EU acquis. MKD-GOV-2024-002-0003
  • Adopt the ICT strategy, align with the Electronic Communications Code and Broadband Cost Reduction Directive, and keep aligning with NIS and the 5G toolbox. MKD-EU-2022-001-0087
  • Align legislation with the European Electronic Communications Code, broadband cost reduction Directive, NIS 2 Directive and 5G toolbox. MKD-EU-2023-001-0121
  • North Macedonia should adopt the ICT and cybersecurity strategies and align with the Electronic Communications Code, Broadband Cost Reduction Directive, NIS 2 and 5G toolbox. MKD-EU-2024-001-0015
  • The country should continue aligning with the European Electronic Communications Code, the Gigabit Infrastructure Act, the NIS2 Directive and the 5G cybersecurity toolbox. MKD-EU-2025-001-0022

Operational cybersecurity capacity of public institutions weak

Problem
The national incident response centre and state institutions lack staff, expertise and secure infrastructure, so government services and digital infrastructure remain exposed to attacks.
Why it matters
Operational national and government CERTs, a staffed competent authority and a secure government network are Reform Agenda payment steps, and the Commission has repeated the need for capacity in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports. The Commission's reform programme assessments also name these deficiencies, and without operating capacity the legal framework has little effect, so the issue is central to the theme. The rating does not rest on the volume of audit and action plan items.
Direction of travel
persistent. The Commission's wording is essentially unchanged across three reports, that state institutions need stronger capacity and infrastructure and the national centre more staff (2023, 2024, 2025), and its reform programme assessments repeat large or major deficiencies in 2025 and 2026, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Incident counts cannot show a trend in capacity, because reporting was not mandatory and the figures are not comparable (1,441 or 1,443 for 2020, 2,804 for 2022, about 170 in 2023 on an unstated definition).
